of the air and the disruption of the hemispheres, the fruitfulness of the lands, and the mysteries of the sea reveal [his sins], and sometimes the striking of lightning shakes the crops, the flowers of the trees, and the vines. The pride of a king and his injustice not only darkens the face of the impious, but also obscures his own children and grandchildren, and those who hold the inheritance of the kingdom after him. On account of the sin of Solomon, the Lord tore the kingdom of the house of Israel from the hand of his sons, and on account of the justice of David the king, He left a lamp for his seed always in Jerusalem. Behold how clearly it appears to those who observe it, how much the justice of a king avails for the age. It is the peace of the people, the struggle of the fatherland. The safety of the commoners. The defense of the peoples. The joy of men and the temperance of the common languor. The serenity of the air. The fruitfulness of the earth. The consolation of the poor. The inheritance of the sons. And for himself and for them, the hope of future blessedness. Nevertheless, let the king know that just as he was established first on the throne of men, so also in punishments, if he has not done justice, he is to have the primacy. For he will have all the sinners whom he had under him in the present, [now] over him in that punishment, in an implacable manner.

¶ The tenth degree of abuse: The negligent bishop.

The tenth degree of abuse is the negligent bishop, who seeks the honor of his station among men, but does not guard the dignity of his ministry before God, through which he is to be led to safety. For first, it is inquired from the bishop what the dignity of his name holds, since the name "bishop" is Greek and signifies a "watchman" <note>original: "speculator"</note>. Why, therefore, is he called a watchman, and what is required of a watchman? The Lord explains this in detail: "I have given you as a watchman to the house of Israel. You will hear the word from my mouth and you will announce it to them from me. But if you see the sword coming and you do not announce it so that the impious man turns from his way, that impious man will indeed die in his iniquity, [but] I will require his blood from your hand. But if you have announced it and he has not turned, he will indeed die in his iniquity, but you have saved your own soul." It behooves the bishop, therefore, to attend diligently to all things in which he is placed as a watchman, and after he has attended, if he is able, [he must] correct [the people] by word and act; and if he is not able, [he must] excommunicate the workers of evil according to the rule of the Gospel. For if, says the Lord in the Gospel, your brother sins against you, correct him between you and him alone; if he hears you, you have won your brother. If he does not hear you, take with you one or two, so that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word may stand.

Sed potius, differentia duarum diuersissimarum Naturarum seruata, vsq; adeò duæ istæ Naturæ inter sese non miscentur, vt potiùs cuiusque Naturæ essentiales proprietates, quotquot sunt, in perpetuum seruandæ & retinendæ: nec vllo modo vel ratione, quacunque id fiat, vnquam inter sese commiscendæ sint.

<header>ON THE PERSONAL VNION.</header>

the person indeed, since the assumed human Nature is not in the least mixed: thus neither is the human with the divine.

V.

But rather, the difference of two most diverse Natures being preserved, those two Natures are so far from being mixed among themselves, that rather the essential properties of each Nature, however many they may be, must be perpetually preserved and retained: nor in any way or manner, by whatever means that may happen, are they ever to be mixed among themselves.

VI.

Furthermore, neither is such a union or Commixture in Christ of those two Natures ever to be imagined or conceded in which, from two Natures, as if from two wholes or corrupted parts, some third singular mixed genus is constituted which is neither perfectly divine nor perfectly human: but which has grown into one certain peculiar mixed substance and Nature, partly from the divine, and partly from the human Nature.

VII.

Which, to be sure, we willingly concede happens in natural things: for both physical Reason and experience itself daily testify: namely, that when qualities are broken and to some extent corrupted within one another, some third Mixed thing is thereby made.

Ceterum istis addemus quod non deest menti sim plicissima quedam forma & perfectissima: m immo adest: per quam & ad quam de simplici tate perſectioneque rerum omnium diiudicat ac se mens, intellectus, sensibile, ratio, ueritas, incorporea, etherea, sempiterna, perfectio
translation: more excellent than the mind itself, it is necessary that it be raised to that which is above itself, thoroughly through the power of that thing. Unless this very thing were something, or existed more truly than the sensible, it certainly could not move the intellect more truly than the sensible moves the sense. But now it moves it far more truly, because it produces it more toward the truth and toward the reason of any truth whatever. Why it is not true by its own reason, and what the reason of truth itself is, and conversely the truth of reason, we perceive not by sense, but by reason. But if someone says that the mind is not moved to understanding by things alien or extrinsic, but that it conceives its own species and its own objects by its own and a certain marvelous virtue, we shall say that it follows from this that the mind is entirely incorporeal and ethereal, if it is moved in no way by another but by itself, and by its own virtue conceives incorporeal and ethereal species or reasons. For the true reason of anything, since it cannot sometimes be otherwise, is everlasting. Furthermore, we shall add to these that a certain most simple and most perfect form is not lacking to the mind; nay, rather it is present, through which and toward which it judges of the simplicity and perfection of all things, and concludes that it itself is much simpler and more perfect than many things, and also that many things are simpler and more perfect.

v. 5. *Perceived* <note>original: "Percepta"</note>.] Gemblacensis: *Precepts* <note>original: "Pracepta"</note>. He called the returning stars *palinōros* <gloss>returning/back-turning</gloss>, as Aratus did.
v. 8. *With the example showing the way* <note>original: "Exemplo monstrante viam"</note>.] For they handed down these annotations to posterity as examples and *rhuseis pragmatikas* <gloss>practical observations</gloss>. Ptolemy: *because of agreeing with them, as they were assigned back to the degrees by the practical observations held by them*. For he calls them *exemplar births*, which they recorded from observations into tables, as we have already shown from Sextus Empiricus.
v. 10. *And the whole alternating* <note>original: "Et totum alterna"</note>.] If it is not an error, he calls "alternating" that which returns into a circle. But I remember that these three words, *aeterna* <gloss>eternal</gloss>, *alterna* <gloss>alternating</gloss>, and *aetheria* <gloss>ethereal</gloss>, are interchanged among themselves in this author by the fault of copyists. Therefore, it is more consistent with the author's mind that *eternal* should be read. For how often is it read thus?
v. 11. *To discern the changes of the Fates by certain signs* <note>original: "Fatorumque vices certis discernere signis"</note>.] Who would doubt that it should be read *to discurre by signs* <note>original: "discurrere signis"</note>, unless someone who had not noticed the lines above? *Discurrere* crept in from the verse that is eighth from this one.
v. 15. *As if mourning for the lost* <note>original: "Tam velut amißis mærens"</note>.] Literally for the Greeks: "The Egyptians, when they saw the sun descending under Cancer and Capricorn, when it was shortening the days from longer ones, would mourn, fearing that the sun might leave them with too little. And that is the time, which is the year of their solstice." When it began to ascend again and make the days longer, they would then celebrate and wear crowns. These things were without doubt written from the *Octaeteris* <gloss>eight-year cycle</gloss> of Eudoxus. In which Eudoxus began the solstice, from which he started his year of *prytaneis*, from the Ides, at which time the sign of the solstice was completed. But see the second book of our work *On the Amendment of Times* regarding this matter.
v. 17. *Nor with the Sun returned* <note>original: "nec Sole regreſſo"</note>.] Gemblacensis and Bonincontrius: *now with the Sun returned* <note>original: "iam Sole regreſſo"</note>. Which is true.
v. 22. *And unknown new* <note>original: "Ignotuſque nouos"</note>.] Better Gemblacensis: *And motionless new* <note>original: "Immotuſque nouos"</note>. He did not speak of "new" spheres in vain because of Britain, discovered by C. Julius Caesar shortly before his own times, which they called a new world.

Quemadmodum verò Majorum Avorumque nostrorum indefessam in litteris Græcis excolendis industriam jure optimo summis evehimus laudibus: Ita seculi hujus meritò accusamus socordiam, dum non pauci Artibus humanioribus discendis consecrati & Studiosi dicti, cum Studiis Græcanicæ lingvæ nihil commercii habere cupiunt, qualicunque Latinitate contenti. Prætendunt enim; omnes omnium Græcorum veterum libros in sermonem Latinum extare versos, ideoque non esse opus, ut ex Grajis voluminibus doctrinæ liberales operosè acquirantur.

O perversum verò judicium horum, qui ad versiones Latinas, tanquam Asylum, refugiunt! Hoc ipsum, quod in subsidium excusationis suæ frivolæ adducunt, eos maximè erroris arguit & convincit. Interpretes enim illi, viri doctissimi & lingvarum elegantium callentissimi, ab authenticis Atticorum Scriptorum, quos cum cura in Latinam orationem transtulerunt, fontibus juventutem neutiquam avocant, sed potius ad illos, tanquam ad exemplar archetypum, remittunt, ut translata cum autoribus ipsis exactè conferant & penitam doctrinam etiam atque etiam excutiant. Nempe translatores seduli, non quodvis pro quovis, tralatitiâ operâ verterunt, sed textum Autorum genuinum vel quoad litteram, vel certè quoad sensum, ut melius intelligeretur, perquisitè sunt interpretati. Invertendum itaque, quod in excusationem suam inanem μισέλληνες convertunt monendique, ut exemplo majorum allaudabili documenta Græca Latinis jungere adnitantur.

Næ cognatæ sunt hæ duæ doctorum lingvæ, & altera alterius ope carere nequit. Latino quidem sermone omnes Disciplinæ docentur; sed nomina illarum â Græcis acceperunt, sine quibus definire illa & cognoscere non possunt. Musica, Dialectica, Physica, Politica & similes termini necessariò retinentur, quia sine complexione, cujusmodi oportet esse definita & themata simplicia, rem certam & subjectam unâ voce notant, quod Latinis negatum est. Proinde rectè scripsit Horatius:

> ->Grajis ingenium, Grajis dedit ore rotundo Musa loqui.<-

Nec tantum nomina Artium, sed & alii termini technici plerumque Græciæ debent natales. Uti ergo Terminus olim in fundamento Capitolii locando cæteris Diis cedere pertinacissimè recusavit: Ita Termini Græci & incomplexi, qui in Disciplinis passim occurrunt, removendi non sunt, sed in consortium Latinitatis semel recepti ab omnibus usurpantur, quia sine verborum ambitu ac alterius vocis adjectione res subjectas planè exprimunt, quod sermo Latinus pleno sensu efferre nescit.

Testes laudo Theologos, qui Scripta Prophetarum & Apostolorum sacra simpliciter vocant Biblia: Si Latinè sine complexione dixeris, nemo intelliget, quos libros indigites. Textus sacri, qui in concione publica populo Christiano explicantur, non nisi Græcè Evangelia & Epistolæ a vulgo etiam nuncupantur. Scriptura divina graphicè admodum appellatur Θεόπνευστος (2. Tim. 3. 16.) Quisquæso Latinorum hoc nomen unâ voce, ut integrum exprimat sensum, effari novit? Idem judicium esto de verbo εὐαγγελίζεσθαι. (Matth. 11. 5.

Quid dicam de Medicis, qui nomina morborum in Pathologiâ suâ terminis Hippocratis, Galeni & aliorum ex Græco illo cætu, frequenter efferunt? Quid memorem de Jurisconsultis & Politicis, qui & ipsi sæpè Græca vocabula adducunt & sermoni vernaculo miscent; ut sunt Archiva, Hypotheca, Amnestia, & hujus farinæ alia; Credunt enim in illis peculiarem quandam significandi vim esse reconditam.

# OF GOD & OF PATRONS

Just as we rightly exalt with the highest praise the tireless industry of our ancestors and forefathers in cultivating Greek letters, so do we deservedly accuse the sloth of this century, while not a few who are consecrated to learning the humane arts and are called students, desire to have no dealings with the studies of the Greek language, content with whatever Latinity. For they pretend that all the books of all the ancient Greeks exist translated into the Latin tongue, and therefore there is no need for liberal doctrines to be laboriously acquired from Greek volumes.

Oh, the perverse judgment of these people, who flee to Latin versions as if to an asylum! This very thing, which they bring forward in aid of their frivolous excuse, argues and convicts them most of error. For those interpreters, most learned men and most skilled in elegant languages, by no means call the youth away from the authentic sources of the Attic writers, which they translated into Latin speech with care, but rather send them back to those sources as to an archetypal exemplar, so that they may exactly compare what has been translated with the authors themselves and examine the deep doctrine again and again. Indeed, the diligent translators did not translate just anything for anything through a perfunctory effort, but searched out and interpreted the genuine text of the authors, either as to the letter or certainly as to the sense, so that it might be better understood. Therefore, what the <term>mishellenes</term> <gloss>haters of Greeks</gloss> convert into their own empty excuse must be inverted, and they must be warned that they should strive to join Greek documents to Latin ones, following the praiseworthy example of their ancestors.

Truly, these two languages of the learned are cognate, and the one cannot lack the help of the other. All disciplines are taught in the Latin tongue, but they received their names from the Greeks, without which one cannot define and know those things. Music, Dialectics, Physics, Politics, and similar terms are necessarily retained because they denote a certain and subject matter with one word, without complexity, which is what the defined subjects and simple themes ought to be; this has been denied to the Latins. Therefore, Horace rightly wrote:

> ->The Muse gave to the Greeks genius, the Muse gave the Greeks to speak with a rounded mouth.<-

And not only the names of the arts, but also other technical terms usually owe their birth to Greece. Therefore, just as the god Terminus once most stubbornly refused to yield to the other gods when the foundation of the Capitol was being laid, so the Greek and simple terms, which occur everywhere in the disciplines, must not be removed but, once received into the fellowship of Latinity, are used by all because they clearly express the subject matters without a circumlocution of words and the addition of another term, which Latin speech does not know how to bring forth with full sense.

I call as witnesses the theologians, who simply call the sacred writings of the Prophets and Apostles the Bible: if you say it in Latin without complexity, no one will understand which books you are indicating. The sacred texts, which are explained to the Christian people in public preaching, are not called by the common people even now as anything other than the Gospels and Epistles in Greek. Divine Scripture is called very graphically <term>theopneustos</term> <gloss>God-breathed</gloss> (2 Tim. 3:16). Who, I ask, of the Latins knows how to utter this name in one word, so that it expresses the complete sense? The same judgment should be held regarding the verb <term>euangelizesthai</term> <gloss>to preach the gospel</gloss> (Matt. 11:5).

What shall I say of the physicians, who frequently express the names of diseases in their pathology through the terms of Hippocrates, Galen, and others from that Greek group? What shall I mention of the jurists and politicians, who themselves often bring forward Greek words and mix them into their vernacular speech, such as "archives," "hypothec," "amnesty," and other things of this sort? For they believe that a certain peculiar force of meaning is hidden in them.

### Chapter 27: Regarding the praise of the preceding doctrine, or the usefulness of his teaching.

<margin>Follow this doctrine 77 a. and you will not need a doctor.</margin>
O Alexander, once you have understood this instruction and put it into practice, it will mean you do not need a doctor for your whole life, with the help of God. You should know that serious illnesses arising from heat or specific cycles <gloss>This term is used for circular movements. In Greek, "periodus" is "circuitus" in Latin, coming from "peri" which means "around" and "odos" which means "way."</gloss>, and which are recognized by the path of the moon, can be identified as either short-lived or long-lasting. Their outcome can also be known from earlier signs. I have taught you faithfully and briefly shown the categories and recognition of illnesses. There is also a proven sign found in water <note>original: "aqua," referring here to the practice of uroscopy, the diagnostic examination of urine.</note> regarding these matters, but the preceding signs are better and more accurate, as I determined in the book about waters. These signs are sufficient for someone who remembers the teachings of that book well, as contained in the work I composed on compound medicines. This includes artificial drinks, prepared ointments, and plasters, according to the order and art of the Greeks, Italians, Indians, and Persians. In these treatments, no experiment was ever found to be false. Since these useful secrets were buried because they were unknown or not found everywhere, I decided it would be unfitting if they remained hidden from your mercy.

It is certainly fitting that you should know the great medicine called "Inestimable Glory," which is also known as the "Philosophers' Treasure." But if it had never been granted to the Roman people that it could be seen as having been rightly incited—that which he taught was often granted—then that case was the most just. Then I transferred and turned the whole speech to rebuking the flight of Cepio, and to lamenting the army again. Thus, he was chafing the pain of those who were mourning their own by his speech, and he was calling back and calling back the minds of the Roman knights, among whom the case was being pleaded then, to the hatred of Q. Cepio, from whom they had been alienated on account of the trials. When I sensed that I had established myself in the possession of the trial and of my own defense, because I had already reconciled the goodwill of the people to me—whose right I had defended even with the conviction of sedition—and I had turned the minds of the judges entirely to our case, either by the calamity of the state, or by the grief and longing of relatives, or by their own hatred toward Cepio, then I began to mix into this genre of vehement and atrocious speech that other genre about which I disputed before, of gentleness and clemency. That I was deciding for my associate, who ought to be in the place of a son to me according to the custom of our ancestors, and for all my own reputation and near fortune, that nothing could happen to me more shameful regarding estimation, nor more bitter regarding pain, than if I, who was thought to have been a savior to men often very strange to me but yet my citizens, had not been able to bring help to my associate. I was begging from the judges that they might concede that to my age, to my honors, to my deeds, if they saw me to have been affected by just and pious pain, especially if they had understood in other cases that I was always advocating everything for the perils of friends, and never for myself. Thus, both that entire defense and the case, which seemed to be placed in art—so that he might speak about the Apuleian law, so that he might explain what it was to diminish the majesty—through which I briefly touched and grazed. By these two parts of speech, one of which has recommendation, the other incitement—which are least polished by the precepts of art—all that case was handled by me then, so that I was both most sharp in renewing the hatred of Cepio, and most gentle in declaring my morals toward my own associates.

For any good Christian ought to prefer that people, seeing him punished for his sins, recognize the justice of God and glorify Him, rather than seeing him left unpunished and speak ill of the providence and justice of God, as people often do when they see the wicked and the criminal living in prosperity. Therefore, after we have said: **Thy kingdom come**, we add: **Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven**. It is as if we were to say: I would indeed wish that all people might turn to You through Your mercy. If, however, You dispose things otherwise because of their sins, let Your will be done as it is in heaven and on earth. This is to say: Just as once in heaven You glorified Yourself through justice regarding the sinning angels, because all who behold such a noble creature that with one sin against You...

<summary>This passage explains that believers should accept God's justice over their own preservation, preferring that His righteousness be recognized even through punishment rather than seeing the wicked prosper. It connects this submission to the petition Thy will be done, referencing the fall of the angels as an example of God’s justice.</summary>

translation:
### XVII.
Arbitrators have the obligation imposed upon them to impose an end to the entire controversy by their sentence, but not the liberty to test whether the parties might allow the dispute to be settled by their counsel or authority.

### XVIII.
They are bound by this necessity only if a penalty—whether monetary or another thing instead of money, whether a fixed sum or uncertain, or whether greater or lesser than the matter in question—has been promised unconditionally, not conditionally, by the parties involved in the compromise, should anyone fail to abide by the arbitrators' sentence.

### XIX.
To this end, the magistrate or ordinary judge is accustomed to interpose his authority so that the arbitrators perform the duty they voluntarily accepted at the beginning in a timely manner.

### XX.
Hence, if the arbitrators attempt to conceal themselves, the magistrate must track them down, and if they do not appear for a long time, he ought to impose a fine against them.

### XXI.
The parties who made the compromise must abide by the sentence of the arbitrators rendered within the established time, whether it is just or unjust, provided it was not rendered contrary to the laws and sacred Constitutions, for fear of the penalty.

### XXII.
Indeed, it is convenient for the sentence to be pronounced in the presence of the litigants: unless it was specifically expressed in the compromise that it be pronounced in the absence of one or both; if this is not done, the absent party incurs the penalty, unless they are prepared to compromise again before the same agreeing arbitrator.

### XXIII.
The penalty from the compromise is sought from the one who has not obeyed the sentence of the arbitrators.

<summary>These conclusions address the arbitrator’s duty to reach a final decision, the role of the magistrate in enforcing their presence, and the requirement for parties to adhere to the final sentence.</summary>
<keywords>Arbitration, Magistrate, Sentence, Penalty, Litigants</keywords>

<note>continues from previous page: of the imaginative power <term>species</term> that the common sense knows. It is necessary that the common sense join its retentive power. It is necessary that the sensible <term>species</term> be diffused from the imaginative</note> power, which is the medium between the <term>estimativa</term> <gloss>estimative power</gloss> and the <term>imaginativa</term> <gloss>imaginative power</gloss>, which composes and divides imagined forms. By this, when we have the imagined form of gold and the imagined form of a mountain, we compose one form of a golden mountain, which we see now. Avicenna places the <term>fantasia</term> <gloss>fantasy/power of active imagination</gloss> as a principle distinct from the others by the composition of form with form, or of the sensed <term>species</term> reserved in the <term>imaginativa</term>. There is another opinion of the holy doctor <note>referring to Thomas Aquinas</note>. He says with Avicenna that it is not necessary to posit more than four interior sensitive powers, namely: the common sense, the <term>imaginativa</term>, the <term>estimativa</term>, and the <term>memorativa</term> <gloss>memorative power</gloss>. To solve the point of Avicenna regarding this opinion, where he attributes to the <term>fantasia</term> what does not appear in other animals besides man, in this, the <term>imaginativa</term> power suffices. Averroes also attributes this action to it in a certain book he wrote concerning sense and the sensible. It is not inconvenient that the <term>imaginativa</term> in man, from the redundancy of reason, has another name and is called <term>fantasia</term>, just as there is <term>estimativa</term>, <term>cogitativa</term> <gloss>cogitative power</gloss>, and <term>memoria</term> <gloss>memory</gloss> regarding <term>reminiscentia</term> <gloss>reminiscence</gloss>. But in the common sense, there is no difference between man and beast. Because of the affinity and proximity to universal reason, those three powers—namely the <term>imaginativa</term>, <term>estimativa</term>, and <term>memorativa</term>—are here joined with a certain repercussion of higher, perfect operations. The <term>imaginativa</term> in man composes image with image, which is the <term>fantasia</term>. Thus, the <term>estimativa</term> in man elicits intentions with a certain discourse, syllogistically or collatively, and is the <term>cogitativa</term>. Also, man has memory of his deeds with a certain discourse, and not suddenly like a beast. Thirdly, this is called <term>reminiscentia</term>. It must be concluded that there are four interior senses. These are sufficient regarding the acts of the interior sensitive soul. For the common sense and the <term>imaginativa</term> suffice for acts concerning <term>species</term> or images. The <term>estimativa</term> and memory suffice for acts concerning intentions.

<meta>A decorative initial 'A' begins the text.</meta>
Aristotle: The act of the <term>cogitativa</term> is to compare, compose, and divide; that is <term>reminiscentia</term>, and a certain syllogism, which is not provided by the act of the <term>estimativa</term> and <term>memorativa</term>. If the act of the <term>fantasia</term> were from the act of the <term>estimativa</term> or <term>cogitativa</term>, and <term>reminiscentia</term> were powers distinct from the <term>estimativa</term> and <term>memorativa</term>, then the <term>fantasia</term> would not be distinct from the <term>estimativa</term>. Therefore, they speak poorly who say the <term>fantasia</term> is comprised under the <term>imaginativa</term>, given its distance. This distance, by which the <term>cogitativa</term> and <term>reminiscentia</term> are here distinct from the <term>estimativa</term> and <term>memorativa</term>, is not because they are primary sensitive powers. If so, why is there some affinity and proximity to universal reason through a certain redundancy? If they are not other powers but the same perfected ones, they would be in other animals besides man. But such is not the case regarding the distance of the <term>fantasia</term> and <term>estimativa</term>, which are the proper sensitive powers. Through this, there is the knowing of <term>species</term> or intentions, and the composing of those known things. Or, regarding the ways in which there are three acts of the <term>fantasia</term> itself: one is to compose an image with an intention, and then sense them with the image or <term>species</term>, and according to this, it is reduced to the <term>imaginativa</term>. Another act is to compose a <term>species</term> with an intention, or vice-versa. The third is to compose the intention, and these two last acts fall under the <term>cogitativa</term> and are reduced to the <term>estimativa</term>, which are uniformly changed by intentions, even if they do not elicit uniformly as was said before. And he who argues: the beast's <term>imaginativa</term> is a receptive thing; see that it does not happen to it to know <term>species</term> and compose those known things. I say doubly: the interior sensitive powers are not reserved in the reserve. If that which reserves also knows in another way, they are said to be reservoirs by comparison to the powers from which they capture similarities, which are like treasuries. Thus, the doctor says this <term>imaginativa</term> power, when taken by itself, is reserved, yet...

<column-break/>

with the implication of the common sense to which it joins and to which it transmits reserved <term>species</term>, and also the <term>cognitiva</term>.

<meta>A decorative initial 'A' begins the text.</meta>
Aristotle: Aristotle afterwards determines about the <term>fantasia</term>. He asks whether it is a special power. He determines that just as this common sense is for external senses and composes and divides sensibles, so the <term>fantasia</term> relates to other interior senses, for it composes images and intentions. But just as the common sense is distinguished from external sensibles, so the <term>fantasia</term> is distinguished from other interior senses. Regarding the first, Aristotle determines below about the <term>fantasia</term>, not as a power, but as an act. To confirm the opinion, that operation comes to the brute's <term>imaginativa</term> or the <term>cogitativa</term> in humans from the reflection of reason. And he defines such a <term>fantasia</term>—which is called the stated <term>fantasia</term>—only in humans. If it were also in other animals, for whom <term>fantasia</term> is the principle of movement, they would follow and animals would move indeterminately through composition and the fantastic images they have of things. It is not true that they judge in this way, and <term>fantasia</term> would move [them] in humans. And according to a rational composed <term>fantasia</term>, they would be moved. And to posit it indeterminately is inconvenient to say.

<meta>A decorative initial 'A' begins the text.</meta>
Doctor: Whether the interior senses are more perfect than the exterior, or vice-versa. I say that the interior ones are more perfect. Because a power is the more perfect the more it possesses a common object, since the power is carried to all those things that pertain to that object. If the object is common, such a power is carried to more things, which argues for nobility. If the interior senses have more common objects, as said before, such powers are more dignified.

<meta>A decorative initial 'A' begins the text.</meta>
Aristotle: The agent is more dignified than the patient. If the exterior senses act upon the interior, and are more dignified than the interior. I say doubly: something acts upon another in one way, by physical and real action, as fire acts upon water, and in this way, the agent is more dignified than the patient. In another way, something acts upon another by intentional action, just as sensibles act upon the senses. And in this way, it is not required that the agent be more dignified than the patient. And rather, that which the patient then receives in the form is more dignified in the agent. And thus the exterior sense is the principle of changing the interior senses according to an intentional <term>species</term>, which is in a more dignified way in the sense than in the sensible. And this can be seen from the sensible and the sense. For it is manifest that the sensible acts upon the sense, and yet the sense is a perfection of the sensible.

Since however the soul is defined by two differences, the motion that is according to place, and that which is in understanding and discerning and sensing. And it seems also that understanding and knowing are as if a certain sensing. In both of these, the soul judges and knows something concerning the things that are.

Afterwards, Aristotle demonstrates that these two operations, namely to perceive through the exterior sense and to discern between the sensibles of diverse senses, do not exceed the faculty of the sensitive principle itself. He wants to inquire whether knowing and understanding exceed the faculty of that same principle. And concerning this, he first shows that knowing and understanding are not for the same subject. Secondly, he shows that the <term>fantasia</term>, which pertains to sense, is not the same as the opinion, which pertains to the intellect. There: <term>Fantasia</term>, etc. Concerning the first, he first puts the opinion of those who posit sense and intellect to be the same. But he refutes it. There: And it would be necessary. He says that in the first place, positing the opinion of the ancients, in common and before, he defined the soul by two things: by the motion that is according to place, and by cognition, which includes intellectual and sensitive discernment.

For example, the ray A F, falling obliquely upon the straight line B C, with the angle A F B, is reflected toward H, where the larger angle A F C looks, yet with equal inclination—that is, with the angle H F C equal to the angle A F D. And this is the principle that the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence (Vitello, 20, 5). The same is true for the rays A E and E G.

8. A thing which is seen through reflection can only be seen at a determined point. For example, if the form H is received in the mirror F, it cannot be seen unless the eye is at some point of the line F A—that is, through the line of reflection alone, which is evident from daily experiments and is treated by Vitello, 24, 5.

9. The perpendicular ray is the strongest of all in direct action; the others, as they recede more or less from the perpendicular, are more or less powerful in their direct action. The opposite happens in reflected action, for the further the ray is from the perpendicular, the stronger it is in reflecting, and the closer it is, the weaker, so that the perpendicular ray itself is the most feeble in its reflection, whereas it was the strongest of all in direct action. For instance, the ray A D, falling perpendicularly on the body B C, is the strongest in direct action; the ray A E is weaker in the same action, though stronger than the ray A F. But in reflected action, the reflected ray F H is stronger than the ray E G, and the perpendicular ray A D is the most weak for reflecting back into itself (Vitello, 47, 2).

The commentator (Scholiast) explains the passage:

“He took Arcturus because it also touches the northern circle or pole, just as the Altar touches the Antarctic. And it is so: Arcturus rises with Leo, count two hours; then Virgo, count four; then Libra, count six; then Scorpio, count eight. And then after the eighth hour, the Altar rises, then Sagittarius, ten hours; Capricorn, twelve; Aquarius, fourteen; then Pisces, sixteen hours; and the Altar's eight hours. Thus, the Altar is set for eight hours; but Arcturus is above the earth for sixteen. For this is above the earth, while that is below, and it travels in the opposite direction. Therefore, the one sets sooner, while the other has larger revolutions.”

# BOOK IV.

The mind of the ascetic, which was inclined towards ignorance and directed outwards—bowed down towards objects, and having the experience of objects as its fruit—is now turned towards discrimination. That is, it enters the right path and is directed inwards toward "Isolation"—it has Isolation as its result, or is possessed of the germ of Isolation.*

Now, by describing the causes of the impediments that occur to the mind flowing in the path of discrimination, he mentions the means of abandoning those obstacles:—†

->तच्छिद्रेषु प्रत्ययान्तराणि संस्कारेभ्यः ॥ २६ ॥<-

*Aph. 26.* In the intervals thereof, other thoughts arise from the self-continuant impressions.

Different thoughts, characterized by "non-abstraction," which arise in the intervals or gaps in the mind of the ascetic abiding in meditation, spring up in the shape of "I," "mine," etc., from the former impressions of the mind produced by the perceptions of non-abstraction, even though these are now weakened.‡

Therefore, such thoughts must be abandoned by extirpating their causes. This is what is to be stated.

He now states that the methods of abandoning these are as they have been described before:§

->हानं तेषां क्लेशवदुक्तम् ॥ २७ ॥<-

*Aph. 27.* The means of the avoidance of these are explained to be as in the case of the afflictions.

<margin>* The mind that was previously leaning toward ignorance, outward-facing, and bearing the fruit of object-enjoyment, is now leaning toward discrimination and the path of truth, bearing the fruit of Isolation or starting the process of Isolation.</margin>
<margin>† He mentions the way to renounce these by explaining their causes in the mind that is flowing toward discrimination.</margin>
<margin>‡ In the intervals of the ascetic's meditation, thoughts of distraction arise from previous impressions of worldly experience, even if those impressions are waning. The meaning is that one must destroy them by cutting off the root of the internal organs.</margin>
<margin>§ He states that the means of removal has been described previously.</margin>

<summary>The author explains that even in meditation, past impressions can create distractions, and these must be cleared using the same techniques previously applied to the "afflictions" (Kleshas).</summary>

Colonel Mure endeavoured at great length, both here and in Germany, to expose fallacies in Welcker’s arguments; but the bitterness of his attack, and the unfairness of much of his reasoning, go far to weaken his otherwise acknowledged authority. Professor Comparetti has recently examined the question with much fairness and erudition, and, with the possible exception referred to above (p. 3, note), has done much to separate fiction from fact; but he does not endorse all Welcker’s conclusions.

Sappho seems to have been the centre of a society in Mitylene, a kind of aesthetic club, devoted to the service of the Muses. Around her gathered maidens from even comparatively distant places, attracted by her fame, to study under her guidance all that related to poetry and music; much as at a later age students resorted to the philosophers of Athens.

The names of many of her girl-friends (ἑταῖραι) and pupils (μαθήτριαι) are preserved. The most celebrated was Erinna of Telos, a poetess of whose genius too few lines are left for us to judge, but we know what the ancients thought of her from this Epigram in the Greek Anthology:

> These are Erinna’s songs : how sweet, though slight !—
> For she was but a girl of nineteen years :—
> Yet stronger far than what most men can write :
> Had Death delayed, whose fame had equalled hers?
> (J. A. Symonds.)

Indeed, according to Otto <note>original: Otho</note>, there was no question that could not be satisfactorily settled in this manner. For example, in 963, Otto was involved in a bitter exchange of accusations with Pope John XII—a conflict that preceded the Saxon emperors' eventual domination of the papacy. When Otto sent Bishop Liutprand to Rome to reject certain accusations made against him, he ordered his ambassador's armed attendants to defend his claims through a duel. The Pope, though he was himself skilled in using weapons, promptly declined this proposal.¹

In fact, a professional duelist seems to have been considered a necessary part of diplomatic missions. In 968, when Otto sent the same Liutprand to Constantinople to arrange a marriage, a dispute arose during the negotiations for the hand of Princess Theophania. The debate concerned the circumstances of Otto's conquest of Italy. The warlike bishop offered to prove his truthfulness through the sword of one of his attendants—an offer that brought the argument to a sudden and triumphant end.²

This willingness to leave the most important interests to the outcome of a judicial duel was not limited to Germany and Lombardy. In 948, at the Synod of Ingelheim, King Louis IV (known as Louis d'Outremer) <note>Louis "from overseas," a Carolingian king of West Francia</note> called for the Church’s help in his desperate struggle against the rising House of Capet. He finished his list of the wrongs he had suffered from Hugh the Great by offering to prove the justice of his complaints in single combat with his enemy.³ Since the battle ordeal was so deeply embedded in the customs of the time, we should not be surprised to find that in a biography of Saint—

<meta>This page continues Humanus's argument that human reason is not a divine gift of our original nature, but rather a consequence of our fallen state, linked to ignorance and mortality.</meta>

<page-num>50</page-num>

And they must live and die together, and all bear the same witness to the fallen state of man. For no creature can come from the hands of God in a state of ignorance concerning anything that is fit and proper for it to know. This is as impossible as it would be for God to have an envious or evil will. Now all right and natural knowledge, in whatever creature it exists, is *sensible* <note>original: "sensible"; here meaning perceived directly and clearly by the senses or the mind, rather than through logical deduction.</note>, *intuitive*, and *its own evidence*. 

But *opinion, reasoning*, or *doubting* (for they are all essentially the same thing) can only begin when the creature has lost its original, correct, and natural state, and has arrived *somewhere*, and become *something*, that it cannot understand. Then doubting begins, and from there *reasoning*, and from there *debating*. This is the "high birth" of our glorified Reason—a birth as noble as *groping* is, which has its beginning in and from *darkness*, or the *loss* of light. 

From this, we have full proof that man has lost the original natural state in which God created him. For *reasoning*, doubt, and perplexity in any creature are the effects of some fall or departure from its first state of nature. It shows that the creature lacks and is seeking something its nature desires, but it does not know how to obtain it. The *beasts* <note>original: "beasts"; referring to animals.</note> do not seek after truth; this is plain proof that truth has no relation to them;

For brevity, let $m + n + l = f$, and $l(l + m)(l + n) = k$, so that $k = fl^2 + lmn$. Since $a = m, \ b = n, \ c = f + l, \ d = 4k$, we have $a + b + c = 2f$, and therefore
-> $p = 2f + 4k.$ <-
Again, since $q = (a + b + c)d + (a + b)c + ab$,
-> $q = 8fk + (m + n)^2 + 2l(m + n) + mn.$ <-
Since $mn + 1 = l^2$, the latter expression becomes
-> $q = 8fk + f^2 - 1.$ <-
Moreover, $s = abcd = 4mnk(f + l)$.
Therefore $1 + q + s = 8fk + f^2 + 4mnk(f + l)$. We must see if the right-hand expression equals $\frac{1}{4}p^2$.
Now $\frac{1}{4}p^2 = f^2 + 4fk + 4k^2$.
Assume then, as a hypothesis, that
-> $8fk + f^2 + 4mnk(f + l) = f^2 + 4fk + 4k^2,$ <-
which simplifies to $4fk + 4mnk(f + l) = 4k^2$.
Dividing throughout by $4k$, we get:
-> $f + mn(f + l) = k = fl^2 + lmn.$ <-
This simplifies to $f + fmn = fl^2$, which is true since $mn + 1 = l^2$.
Consequently, it is proved that
-> $1 + q + s = \frac{1}{4}p^2,$ or $(\frac{1}{4}q - \frac{1}{8}p^2) = -\frac{1}{2}(s + 1).$ <-

Example 1: Assume $m = 1, \ n = 3$, so that $l = 2$; therefore
-> $a = 1, \quad b = 3, \quad c = 8, \quad d = 120,$ <-
whence $p = 132, \quad q = 1475, \quad r = 4224, \quad s = 2880$. We deduce that:
-> $z = \frac{4 \cdot 4224 + 264 \cdot 2881}{2879^2} = \frac{777480}{8288641}.$ <-

The conditions are satisfied, for
-> $ab + 1 = 2^2, \quad ac + 1 = 3^2, \quad ad + 1 = 11^2,$ <-
-> $bc + 1 = 5^2, \quad bd + 1 = 19^2, \quad cd + 1 = 31^2,$ <-
... (the remaining terms follow the same pattern).

The *First Song* was then sung, in which all participated <note>During the singing, Shókhunyoma ceased working. Lolúlomai was absent, having gone after wood for the fire. The singing began about 4 o'clock P.M.</note>. Koyónainiwa placed four cornmeal lines on the four <term>kiva</term> walls from a small tray containing finely ground cornmeal and threw a little meal four times toward the <term>kiva</term> roof above the medicine tray and on the floor. He held his bow, arrows, and an old white corn ear in his left hand throughout the ceremony.

*Second Song.* Koyónainiwa threw a little cornmeal into the medicine tray from the north side and then onto the stones lying on that side. He then repeated the action from the west and the other four sides.

*Third Song.* Koyónainiwa threw a pinch of meal into the medicine tray from the north side, took the long black feather from that side, and forcibly thrust it into the medicine tray, uttering the word "pooh" in a high-pitched voice. He did the same with the five other feathers, each time circling the feather over the stones in the tray first. He then withdrew the six feathers from the tray and handed them to Taláskwaptiwa, who tied them into a bundle and returned them to Koyónainiwa, who used them to beat time during the remainder of the ceremony.

*Fourth Song.* Koyónainiwa poured some water into the tray, took all six feathers, and beat time with them, dipping them into the water and sprinkling it occasionally. He then shouted loudly into the bowl: "Haih, aih, aih, hai, hai." He took the feathers into his left hand, stirred the stones and water in the tray with his right hand, and sprinkled them with his fingers. He did this six times, placing a little cornmeal into the tray before each stirring.

*Fifth Song.* Tanákyeshtiwa <note>In 1889 this office was performed by Lomáboyaoma, the son of Lolúlomai.</note> dipped some water from the medicine tray with a shell and used it to wet the clay placed near the bowl. He then took a small lump in one hand and smeared a little on the chest and back of each person present; on his own body, he made additional marks on his upper and lower arms and legs. Lolúlomai arrived during this song, disrobed, combed his hair, and smoked.

*Sixth Song.* Talássyamtiwa lit the cloud blower and handed it to Koyónainiwa, who blew smoke over the medicine tray and returned the pipe to Talássyamtiwa. He then performed aspergation <note>The act of sprinkling holy water.</note> occasionally and went up the ladder, spat honey, and sprinkled it out of the hatchway.

The intercourse is that of a most highly cultured man who, in his relation to others, never places anything personal in all his wit, and sets aside all that is unpleasant.  Thus Xenophon's, but particularly Plato's Socratic Dialogues belong to the highest type of this fine social culture.

Because the philosophy of Socrates is no withdrawal from existence now and here into the free, pure regions of thought, but is in a piece with his life, it does not proceed to a system ; and the manner of his philosophizing, which appears to imply a withdrawal from actual affairs as it did to Plato, yet in that very way gives itself this inward connection with ordinary life.  For his more special business was his philosophic teaching, or rather his philosophic social intercourse (for it was not, properly speaking, teaching) with all ; and this outwardly resembled ordinary Athenian life in which the greater part of the day was passed without any particular business, in loitering about the market-place, or frequenting the public Lyceum, and there partly partaking of bodily exercises, and partly and principally, talking with one another.  This kind of intercourse was only possible in the Athenian mode of life, where most of the work which is now done by a free citizen—by a free republican and free imperial citizen alike—was performed by slaves, seeing that it was deemed unworthy of free men.  A free citizen could in Athens certainly be a handicraftsman, but he had slaves who did the work, just as a master now has workmen.  At the present day such a life of movement would not be suitable to our customs. <header>HISTORY OF PHILOSOPHY.</header>

...living relationship to the individual and applies to the specific case at hand. His social interaction is that of a highly cultured man who, in his relationships with others, never makes his wit personal and avoids anything unpleasant. Therefore, the Socratic dialogues of Xenophon, and especially those of Plato, represent the highest form of this refined social culture.

Because Socrates' philosophy is not a retreat from immediate existence into the pure regions of thought, but is inseparable from his life, it does not develop into a formal system. His method of philosophizing might seem to imply a withdrawal from practical affairs—as it did for Plato—but in reality, that very method connects it deeply with everyday life. His primary work was his philosophical teaching, or more accurately, his philosophical social interaction (since it was not formal teaching). This lifestyle outwardly resembled typical Athenian life, where citizens spent most of the day without specific business, loitering in the marketplace or visiting the public Lyceum <note>A public meeting place and gymnasium in Athens where philosophers often gathered</note>. There, they engaged in physical exercises and, most importantly, talked with one another.

This type of social life was only possible in the Athenian way of life. In that society, slaves performed most of the work that modern free citizens—whether in a republic or an empire—now do for themselves, as manual labor was considered unworthy of free men. An Athenian citizen could certainly be a craftsman, but he had slaves to perform the labor, much like a modern employer has workers. Today, such a lifestyle of constant movement would not fit our social customs. Socrates spent his time in this same way, living through constant discussions of ethical questions.¹ Thus, what he did came naturally to him and can generally be described as moralizing. <meta>This page continues Dürer’s geometric demonstration of how to manipulate solid blocks in space. He transitions from rigid, straight-edged geometric forms to the more organic, curved shapes required to accurately represent the human body's "soft" tissues during movement.</meta>

As was shown before, when two squared **bodies** <term>corpora</term> <note>geometric blocks used here to represent structural segments of the human figure, such as the torso and pelvis</note> are stacked upon one another, the upper body may be turned to one side or bent, and likewise it may be bent forward or backward. The lower body may also be handled in the same way. As one wishes, one may choose to let one remain stationary while moving the other, or move both of them together as the specific use requires. 

However, when such things are **projected** <term>aufgerissen</term> <note>the technical process of drafting or drawing out a three-dimensional form onto a two-dimensional surface</note>, their hard edges and planes intersect one another quite strangely in both the vertical and flattened **ground plans** <term>grund</term> <note>a two-dimensional geometric projection or plan view</note>, as you can see before your eyes. For in some places, the bodies merge into one another, while on the opposite side, they move outward or away from each other. 

And when this is applied to soft things <note>Dürer is shifting his focus from pure geometry to the pliable nature of human flesh and muscle.</note>, one part stretches while the other part **bunches up** <note>original: "krupfft" – referring to the way skin and muscle fold or contract when a limb or torso is bent.</note> over itself. Because of this, in a finished work, what is taken from one part must be given to the other, so that the gaps are filled.

The presence of a membrane enveloping the plasmodium is incompatible with these facts, not to mention the phenomena of fusion. <note>Cienkowski is arguing against the idea that these organisms have a fixed cell wall during this stage, as a rigid membrane would prevent the engulfing of food and the merging of branches.</note>

The plasmodium thus provides an indubitable example of a fluid developmental stage of an organism. We shall presently see to what extent this assumption is supported by the mode of origin of the <term>protoplasmic mass</term> of the <term>myxomycetes</term> (slime molds) and by analogous phenomena in other organisms.

# II.

Through the investigations of de Bary,*) we have learned that the myxomycetes do not possess a filamentous germination like other fungi, but rather form a <term>swarmer</term> (*Schwärmer*—a motile spore) from the spore that moves freely in the water. Its form is similar to an *Euglena*; at its forward end there is a <term>cilium</term> (a hair-like appendage for movement), and at the opposite end a <term>contractile vacuole</term> (a water-regulating organelle) is present. Therefore, those who consume far too much salt eventually have to deal with salted humors, <term>die Kräke</term> <gloss>the itch or scabies</gloss>, <term>den Schorbock</term> <gloss>scurvy</gloss>, and finally <term>Aussatz</term> <gloss>leprosy</gloss>, because the use of too much salt causes a body to rot, just as a moderate amount protects it from rotting. We see an example of this in seafaring, where the long-term consumption of salted foods introduces scurvy. And, certainly, here in Bavaria, where the common man salts his food very heavily because of the abundance and cheapness of salt—thinking to protect himself from rot in this way—people fall into heavy, dangerous diseases, especially leprosy. There is a great number of people afflicted with this throughout all of Bavaria. Although some attribute it to pork, which the inhabitants use the most, I blame the excessive use of salt. In other places, people also eat a lot of pork and do not become susceptible to this in the same way. Thus, salt brings great benefit, but no less trouble when it dissolves into a rot. This is not a simple rot, but because of the mixed-in acrimony, it impresses a sharp greed upon the blood and makes everything in the human body acrid, raging within its own frame. representatives of a culture leaning toward the grave were reinstated in their rights, and even consulted by the emperor himself before his departure for the Persian war <note>1</note>—naturally, to complete the illusion, with Delphi, Dodona, and Branchidae above all. Thus, Julian speaks in his letters of the oracles as if they were self-evident things <note>2</note> and mentions in particular the Branchidae oracle, which was closely related to Klaros. <note>3</note> His contemporary Themistios of Constantinople—and his testimony carries more weight—highlights Klaros and Branchidae as particularly famous among the oracles (he mentions Trikka, Epidauros, Delphi, Klaros, Branchidae, and a Paphlagonian oracle) in a remarkable speech that shows how firmly the old institutions were still rooted in the people. "Indeed," he says, "I admire Miletus and Kolophon for the sake of their ancient seats of Apollo; but if the god were now to settle and prophesy somewhere near here, I would not go far away, but there, even if it were an unrenowned city, or a village, a field, or a tree, whatever might please him." For one should not roam far away when the good lies near: this is what the speech intends to prove. <note>4</note> Himerios also speaks of these same two much-visited tripods; <note>5</note> and to the apostate emperor's deified teacher, Iamblichus, we owe the most precise description of the Klarian sanctuary, which agrees strikingly with that of Tacitus—and he speaks of something generally familiar. <note>6</note>

# Die Hessischen auß Neuß haben eine gute Fortun/ versehens aber heftlich.

<margin>
Aprilis
Anno
1644.
</margin>
Der Eingang deß Aprilis hatte sich bey der Hessischen Partie auß Neuß (welche Statt sie der Zeit mit 7. Bollwercken zu einer Real-Vestung gemacht:) ziemlich wol angelegt. All dieweil sie sich aber allzu sicher erzeigt/ unnd der Fortun zu viel getrawet/ hat ihnen selbige einen unversehenen Streich versetzt/ und damit/ wie wenig ihr zu trawen/ stattlich erwiesen/ welches also zugangen.

Nachdem mehrgedachte Hessische verkundschafftet/ daß vier Lothringische Regimenter/ als das Leib-Regiment/ Obr. Bellemont/ zu Fuß/ Obrister de Fauge/ und Obr. Baltin zu Pferd/ mit dem Geschütz unweit vom Schloß Merode/ im Dorff Merode aber Obrister de Gierecourt zu Fuß/ und Obr. de Mondragou zu Pferd im Quartier gelegen; seynd selbige Völcker auß Neuß/ Kempen und Calcar/ underm Begleite deß Obristen Rabenhaupts/ deß Nachts mit 500. Reuttern/ 300. Dragonern/ und 400. Musquetierern außgegangen/ haben Sonntags den 1. 11. Aprilis das Lothringische Hauptquartier überfallen/ und ist ohnerachtet grosser Gegenwehr/ der Obriste Bellmont/ auch in 200. gemeine Lothringische todt geblieben/ 160. Reutter gefangen/ sampt 200. Pferden und 2. Stück Geschütz/ auch was sonsten im Quartier gefunden/ bekommen worden. In wehrendem Scharmütziren hat/ nach deß Obr. Bellemonts Tod/ Obrister de Fauge sich noch uber ein halbe Stund auffgehalten/ biß endlich das Pferd under ihm erschossen/ und er darüber gefangen worden/ da dann die Lothringischen endlich sich nach deß Obristen Gierecourts Quartier retiriren müssen. Als nun indessen Hertz-Graff Christian zu Nassaw/ Siegen/ etc. hiervon Nachricht erlangt/ hat er mit 300. Reuttern/ sampt dem Mandeslohischen Regiment hinzu geeilet/ unnd die zerstreuwete Lothringische Trouppen in Eyl widerumb gesamblet/ auch auff die Hessischen (welche ohnnöthiger Weise lang im Feld geblieben/ unnd auß denen eroberten Stücken geschossen:) mit gefaßter Resolution angangen/ selbige bey Ober-Em am Holz/ die Hölle genannt/ angetroffen/ da es dann erst rechte Stöß geben/ und beydersseits Männlich zusammen geschlagen worden/ biß endlich die Hessische Partie in Unordnung gerathen/ unnd von beyden Theilen in 500. auff der Stelle todt blieben: wobey dann die vorhin von den Hessischen gefangene Lothringische Obristen und andere/ sampt denen 2. eroberten Stücken/ unnd mehrere Beutten wider: Item viel gesattelte Pferde erobert/ die Hessischen Obristen/

# The Hessians from Neuss have good fortune, yet they are quite careless.

<margin></margin>
April
Year
1644.
</margin>
The beginning of April started quite well for the Hessian party from Neuss, which city they have currently transformed into a true fortress with seven bastions. However, because they showed themselves to be overly confident and trusted their fortune too much, fortune dealt them an unexpected blow, thereby demonstrating how little she is to be trusted. This is how it came to pass.

After the aforementioned Hessians scouted that four Lorraine regiments, namely the Life Guard Regiment under Colonel Bellemont on foot, Colonel de Fauge, and Colonel Baltin on horseback, were quartered not far from Merode Castle, and in the village of Merode itself Colonel de Gierecourt on foot and Colonel de Mondragou on horseback, those troops set out from Neuss, Kempen, and Calcar under the escort of Colonel Rabenhaupt at night with 500 cavalry, 300 dragoons, and 400 musketeers. On Sunday, April 1st <note>original: 11. Aprilis; the difference represents the Julian vs. Gregorian calendar</note>, they ambushed the Lorraine headquarters. Despite heavy resistance, Colonel Bellemont and some 200 common Lorraine soldiers remained dead, 160 cavalrymen were captured, along with 200 horses and two pieces of artillery, as well as whatever else was found in the quarters. During the ongoing skirmish, after Colonel Bellemont's death, Colonel de Fauge held his ground for more than half an hour until finally his horse was shot from under him, and he was captured as a result. The Lorraine forces then had to retreat toward Colonel Gierecourt's quarters. When Count Christian of Nassau-Siegen and others meanwhile received news of this, he hurried there with 300 cavalrymen and the Mandesloh Regiment. He quickly gathered the scattered Lorraine troops and attacked the Hessians, who had remained in the field unnecessarily long and were firing from the captured cannons. He encountered them at Ober-Em near the woods, called the Hell, where the real struggle began. Both sides fought manfully until the Hessian party fell into disorder, and about 500 men from both sides remained dead on the spot. In this process, the Lorraine colonels and others previously captured by the Hessians, along with the two recaptured cannons and much other loot, were taken back. Eine ausführliche und zusammenhängende Darstellung der Art und der Folgen dieser κίνησις, des Sündenfalls, finden wir dann in dem Brief an die Melania (Frankenberg 613 ff.). Durch den Sündenfall — das ist ebenfalls eine uns schon bekannte Gedankenreihe — hat der Nus die Einheit seines Wesens verloren. Er ist aus der Wesenheit der göttlichen Monas gefallen und in die Welt der „Zahl“ eingegangen (s. o.): ἀριθμοὶ οἳ διὰ τὴν κίνησιν εἰς τὸν νοῦν ὑπεισῆλθον (Frankenberg 617). Genauer ist die Gespaltenheit des menschlichen Wesens in Nus, Seele und Leib eine Folge der κίνησις (617. 190 b α). Noch charakteristischer ist der Satz (Frankenberg 618) ἔστι δὲ ὅτε διὰ τὸ αὐτεξούσιον αὐτοῦ τῆς πρώτης αὐτοῦ καταστάσεως ἀποπεσὼν ὠνομάσθη ψυχὴ καὶ πάλιν κατολισθήσας .... προσηγορεύθη σῶμα¹), und so ist nun ein und dasselbe Wesen Leib, Seele und Nus διὰ τὰς μεταβολὰς τῶν αὐτοῦ προαιρέσεων. Euagrios lehrt also ganz deutlich eine Degradation des Nus zur Psyche und wiederum der Psyche zur leiblichen Wesenheit durch den Fall²). In etwas anderer Weise und strenger Anlehnung an Platonische Psychologie wird das VI 85 auch so zum Ausdruck gebracht: εἰ τὴν ἐπιθυμίαν καὶ τὸν θυμὸν ἐπικοινῶς (ὁμοίως) τοῖς θηρίοις κεκτήμεθα γνωστόν ὅτι ἀρχῇ τῆς κτίσεως ταῦτα μεθ’ ἡμῶν οὐκ ἔκτισται ἀλλὰ μετὰ τὴν κίνησιν εἰς τὴν λογικὴν ψυχὴν παρεισῆλθεν³).

Mühelos erkennen wir hier überall die Gedankenwelt und auch die Terminologie des Origenes wieder. Auch für Origenes ist der Fall der Geschöpfe eine κίνησις, wenn auch der Terminus zu fehlen scheint: *voluntarios enim et liberos motus a se conditis mentibus creator indulsit* (II 9, 2 p. 165 25). Er redet von *„animae ipsius ambigui fragilesque motus“* (I 8, 4. 102, 6). — Auch bei ihm taucht das Schlagwort auf, daß der Mensch durch seine ἀμέλεια (s. o.) zu Fall gekommen sei⁴). Ich erinnere weiter daran, daß ein Logienpaar des Euagrios, dessen Sinn auf der terminologischen Unterscheidung von νοῦς und ψυχή beruht, sich uns als wörtliches Zitat aus Origenes erwiesen hat: κιθάρα ἐστὶν ψυχὴ πρακτική .... ψαλτήριόν ἐστι νοῦς καθαρός (VI 46. 48 s. o. S. 291).

Die Theorie von der Minderwertigkeit der menschlichen ψυχή, auf welcher die Gesamtauffassung des Euagrios ruht, entwickelt Origenes ferner ausführlich in seinem Kapitel *περὶ ἀρχῶν* II 8. <meta>This page continues the investigation into the Origenist roots of Evagrius's theology, specifically focusing on the "movement" (kinesis) or the Fall that caused minds to become souls and bodies.</meta>

enumerated before and after the movement <note>original Greek: κίνησις (*kinesis*)</note> (cf. VI 75). In VI 36, it is stated that it was Satan who began the movement. According to VI 75, free will <note>original Greek: τὸ αὐτεξούσιον (*to autexousion*)</note> is named as the author of the movement.

A detailed and coherent presentation of the nature and consequences of this movement—the Fall—is then found in the *Letter to Melania* (Frankenberg 613 ff.). Through the Fall—this is also a line of thought already familiar to us—the Mind <note>original Greek: *Nus*</note> has lost the unity of its essence. It has fallen from the essence of the divine Monad <note>The "Monad" refers to the ultimate, indivisible divine unity</note> and entered the world of "number" (see above): "numbers which entered into the Mind because of the movement" <note>original Greek: ἀριθμοὶ οἳ διὰ τὴν κίνησιν εἰς τὸν νοῦν ὑπεισῆλθον</note> (Frankenberg 617). More precisely, the fragmentation of the human being into Mind, soul, and body is a consequence of the movement (617. 190 b α). Even more characteristic is the sentence (Frankenberg 618): "it happens that because of its free will, having fallen from its first state, it was named 'soul' and, having slipped down again... it was called 'body'" ¹), and so one and the same being is now body, soul, and Mind "through the changes of its own choices" <note>original Greek: διὰ τὰς μεταβολὰς τῶν αὐτοῦ προαιρέσεων</note>. Evagrius thus teaches quite clearly a degradation of the Mind to the soul, and again from the soul to the bodily essence through the Fall ²). In a slightly different way and in strict adherence to Platonic psychology, this is expressed in VI 85 as follows: "If we possess desire and anger in common with the beasts, it is clear that these were not created with us at the beginning of creation, but they crept into the rational soul after the movement" ³).

We effortlessly recognize the world of thought and terminology of Origen here throughout. For Origen, too, the fall of creatures is a movement, even if the specific term seems to be missing: "for the Creator allowed voluntary and free movements to the minds he had established" <note>original Latin: *voluntarios enim et liberos motus a se conditis mentibus creator indulsit*</note> (II 9, 2 p. 165 25). He speaks of "the ambiguous and fragile movements of the soul itself" <note>original Latin: *animae ipsius ambigui fragilesque motus*</note> (I 8, 4. 102, 6). — With him, too, the catchphrase appears that man fell through his "negligence" <note>original Greek: ἀμέλεια (*ameleia*)</note> (see above) ⁴). I further recall that a pair of sayings by Evagrius, whose meaning rests on the terminological distinction between Mind <note>original Greek: *νοῦς*</note> and soul <note>original Greek: *ψυχή*</note>, has proven to be a literal quotation from Origen: "the soul that acts is a lyre... the pure Mind is a psaltery" <note>original Greek: κιθάρα ἐστὶν ψυχὴ πρακτική .... ψαλτήριόν ἐστι νοῦς καθαρός</note> (VI 46. 48 see above p. 291).

The theory of the inferiority of the human soul <note>original Greek: *ψυχή*</note>, upon which Evagrius's entire outlook rests, is further developed by Origen in detail in his chapter *On First Principles* <note>original Greek: *περὶ ἀρχῶν* (*Peri Archon*)</note> II 8. He demonstrates here how the soul, the "imaginative and impulsive essence" <note>original Greek: οὐσία φανταστικὴ καὶ ὁρμητική</note>, is common to both humans and animals, how the angels are never called "souls" in Scripture, and how the "soul of God" is only spoken of exceptionally and improperly, while it is with

2) In connection with this are the terms "density" or "thickness" <note>original Greek: παχύτης, παχύς</note>, which Evagrius likes to use in relation to the bodily essence of humans. Cf. IV 46 "the density of this world," II 68 "dense bodies," II 62 "then the density of the bodies shall also be removed from our midst." *Letter* in Migne 32. 260 A "denser teaching" (cf. 256 B). *Practicus* 29 "the Mind having become thickened." — That Evagrius is dependent on Origen's usage here is proven by the circumstance that *Centuries* IV 36, where the "intelligible fat" is interpreted as the "density" of our Mind, stems literally from Origen, *Selections on the Psalms* (Lommatzsch XII 51). Cf. the latter's speculation on the "garments of skins" (Koetschau *On First Principles* p. 159 note) and *Against Celsus* III 35.
3) We find slightly different phrasing for the degradation of the Mind in the *Letter* in Migne 32. 257 c: "since our Mind, having become thickened, is bound to the dust and mingled with the clay." 260 A, 263 A "the Mind bound to the flesh." — *Practicus* 70 = *Centuries* VII 26: "the passions binding it [the Mind] through thoughts to things and to sensible objects." Cf. VII 52. 56, IV 62. 70, V 57.
4) I 4, 1. 63 27. 64 9, II 9, 2. 165 28.

<summary>This page analyzes Evagrius's theory of the Fall as a "movement" (kinesis) of the Mind away from divine unity, resulting in its degradation into soul and body. It highlights how these ideas and specific terminologies, such as "negligence" and "density," are directly inherited from Origen's psychological and cosmological framework.</summary>

I mean, therefore, the human as a composite of soul and body, and for such a human to become accountable for all things done, and to receive this honor or punishment on account of these. But if the just judgment brings the penalty for the things worked against the composite, and [if] it is not fitting for the soul alone to carry away the rewards for the things done together with the body—for it is impassive by itself regarding the transgressions occurring around bodily pleasures or nourishment and treatments—nor for the body alone—for it is incapable of judging laws and justice by itself—then the human who is from these [two] will receive the judgment for each of the things worked by him. But the discourse finds that this does not happen in this life. For justice according to merit is not preserved in the present life, because many, who are godless and who practice every lawlessness and wickedness, continue until the end without experiencing evils. And on the contrary, those who have shown their life to be examined according to every <term>arete</term> <gloss>virtue</gloss> live in pain, in abuse, in false accusations, in beatings, and in all kinds of suffering. Nor does it happen after death. For the composite is no longer [there], as the soul is separated from the body, and the body itself is scattered as those things from which it was gathered, and it no longer preserves anything of its former nature or form, or even the memory of what was done. # [PROCOPIUS ON THE GOTHIC WAR IV. 29.]

<margin>12</margin>
...the hill that happened to be there. Therefore, it was necessary for both sides to value it highly: for the Goths, so that by encircling the enemy in the engagement they might place them in a difficult position; for the Romans, so that they might not suffer this. But Narses, anticipating them, selected fifty infantrymen from the roll <note>a list of enlisted soldiers</note> and sent them in the dead of night to seize and hold it. They, with no one from the enemy standing in their way, arrived there and remained quietly. There is a mountain torrent in front of the hill, beside the path I just mentioned, and opposite the ground where the Goths had encamped, where the fifty men stood, huddled close together, drawn up in a phalanx as they were in a narrow space. At daybreak, Totila, seeing what had happened, was eager to drive them away. He immediately sent a squadron of cavalry against them, ordering them to drive them out as quickly as possible. The cavalry rushed at them with much noise and shouting, as if they would carry them off in one charge, but they, drawn up in a small group and shielding themselves with their shields and holding their spears out, stood their ground. Then the Goths, attacking with zeal, caused confusion and drove at them, but the fifty, through the pushing of their shields and the very dense and unbroken array of their spears, defended themselves against the attackers most stoutly, deliberately making a clatter with their shields, thereby constantly frightening the horses and the men with the points of their spears.

(166) καὶ ἐπὶ πλέον ἐπειρῶντο τὴν μνήμην γυμνάζειν· οὐδὲν γὰρ μεῖζον πρὸς ἐπιστήμην καὶ ἐμπειρίαν καὶ φρόνησιν τοῦ δύνασθαι μνημονεύειν. ἀπὸ δὴ τούτων τῶν ἐπιτηδευμάτων συνέβη τὴν Ἰταλίαν πᾶσαν φιλοσόφων ἀνδρῶν ἐμπλησθῆναι, καὶ πρότερον ἀγνοουμένης αὐτῆς ὕστερον διὰ Πυθαγόραν μεγάλην Ἑλλάδα κληθῆναι, καὶ πλείστους παρ’ αὐτοῖς ἄνδρας φιλοσόφους καὶ ποιητὰς καὶ νομοθέτας γενέσθαι. τάς τε γὰρ τέχνας τὰς ῥητορικὰς καὶ τοὺς λόγους τοὺς ἐπιδεικτικοὺς καὶ τοὺς νόμους τοὺς γεγραμμένους παρ’ ἐκείνων εἰς τὴν Ἑλλάδα συνέβη κομισθῆναι. καὶ περὶ τῶν φυσικῶν ὅσοι τινὰ μνείαν πεποίηνται, πρῶτον Ἐμπεδοκλέα καὶ Παρμενίδην τὸν Ἐλεάτην προφερόμενοι τυγχάνουσιν, οἵ τε γνωμολογῆσαί τι τῶν κατὰ τὸν βίον βουλόμενοι τὰς Ἐπιχάρμου διανοίας προφέρονται, καὶ σχεδὸν πάντες αὐτὰς οἱ φιλόσοφοι κατέχουσι. <note>Zu § 163 vgl. Cramer An. Par. I 172 ὅτι οἱ Πυθαγορικοί, ὡς ἔφη Ἀριστόξενος, καθάρσει ἐχρῶντο τοῦ μὲν σώματος διὰ τῆς ἰατρικῆς, τῆς δὲ ψυχῆς διὰ τῆς μουσικῆς. Stob. III 1, 71 H. Diod. x 5, 1. Zu § 164 vgl. They certainly honored memory very much and applied great exercise and care to it. In learning, they would not let go of what was being taught until they had firmly grasped the things of the first lesson, and they practiced recollection of things said daily in the following manner. (165) A Pythagorean man did not rise from his bed before he had recollected the events of the previous day. He performed the recollection in this way: he tried to recover in his mind what he first said or heard or ordered for the household after rising, and what was second, and what was third. The same logic applied to subsequent events. And again, upon going out, whom he first met and whom second, and what words were spoken first, second, and third; and the same logic for all other things. For he tried to recover in his mind everything that happened in the whole day, desiring to remember them in the order in which each of them happened to occur. If he had more leisure upon waking, he tried to recover the events of the third day in the same way. (166) They tried even more to exercise the memory, for nothing is greater for knowledge, experience, and wisdom than the ability to remember. From these practices, it happened that all of Italy was filled with philosopher men, and though it was previously unknown, it was later called Great Greece because of Pythagoras, and many philosophers, poets, and lawmakers arose among them. For the rhetorical arts, the demonstration speeches, and the written laws were brought from them into Greece. And regarding natural philosophers, whoever makes mention of them, they happen to bring forward Empedocles and Parmenides the Eleatic first; and those wishing to say something wise about life bring forward the thoughts of Epicharmus, and almost all philosophers possess them. <note>Regarding section 163, compare Cramer's notes: the Pythagoreans, as Aristoxenus said, used purification of the body through medicine and of the soul through music. Also Diodorus x 5. Regarding section 164, compare Iamblichus 110-111.</note>

2. Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras* 137. I wish to show from the beginning the principles of the worship of the gods which Pythagoras and the men after him established. Everything they define regarding acting or not acting is aimed at communion with the divine; this is the starting principle, and their whole life is organized toward following God. The logic of this philosophy is that men act ridiculously when seeking the good from anywhere other than from the gods. It is similar to a person in a kingdom who serves a minor official of the citizens but neglects the ruler and king of all. For they think humans do such a thing. Since there is a God and He is the lord of all, and it is agreed that one must ask the lord for the good—and everyone gives good things to those they love and in whom they delight, but the opposite to those they are against—it is clear that those things must be done in which God happens to delight.

36 The north-east and the south-west winds are the wettest. Hail comes with the north, the north-north-east, and the north-west. Snow comes with the north-north-east <note>original: "ἢ βορέας" <gloss>or north</gloss>—likely a gloss on <term>aparktias</term> <gloss>north-north-east</gloss></note> and the north. Heat is brought by the south, the west, and the south-east winds; some have this effect on the places they strike when coming from the sea, others on those they visit when coming over land. The winds which most thicken the sky with clouds and cover it are the north-east, and then the south-west. While other winds push clouds away from themselves, the north-east alone attracts them as it blows. The winds which best bring a clear sky are the north-west and the north-north-west, and of the others, the north. Those which most have the character of a hurricane are the north, the north-north-west, and the north-west.

37 These acquire the character of a hurricane when they blow into one another, most especially in autumn, though also in spring. The winds accompanied by lightning are the north-north-west, the north-west, the north, and the north-north-east. <meta>This page continues Clement’s discussion on the biological and spiritual connection between blood and milk, moving into the symbolic use of milk, honey, and water in Christian initiation.</meta>

## THE INSTRUCTOR, BOOK I

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, the same substance, both blood and milk, serves as a symbol of the Lord’s passion and his teaching. It is permitted for each of us who are infants to boast in the Lord, saying:

->I boast to be of a good father and of such blood.<-
->[To be.]<-

It is already clear that milk is formed from blood through a process of change. However, we can also learn this from looking at flocks of sheep and herds of cattle. During the season of the year we call spring, the atmosphere is more humid. The grass and pastures are full of juice and moisture at that time. The animals first become full of blood, which is shown by the way their veins distend and their vessels become rounded. From this blood, milk flows more abundantly. <margin>B</margin> Conversely, in the summer, the blood is constricted and dried out by the heat. This stops the transformation, and so they produce less milk when they are milked. Furthermore, milk has a very natural kinship with water, just as the spiritual bath <note>original: λουτρὸν (loutron); referring to baptism</note> has a kinship with spiritual nourishment. Those who sip a little cold water with the aforementioned milk find it helpful immediately. The fellowship with water does not allow the milk to turn sour <note>original: ἀποξύνεσθαι (apoxynesthai)</note>. This happens not through some kind of opposition, but through a natural affinity as it ripens. The relationship that the Word <note>original: Λόγος (Logos)</note> has with baptism is the same as the connection milk has with water. Milk is the only liquid that accepts a mixture with water, being received for the purpose of cleansing, just as baptism is received for the forgiveness of sins. <margin>C</margin> It is also naturally mixed with honey, and this again is for cleansing along with sweet nourishment. For when the Word is mixed with love for humanity, he heals our passions and cleanses our sins. The saying:

> ... Speech flowed sweeter than honey,

seems to me to have been spoken about the Word, who is honey. In many places, prophecy raises him above honey and the honeycomb. Furthermore, milk is also mixed with wine.
