(44) **Father.** Diomedes says this in Homer, *Iliad* 14, line 113: *I also boast that my birth is from a good father.* (45) **To turn sour.** The Bodleian manuscript reads *epoxynesthai*, but another hand wrote an *a* over the first *e*. (46) **Cleansing.** There is no doubt this should be read as *epi katharsei* (for cleansing) as it appears shortly after. (47) **Honey.** This refers to the custom of the early Christians, who gave those newly baptized a taste of honey and milk mixed together. Clement seems to have alluded to this a little earlier on page 125: *As soon as we are reborn, we are honored with the hope of rest, the Jerusalem above, in which it is written that milk and honey rain down.* Tertullian mentions the same rite in *On the Crown*, chapter 3: *Then, having been received from baptism, we taste a mixture of milk and honey.* In his work *Against Marcion*, book 1, chapter 14, he says that Marcion does not reject the Creator's water with which he washes his own, nor the oil with which he anoints them, nor the fellowship of honey with which he treats them as infants. For infants were once nourished with milk and honey. Barnabas says in chapter 6: *Why then milk and honey? Because the infant is first made alive with honey, and then with milk.*

<column-break/>

<margin>A</margin> Therefore, the same blood and milk are symbols of the Lord's suffering and his doctrine. It is allowed for each of us who are children to boast in the Lord and say:

->*I boast to be of a good father and of such blood.*<-

It is now evident that milk is made from blood through change. We can observe this in cattle and oxen. In the spring time, when the air is more moist and the grass is more succulent, animals are first filled with blood. This can be known from the swelling of the veins. From this blood, milk is <margin>B</margin> poured out more richly. In the summer, however, the blood is dried by the heat and stops its transformation, so less is milked. Indeed, milk has a very natural connection with water, just as the spiritual washing has with spiritual food. Those who swallow a little cold with the milk are helped. The water prevents the milk from souring, not by conflict, but by ripening it through an inward connection. The same fellowship the Word has with baptism, milk has with water. This is the only liquid that mixes with water for the purpose of purifying, just as baptism is for the remission of sins. It is also <margin>C</margin> aptly mixed with honey for purification along with sweet food. The Word, mixed with kindness, heals the affections of the soul and clears away sins. The line:

> .... *Speech flows sweeter than honey*,

seems to me to be said of the Word, who is honey. In many places, prophecy exalts him *above honey and the honeycomb* <margin>Psalm 18:11; 118:103</margin>. Moreover, milk is also mixed...

---

*The infant is first given life with honey, then with milk.* Callimachus, in his *Hymn to Jupiter*, line 48:
<margin>D</margin>
> ... you sucked the rich breast 
> of the goat Amalthea, and ate sweet honeycomb besides.

Since baptism was a second birth, they gave the baptized honey mixed with milk to taste after the washing, as if they were tender infants. Compare Jerome, *Against the Luciferians*, chapter 4; Third Council of Carthage, canon 24.
(48) **Honey.** Homer, *Iliad* 1, line 248, says of Nestor:
> ... the clear-voiced orator of the Pylians, 
> from whose tongue speech flowed sweeter than honey.
(49) **Milk and wine.** Jerome notes on Isaiah 55:1 that the Western Churches gave wine and milk to the newly baptized.

<summary>Clement explains the biological transformation of blood into milk in animals and humans, using it as a metaphor for how Christ’s suffering (blood) becomes spiritual nourishment (milk) for believers. He also discusses the early Christian liturgical practice of giving honey and milk to the newly baptized to symbolize their rebirth as spiritual infants.</summary>

<margin>On the Coan [Prognostics]</margin>
### CLXXXVII. When the brain has suffered <term>sphacelismus</term> <gloss>mortification or gangrene</gloss>, some die on the third day, others on the seventh. Those who escape these are saved. Among those who have been opened, if the bone is found to be decayed, they perish.

### CLXXXVII. *When the brain is endangered by sideration <note>meaning a sudden injury or "striking" of the brain, leading to inflammation</note>, some die in three days, others in seven, and those who survive these are saved. Of that number, those perish in whom the bone appears separated by the incision.*

1. That is, it tends from inflammation to a deadening of the part. Here <term>sphacelismus</term> is taken for a not-yet-confirmed deadening, and for that progress which leads toward corruption. Therefore, it would be better read as "when the brain is becoming gangrenous."

2. [This varies] according to the varying condition and location of the affected part. Death comes more quickly when the crown of the head is affected in a boy than [when it is] the occiput, and [the same applies] in an adult.

semper est extra. Cuius hoc indicium est: nam & annulorum eos, qui pala carent, infinitos, homines dicunt, quia semper aliquid est extra sumendū: per similitudinē tamē quandā, & non propriè. Oportet enim & hoc nunquā idē insuper sumi. In circulo verò non ita fit: sed semper quod deinceps sumitur, est solùm aliud. Infinitū igit id est, cuius semper aliquid extrà, ratione quātitatis accipi potest: cuius verò nihil est extra, id est perfectū, ac totū. Hoc. n. pacto totum consueuimus definire, totum dicentes id esse, cuius nil pror-sus abest: vt hominē totū, aut cistellam. Atq. vt quodque, sic & id quod propriè totū est: veluti totū ipsū cuius nihil est extra. Cuius verò aliquid abest, id quicquid abest, vniuersum non est. Totum autem, & perfectum aut idem penitus sunt, aut naturam finitimā habent. Perfectum verò nihil est prorsus, quod non habeat finem. Quocirca putandum est melius Parmenidem Melisso dixisse. Hic enim ipsum infinitum totum appellat: Parmenides autem, totum dicit esse finitum, à medio æquè distans. Fieri enim non potest, vt infinitū cū toto, ac vniuerso, perinde atque cuin lino linum nectatur. Nà hinc & hanc præclarā de infinitò conditionē accipiunt, omnia, inquam, ipsum continere, & vniuersum in se ipso complecti: habet enim similitudinem quandam ad totum. Infinitū enim materiæ perfectionis magnitudinis est, & id, quod est potentia totum, non actu. Est autem diuisibile, ad diminutionem, & ad additionem contrariam, totūmque atque finitum, non per se, sed per aliud: & non continet, sed vt infinitum est, continetur. Quapropter & ignotum est, ea ratione, qua est infinitum. materia nanque formam non habet. Quare patet, partis magis infinitum, quàm totius rationem subire. Materia nanque pars est totius, perinde ac æs, est æneæ statuæ pars. Nam si in rebus sensibilibus continet, & intelligibilibus, etiam ipsum magnum, & paruum cōtinere res intelligibiles oportebat. At absurdum est profectò, ac impossibile, id, quod est ignotum atque indefinitum, continere, ac definire.

### CAPVT VII.
*Quo pacto ex definitione infiniti, assignanda sit ratio eorum quæ de infinito dicuntur.*

Atqui cum ratione etiam fit, vt id quidem, quod in additione cōstitit, nō videatur esse sic infinitū, vt omnē exuperet magnitudine: id verò, quod in diuisione constitit, infinitū esse istiusmodi videatur. Infinitū enim intus perinde atque materia cōtinetur, forma autem continet. Cum ratione etiam accidit, in numero quidē versus minus, minimum esse, finémque: versus autem plus, omnem semper multitudinem exuperare. In magnitudine verò, cōtrarium: versus quidem minus, omnem magnitudinem exuperare: versus autem maius, non esse magnitudinem infinitam. Hæc enim propterea fiunt, quòd ipsum vnum quicquid tādem id sit, indiuisibile est, homo nanque vnus est homo, nō multi. Numerus autem est, vna, plura, quantáve quædam. Quare ad indiuisibile stetur necesse est. duo enim, ac tria, denominatiua nomina sunt: & cæterorum quisque numerorum simili modo. Versus autem plus, fit vt semper intelligatur. Diuisiones enim magnitudinis duas in partes æquales, sunt infinitæ. Quare potentia quidem est, actu non est: sed semper id, quod accipitur, multitudinem omnem exuperat definitam. Sed non est separabilis is numerus diuisionis, nec infinitio permanet: sed fit & quemadmodum tempus, & ipse numerus temporis. In magnitudinibus autem contrarium est. Nam diuiditur quidem in infinita, continuum ipsum: versus autem maius, non est infinitum. quantum enim contingit potentia esse, tantum & actu esse contingit. Quare cùm infinitum nullum sit sensibile corpus, non contingit definitæ magnitudinis omnis exuperationē esse. Alioqui, mauis cælo aliquid erit. Ipsum autem infinitum nō est idem in motu, magnitudine, atque tempore: vt vna quædam natura. Sed posterius dicitur ob prius. Veluti motus quidem dicitur infinitus, quia prius dicitur magnitudo super qua fit motus, & quę alteratur, aut accrescit, tempus autem propter motum. Atque nunc quidem vtimur hisce: posteriùs autem, & quidnam sit horum vnumquodque, & cur omnis magnitudo diuisibilis sit in magnitudines, dicere enitemur. Atqui neque mathematicorum contemplationem ea ratio aufert, quæ infinitum hoc pacto è medio tollit, vt ad incrementum abeat actu sine transitione. Neque enim nunc ipso indigent infinito, neque vtuntur, sed tantam solùm lineam polluant quantum volunt finitam: atque quamuis aliam magnitudinem eadē diuidere ratione, qua diuisa est magnitudo maxima licet. Quare ad ostendendum quidem illo pacto nihil refert prorsus: esse autem ipsum in his est magnitudinibus, quæ in rerum sunt ratione. Cùm verò causæ in quatuor sint distinctæ, patet, infinitum vt materiam causam esse, & esse quidem ipsius priuationem esse: per se autem subiectum, continuum ipsum atque sensibile esse. Cæteri etiam omnes ipso infinito vt materia vti videntur. Quapropter & absurdum est sanè, ipsum id esse quod continet, & nō id quod continetur, asserere.

οὐ γὰρ ἂν λίνον λίνῳ ὅδε συνάπτειν τῷ παντὶ καὶ τῷ ὅλῳ τὸ ἄπειρον· ἐπεὶ ἐντεῦθέν γε λαμβάνουσι τὴν σεμνότητα κατὰ τοῦ ἀπείρου, τὸ πάντα περιέχειν, καὶ τὸ πᾶν ἐν ἑαυτῷ ἔχειν, διὰ τὸ ἔχειν τινὰ ὁμοιότητα τῷ ὅλῳ· ἔστι γὰρ τὸ ἄπειρον, τῆς τοῦ μεγέθους τελειότητος ὕλη, καὶ τὸ δυνάμει ὅλον, ἐντελεχείᾳ δὲ οὔ· διαιρετὸν δὲ, ἐπί τε τὴν καθαίρεσιν καὶ τὴν ἀντεστραμμένην πρόσθεσιν· ὅλον δὲ καὶ πεπερασμένον οὐ καθ’ αὑτὸ, ἀλλὰ κατ’ ἄλλο· καὶ οὐ περιέχει, ἀλλὰ περιέχεται, ᾗ ἄπειρόν ἐστι· διὸ καὶ ἄγνωστον, ᾗ ἄπειρον. εἶδος γὰρ οὐκ ἔχει ἡ ὕλη. ὥστε φανερὸν, ὅτι μᾶλλον ἐν μορίου λόγῳ τὸ ἄπειρον, ἢ ἐν ὅλου· μόριον γὰρ ἡ ὕλη τοῦ ὅλου, ὥσπερ ὁ χαλκὸς τοῦ χαλκοῦ ἀνδριάντος· ἐπεὶ εἴγε περιέχει ἐν τοῖς αἰσθητοῖς καὶ ἐν τοῖς νοητοῖς τὸ μέγα καὶ τὸ μικρὸν, ἔδει περιέχειν τὰ νοητά. ἄτοπον δὲ καὶ ἀδύνατον, τὸ ἄγνωστον καὶ τὸ ἀόριστον περιέχειν καὶ ὁρίζειν.

Parmenides τῆ ὅλον εἶπε αἰτ. Πᾶν τυχὸν ἐν κύκλου σφαίρας ἐναλίγκιον ὄγκῳ. Μεσόθεν ἰσοπαλὲς πάντη.
</margin>

### Κεφάλαιον ζ'.
*Πῶς χρὴ ἐκ τοῦ ὁρισμοῦ τοῦ ἀπείρου λόγον ποιεῖσθαι τῶν αἰεὶ ἀπειρουμένων.*

Κατὰ λόγον δὲ συμβαίνει καὶ τὸ κατὰ πρόσθεσιν, ὡς μὴ δοκεῖν ἄπειρον οὕτως, ὥστε παντὸς ὑπερβάλλειν τὸ μέγεθος· ἐπὶ τὴν διαίρεσιν δὲ, ὑπερβάλλειν. καὶ γὰρ ὡς ἡ ὕλη ἐντὸς, καὶ τὸ ἄπειρον· περιέχει δὲ τὸ εἶδος. εὐλόγως δὲ καὶ τὸ, ἐν μὲν τῷ ἀριθμῷ ἐπὶ τὸ ἐλάχιστον πέρας· ἐπὶ δὲ τὸ πλεῖον, αἰεὶ παντὸς ὑπερβάλλειν πλήθους· ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν μεγεθῶν τοὐναντίον· ἐπὶ μὲν τὸ ἔλαττον, παντὸς ὑπερβάλλειν μεγέθους· ἐπὶ δὲ τὸ μεῖζον, μὴ εἶναι μέγεθος ἄπειρον. αἴτιον δ’, ὅτι τὸ ἕν ἐστιν ἀδιαίρετον, ὅπερ ἂν ᾖ, οἷον ἄνθρωπος εἷς ἄνθρωπος, καὶ οὐ πολλοί· ὁ δ’ ἀριθμός ἐστιν ἕνα πλείω, καὶ ποσὰ ἄττα· ὥστ’ ἀνάγκη στῆναι ἐπὶ τὸ ἀδιαίρετον· τὰ γὰρ δύο καὶ τρία παρώνυμα ὀνόματά ἐστιν, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ τῶν ἄλλων ἀριθμῶν ἕκαστος· ἐπὶ δὲ τὸ πλεῖον αἰεὶ ἔστι νοῆσαι· ἄπειροι γὰρ αἱ διχοτομίαι τοῦ μεγέθους· ὥστε δυνάμει μὲν ἔστιν, ἐνεργείᾳ δ’ οὔ· ἀλλ’ αἰεὶ ὑπερβάλλει τὸ λαμβανόμενον, παντὸς ὡρισμένου πλήθους· ἀλλ’ οὐ χωριστὸς ὁ ἀριθμὸς οὗτος τῆς διχοτομίας, οὐδὲ μένει ἡ ἀπειρία, ἀλλὰ γίνεται, ὥσπερ καὶ ὁ χρόνος καὶ ὁ ἀριθμὸς τοῦ χρόνου. ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν μεγεθῶν, τοὐναντίον ἐστίν· καὶ διαιρεῖται μὲν γὰρ εἰς ἄπειρα τὸ συνεχές. ἐπὶ δὲ τὸ μεῖζον οὐκ ἔστιν ἄπειρον. ὅσον γὰρ ἐνδέχεται δυνάμει εἶναι, καὶ ἐνεργείᾳ ἐνδέχεται τοσοῦτον εἶναι. ὥστ’ ἐπεὶ ἄπειρον οὐδέν ἐστι μέγεθος αἰσθητὸν, οὐκ ἐνδέχεται παντὸς ὑπερβολὴν εἶναι ὡρισμένου μεγέθους· εἴη γὰρ ἄν τι τοῦ οὐρανοῦ μεῖζον. τὸ δ’ ἄπειρον, οὐ ταὐτὸν ἐν κινήσει, καὶ μεγέθει, καὶ χρόνῳ, ὡς καὶ μία τις φύσις, ἀλλὰ τὸ ὕστερον λέγεται κατὰ τὸ πρότερον· οἷον, κίνησις μὲν, ὅτι τὸ μέγεθος, ἐφ’ οὗ κινεῖται, ἢ ἀλλοιοῦται, ἢ αὐξάνεται, ὁ χρόνος δὲ διὰ τὴν κίνησιν. νῦν μὲν οὖν χρώμεθα τούτοις, ὕστερον δ’ ἐροῦμεν τί ἐστιν ἕκαστον, καὶ διότι πᾶν μέγεθος εἰς μεγέθη διαιρετόν. Οὐκ ἀφαιρεῖται δὲ ὁ λόγος οὐδὲ τοὺς μαθηματικοὺς τὴν θεωρίαν, ἀναιρῶν οὕτως εἶναι τὸ ἄπειρον, ὡς ἐνεργείᾳ εἶναι ἐπὶ τὴν αὔξησιν, ὡς ἀδιεξίτητον· οὐδὲ γὰρ νῦν δέονται τοῦ ἀπείρου, οὐδὲ χρῶνται, ἀλλὰ μόνον εἶναι, ὅσην ἂν βούλωνται, πεπερασμένην· τῷ δὲ μεγίστῳ μεγέθει τὸν αὐτὸν ἔστι τετμῆσθαι λόγον ὁπηλικονοῦν μέγεθος ἕτερον. ὥστε πρὸς μὲν τὸ δεῖξαι ἐκείνοις, οὐδὲν διοίσει τὸ εἶναι ἐν τοῖς οὖσιν ἔστη μεγέθεσιν. ἐπεὶ δὲ τὰ αἴτια διῄρηται τέσσαρα, φανερὸν ὅτι τὸ ἄπειρον αἴτιόν ἐστι καὶ ὅτι, τὸ μὲν εἶναι αὐτῷ στέρησίς ἐστι, τὸ δὲ καθ’ αὑτὸ ὑποκείμενον, τὸ συνεχὲς καὶ αἰσθητόν. φαίνονται δὲ πάντες καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι ὡς ὕλῃ χρώμενοι τῷ ἀπείρῳ· διὸ καὶ ἄτοπον τὸ περιέχον ποιεῖν αὐτὸ, ἀλλὰ μὴ τὸ περιεχόμενον.

<margin>
Sic legendum hoc est, μονάδες πλείους, νῦν δὲ τὸ πλ. ἀλλὰ πλείω, perperam vtrumque.
</margin>

always is outside. The proof of this is as follows: for people say that even rings which lack a bezel are infinite, because there is always something outside to be taken: though this is by a certain similarity, and not properly. For it is necessary that this same thing is never taken over and above. In a circle, however, this does not happen: but what is taken next is always merely another thing. The <term>infinitum</term> <gloss>infinite</gloss> is, therefore, that which, in terms of quantity, always has something outside that can be taken: but that which has nothing outside it, is perfect and whole. For in this manner we are accustomed to define the whole, calling that a whole from which nothing at all is missing: as a whole man, or a whole basket. And as it is with each thing, so it is with that which is properly whole: such as the whole itself, of which nothing is outside. But if anything is missing from it, then whatever is missing means it is not a universe. The whole and the perfect are either entirely the same, or have a nature bordering upon one another. Nothing is perfect, however, which does not have an end. Wherefore it must be thought that Parmenides spoke better than Melissus. For the latter calls the infinite itself a whole; Parmenides, however, says the whole is finite, equidistant from the center. For it cannot happen that the infinite is joined to the whole and the universe, just as one thread is joined to another. From this, indeed, they receive this noble condition regarding the infinite, namely, that it contains all things, and embraces the universe within itself: for it has a certain similarity to the whole. For the infinite is the matter of the perfection of magnitude, and it is a whole in potentiality, but not in actuality. It is divisible, toward diminution and toward the opposite, addition, and it is a whole and finite, not of itself, but through another: and it does not contain, but insofar as it is infinite, it is contained. Wherefore it is also unknown, for the reason that it is infinite. For matter has no form. Wherefore it is clear that the infinite is subject to the reason of a part rather than a whole. For matter is a part of the whole, just as bronze is a part of a bronze statue. For if it contains in sensible and intelligible things, it ought also to contain intelligible things within the great and the small. But it is absurd, indeed, and impossible, that that which is unknown and indefinite should contain and define.

### CHAPTER VII.
*How, from the definition of the infinite, the account of those things which are said about the infinite is to be assigned.*

And yet, it happens with reason that that which consists in addition does not seem to be infinite in such a way that it surpasses every magnitude: but that which consists in division seems to be infinite in this way. For the infinite is contained within just as matter is, while form contains. It also happens with reason that, in number, toward the less, there is a minimum and an end: but toward the more, it always surpasses every multitude. In magnitude, however, the opposite occurs: toward the less, it surpasses every magnitude: but toward the greater, there is no infinite magnitude. These things happen because the one, whatever it may be, is indivisible; for one man is a man, not many. Number, however, is one, many, and certain quantities. Wherefore it is necessary to stand upon the indivisible. For two and three are denominative names: and each of the other numbers in a similar way. But toward the more, it happens that it can always be understood. For divisions of a magnitude into two parts are infinite. Wherefore it is in potentiality, but not in actuality: but that which is taken always surpasses every defined multitude. But this number of division is not separable, nor does the infinity remain: but it comes to be just like time and the number of time. In magnitudes, however, the opposite is true. For the continuous itself is indeed divided into infinite parts: but toward the greater, it is not infinite. For as much as it happens to be in potentiality, it also happens to be in actuality. Wherefore, since no sensible body is infinite, it does not happen that there is an excess over every defined magnitude. Otherwise, something would be greater than the heavens. The infinite itself is not the same in motion, magnitude, and time, as if it were one certain nature. But the later is said because of the earlier. Just as motion is called infinite because the magnitude over which it occurs, and which is altered or grows, is called so first, and time is called so because of the motion. And now indeed we are using these terms: but later we shall endeavor to say what each of these is, and why every magnitude is divisible into magnitudes. Nor does this account remove the contemplation of the mathematicians, which destroys the infinite in this way, so that it might go toward increment in actuality without transition. For they do not need the infinite now, nor do they use it, but they only postulate a line as finite as they wish: and it is permitted to divide any other magnitude by the same reason by which the largest magnitude is divided. Wherefore, in order to demonstrate that, it makes no difference at all that it exists among these magnitudes which are in the realm of reason. Since causes are distinguished into four, it is clear that the infinite is a cause as matter, and that its being is a privation: but the subject in itself is the continuous and sensible. All others also seem to use the infinite itself as matter. Wherefore it is also absurd, indeed, to assert that it is that which contains, and not that which is contained.

<column-break/>

And because outside, but that of which there is always something outside, this is infinite. A sign of this is that they even say that rings which do not have a bezel are infinite, because there is always something outside to take, speaking by a certain similarity, but not properly; for it is necessary that this should exist in this way, and that the same thing should never be taken. But in a circle, this does not happen, but the next thing is always merely another. Therefore, the infinite is that of which, as we take it according to quantity, there is always something outside to take. And that of which there is nothing outside, that is perfect and whole; for thus we define the whole, of which nothing is absent, such as a whole man or a whole chest. And as it is with each thing, so it is with that which is properly so; such as the whole, of which nothing is outside; but that from which something is outside, is not all, whatever is absent. The whole and the perfect are either entirely the same or near to each other in nature. Nothing is perfect that does not have an end; and the end is a boundary. Therefore, one must think that Parmenides spoke better than Melissus; for the former says the infinite is the whole; the latter, that the whole is bounded,
<margin>
* Equidistant from the center.
</margin>
for he would not join thread to thread to the universe and the whole, regarding the infinite; since from this they receive the majesty regarding the infinite, that it contains all things, and has the universe within itself, because it has a certain similarity to the whole; for the infinite is the matter of the perfection of magnitude, and it is a whole in potentiality, but not in actuality; and it is divisible, regarding the process of diminution and the reversed process of addition; but it is a whole and finite, not of itself, but according to another; and it does not contain, but is contained, insofar as it is infinite; wherefore it is also unknown, insofar as it is infinite. For matter has no form. So it is clear that the infinite is rather in the account of a part than in that of a whole; for matter is a part of the whole, just as bronze is of a bronze statue; since if the great and the small contain in sensible and intelligible things, they ought to contain intelligible things. But it is absurd and impossible for the unknown and the indefinite to contain and define.

<margin>
Parmenides said "the whole" [in these words]: "All things equal to the bulk of a sphere. Equidistant from the center everywhere."
</margin>

### CHAPTER VII.
*How one must make an account of those things that are always being infinitized from the definition of the infinite.*

It happens with reason that even that which is according to addition does not seem to be infinite in such a way as to surpass every magnitude; but toward division, it does surpass. For as matter is within, so is the infinite; but form contains. It happens reasonably that in number there is a limit toward the least; but toward the more, it always surpasses every multitude; but in magnitudes, the opposite is true; toward the less, it surpasses every magnitude; but toward the greater, there is no infinite magnitude. The cause is that the one is indivisible, whatever it may be, such as one man is one man, and not many; but number is more than one, and certain quantities; so it is necessary to stop at the indivisible; for two and three are denominative names, and in the same way, each of the other numbers; but toward the more, it is always possible to think; for the divisions of a magnitude are infinite; so it is in potentiality, but not in actuality; but the thing taken always surpasses every defined multitude; but this number of division is not separable, nor does the infinity remain, but it comes to be, just as time and the number of time. But in magnitudes, the opposite is true; for the continuous is divided into infinite parts. But toward the greater, it is not infinite. For as much as it is possible to be in potentiality, so much is it possible to be in actuality. So since no sensible magnitude is infinite, it is not possible for there to be an excess over every defined magnitude; for there would be something larger than the heavens. But the infinite is not the same in motion, and magnitude, and time, as if it were one certain nature, but the later is said according to the former; as, motion is [infinite], because the magnitude over which it moves, or is altered, or grows, [is so], and time [is so] because of the motion. Now we are using these, but later we shall say what each is, and why every magnitude is divisible into magnitudes. Nor does the account remove the contemplation of the mathematicians, destroying the infinite in such a way that it is in actuality toward increase, as if it were untraversable; for they do not need the infinite now, nor do they use it, but only [require it] to be finite, as much as they wish; and it is possible to cut the same proportion upon the largest magnitude with another magnitude of any size. So, regarding proving those things to them, it will make no difference that it exists among the existing magnitudes. And since causes are divided into four, it is clear that the infinite is a cause, and that its being is a privation, but the subject in itself is the continuous and sensible. And all others seem to use the infinite as matter; wherefore it is absurd to make it the container, and not the contained.

<margin>
This should be read thus: "monads more," but now "the multitude" is "but more," both are incorrect.
</margin>

<summary>Aristotle discusses the distinction between the infinite in potentiality and actuality, emphasizing that the infinite acts as matter—the container that is itself contained—rather than as a complete, formal whole. He explains how mathematical division and physical addition differ in their relationship to the infinite, concluding that the infinite is not a primary nature but a subordinate consequence of magnitude, motion, and time.</summary>

The <term>commander</term> <note>original: "chiliarchos," a Roman military tribune in charge of a cohort of about 1,000 men.</note> said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman?” He said, “Yes.” 28 The commander answered, “I bought this citizenship* for a large sum of money.” But Paul said, “But I was actually born a citizen.” 29 Immediately, therefore, those who were about to examine him withdrew from him; and the commander was also afraid, realizing that he was a Roman and that he had bound him. 30 On the next day, wishing to know for certain why he was being accused by the Jews, he released him and ordered the chief priests and the whole <term>Sanhedrin</term> <note>original: "synedrion," the supreme judicial and religious council of the Jews.</note> to assemble; and bringing Paul down, he placed him before them.

<margin>CAP. 23</margin>

1 Looking intently at the Council, Paul said, “Brothers, I have lived my life with a perfectly good conscience before God until this day.” 2 But the high priest Ananias ordered those standing near him to strike him on the mouth. 3 Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, you <term>whitewashed wall</term> <note>A metaphor for hypocrisy, referring to a wall that looks clean and sturdy on the outside but is structurally unsound or covers filth.</note>! Do you sit there *judging* <gloss>2. m. κρίνων</gloss> me according to the law, and yet, contrary to the law, you order me to be struck?” 4 Those standing by said, “Do you insult the high priest of God?” 5 Paul said, “I did not know, brothers, that he is the high priest; for it is written: ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’” 6 But when Paul perceived that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the Council, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees; I am on trial concerning the hope and the resurrection of the dead!” 7 When he had said this, a dispute *fell upon* <gloss>1. m. ἐπέπεσε</gloss> the Pharisees and Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. 8 For the Sadducees say there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. 9 There was a great outcry; and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ party stood up and argued forcefully, saying, “We find nothing wrong with this man; what if a spirit spoke to him...”

<summary>Paul avoids interrogation by revealing he is a Roman citizen by birth and later cleverly divides his accusers by highlighting the theological rift between Pharisees and Sadducees regarding the resurrection.</summary>

->679.—ANONYMOUS<-

->*On an Aqueduct at Assus*<-

All cities worship Axiochus, for, on his progress, like a god he has healed the ills of each. Especially on rugged Assus did he bestow running water, cutting through the hard face of many rocks. No longer run off to a distance, all ye travellers. I overflow with the cold water of Axiochus.

---

->680.—ANONYMOUS<-

->*On a Sea-side Garden at Antioch in which was a Bath*<-

Thou seest in me the three Graces, stranger. Poseidon wrought the one from the neighbouring sea, the second is the work of my garden rich in produce, and the remaining one is supplied by this bath.

---

->681.—LEONTIUS SCHOLASTICUS<-

->*On a Shell with a Carving of Aphrodite*<-

It is a great favour I grant thee, Dionysus. Cypris bathes in me, and from her I bring thee the cup.

---

->682.—ANONYMOUS<-

->*On the Obelisk in the Hippodrome*¹<-

It was only the Emperor Theodosius who undertook to raise the four-sided column which had ever lain a burden on the earth. He committed the task to Proclus,² and so great a column stood erect in thirty-two days.

I believe I can also ensure that Spinoza, Collins, and Hobbes would hardly have been amused by it. But so that one does not believe we have embellished the narration of this feast, we will place here, following our custom, the original words of the historian.

<note>original Latin: "On the last Sunday of the month of October, fifty honest prostitutes, called courtesans, held a supper with the Duke of Valentinois in his room in the Apostolic Palace. After supper, they danced with the servants and others present, first in their clothes, then naked. After supper, the table candlesticks with burning candles were placed on the floor, and chestnuts were thrown on the ground before the candlesticks, which the naked prostitutes gathered up on their hands and feet as they moved. The Pope, the Duke, and Lucrezia his sister were present and watching. Finally, gifts were displayed, silk tunics, pairs of shoes, caps, and other things for those who could carnally know the most of these prostitutes, who were carnally handled there in the hall publicly at the discretion of those present, and the gifts were distributed to the winners. ## ARTICLE I.

# LES VINGT-HUIT CONSTELLATIONS CHINOISES (BT),

# EUL-CHE-PA-SIEOU 二十八宿.

Les vingt-huit astérismes chinois se partagent en quatre groupes, renfermant chacun **7** constellations ; elles ont été scientifiquement classées dans l'ouvrage du P. Zottoli. *Cursus litteraturæ sinicæ*. Tom. II. p. 51. et dans le Calendrier-annuaire de Zi-ka-wei ; nous renvoyons le lecteur à ces données. Notre but ici est de donner les noms des esprits de chacune de ces constellations, l'influence heureuse ou néfaste de ces étoiles sur les principaux actes de la vie humaine, et les pronostics des astrologues, qui prétendent qu'elles influent sur la température et l'état atmosphérique, au point de produire les vents, les pluies ou le beau temps.

La notice sur chaque constellation sera divisée en trois alinéas.

1º Le nom de l'astérisme, auquel nous joindrons l'animal correspondant, sa classification d'après les cinq éléments *kin* 金, *mou* 木, *choei* 水, *houo* 火, *t'ou* 土, auxquels on ajoute : *je* 日 : le soleil, *yué* 月 : la lune.

Enfin le nom de l'esprit stellaire ; le tout d'après l'ouvrage taoïste : *Tseng-koang-yu-hia-ki* 增 廣 玉 匣 記 (1). ## ARTICLE I.

# THE TWENTY-EIGHT CHINESE CONSTELLATIONS (BT),

# EUL-CHE-PA-SIEOU 二十八宿.

The twenty-eight Chinese asterisms are divided into four groups, each containing **7** constellations; they have been scientifically classified in the work of Father Zottoli, <italic>Cursus litteraturæ sinicæ</italic>, Vol. II, p. 51, and in the <italic>Calendar-Yearbook of Zi-ka-wei</italic>; we refer the reader to these data. While previous folios focused on mechanical components like spindles and gears, these notes transition into the large-scale mechanics of the Earth—specifically how the movement of water and silt shifts the planet's center of gravity—and the physiological response of the eye to light.</meta>

### [THE SPHERE OF WATER AND THE CENTER OF THE WORLD. — OPTICS].

<margin>[Continuation of folio 14 recto:] (This is proven by viewing a white line on a black field with two eyes, one of which looks through a <term>blowpipe<note>original: "cier-bottana" (Italian) or "sarbacane" (French); a hollow tube used here as an optical aperture to restrict light.</note></term> and the other through the luminous air).</margin>

THE SURFACE OF THE SPHERE OF WATER ALWAYS BECOMES MORE DISTANT FROM THE CENTER OF THE WORLD —

This occurs because of the terrain carried by the floods of <term>turbid rivers<note>Rivers carrying a high load of suspended sediment or silt.</note></term>, which discharge the soil from their turbulence onto the sea shores and narrow the borders of that sea; furthermore, they raise its bottom, so that by necessity the surface of such an element must rise —

THE CENTER OF THE WORLD ALWAYS SHIFTS ITS POSITION *oppositely* WITHIN THE BODY OF THE EARTH, FLEEING *mo* TOWARD OUR HEMISPHERE —

This is demonstrated by the aforementioned terrain which is continually taken from the shores or the sides of mountains and carried to the seas; the more that is removed from here, the more it lightens, and consequently, the more it becomes heavy where such terrain is discharged by the marine waves; therefore, it is necessary that such a center changes its position.

---

THE SURFACE OF THE SPHERE OF WATER ALWAYS BECOMES MORE DISTANT FROM THE CENTER OF THE WORLD.

This takes place through the lands carried by the overflows of turbid rivers. These discharge the lands that cloud them onto the maritime shores and restrict the shore of the sea; besides this, they raise their bottom, so that by necessity the surface of such an element comes to rise.

THE CENTER OF [OUR] WORLD <note>1. See folio 17 recto.</note> ALWAYS CHANGES PLACE, *opposite to* WITHIN THE BODY OF THE EARTH, FLEEING *mo* TOWARD OUR HEMISPHERE.

This is shown by the aforementioned lands which are continually removed from the beaches [slopes] or sides of the mountains, and carried to the seas; the more that is removed, the more there is a lightening, and consequently, the more there is a weighing down where these lands are discharged by the marine waves; from then on, it is necessary that such a center changes its place.

<note>1. Leonardo is referring to the Earth's center of gravity. As weight (silt and earth) moves from the mountains to the ocean floor, the balance of the planet shifts, causing the geometric center and the gravitational center to move in relation to one another.</note>

<meta>This page continues the catechism of the Perfect Elect degree, transitioning from the symbolic journey through the corridor to the discovery of the "Lost Word" and the conclusion of the ritual drama regarding the assassins of Hiram Abiff.</meta>

<header>OF MASONRY.</header>

*Q.* What did you find before the Corridor?
*A.* A respectable <term>Elect</term>, who asked me for the password.
*Q.* How did you give it to him?
*A.* <term>Chibot</term> three times. <note>original: "Chibot." This is a phonetic variation of "Shibboleth," a Hebrew word meaning an ear of grain or a flowing stream, used as a password in several Masonic degrees.</note>
*Q.* What does the sacred vault contain?
*A.* The <term>Word</term>. <note>In Masonic tradition, the "Lost Word" represents divine truth or a secret name of God that was lost upon the death of the master builder, Hiram Abiff.</note>
*Q.* What is this word?
*A.* That which was lost in the ruins of the Temple.
*Q.* To whom was this word given in the first place?
*A.* To Moses, in a <term>burning bush</term>. <note>A reference to the biblical account in Exodus where God reveals His name to Moses.</note>
*Q.* To whom was it transmitted?
*A.* To the Perfect Elect alone.
*Q.* What was this word used for?
*A.* By those who sought the murderers of <term>Hiram</term>. <note>Hiram Abiff is the central character of Masonic allegory, the chief architect of King Solomon's Temple whose murder by three "unworthy craftsmen" forms the basis of the ritual.</note>
*Q.* Give it to me.
*A.* I cannot, <term>Most Respectable</term>. <note>original: "très-Respectable." This is the formal title used to address the Master of the Lodge in this degree.</note>
*Q.* Have you found the murderer?
*A.* I have punished him.
*Q.* Where did you find him?
*A.* In the dark cavern, near the fountain of <term>Siloam</term>. <note>original: "Siloé." This refers to the Pool of Siloam in Jerusalem, which in this ritual context serves as the setting for the capture of the assassins.</note>
*Q.* In what posture was he?
*A.* In this one, Most Respectable,
*(while performing it.)*

Nous les avons pris pour des vertèbres lombaires: voilà donc trois sortes de vertèbres.

3º. Outre les vertèbres contenues dans ces deux blocs il y a encore un nombre considérable de vertèbres ou de fragments de vertèbres détachés. Parmi celles-ci il s'en trouve 5 à 6 qui ont d'apophyses semblables aux grandes vertèbres du premier bloc, plusieurs à 3 apophyses comme celles que nous avons regardées comme vertèbres lombaires; & un beaucoup plus grand nombre encore de vertèbres oblongues pareilles à celles dont le grand bloc en contient cinq. Ces vertèbres oblongues font une suite décroissante interrompue ça & là à cause des vertèbres égarées & qui va se terminer presque en pointe. La somme totale de toutes les vertèbres disposées par l'école centrale monte à plus de 80. Il en existe encore plusieurs entre les mains de quelques particuliers qui les ont eu des ouvriers avant que l'acquisition fût faite par l'école. Je me flatte que la plus part au moins de ces particuliers donneront au Cabinet les vertèbres qu'ils possèdent. Jusqu'ici on n'a trouvé autant que je sais que quatre dents, dont une & les fragments d'une autre se trouvent au cabinet. Elles sont creuses jusqu'à la pointe qui est un peu recourbée. La comparaison de ces dents avec les superbes machoires qui sont à paris suffira seule pour prouver contre ce que le C. <term>Faujas</term> a dit dans sa lettre que l'animal dont il s'agit & celui dont la tête est à Paris sont de différentes espèces.

Il y a un os dans un petit bloc que quelques uns regardent comme une côte & d'autres comme un tibia. Voilà en gros ce qui est déposé au Cabinet.

On a trouvé depuis un autre bloc & plusieurs ossements détachés. Dans ce bloc il y a une suite de dix vertèbres, disposées comme dans l'animal vivant, leur hauteur est de 16 lignes, celle de chacune des vertèbres de notre grand bloc. Leurs <term>apophyses epineuses</term> sont aussi plus larges & longues de six pouces. A côté de ces vertèbres on voit les empreintes de 9 côtes, d'une partie de côte longue de 8 à 9 pouces. J'ai été bien fâché en voyant qu'on avait scié ce bloc à l'endroit des côtes & qu'aucune cote n'a été conservée entière; mais les ouvriers disent que cela leur a été impossible vu l'état de consomption dans lequel se trouvent les côtes à cause des infiltrations des

<column-break/>

eaux qui ont eu lieu à cet endroit. Ils disent que ces côtes avaient plus de trois pieds de long & qu'elles se sont mises en pièce dès qu'ils les ont touché ce qui parait croyable, car j'ai trouvé des ossements détachés entièrement friables. Le morceau de côte qui se trouve dans le bloc est presque rond très peu applatis & ayant une courbure. Parmi les ossements qui sont encore à sécher il se trouve cinq ou six vertèbres tout à fait différentes de celles qui se trouvent au Cabinet. Elles paraissent avoir été les vertèbres du cou. L'apophyse epineuse y est bien prononcée, & les apophyses transverses d'une forme différente de celle des vertèbres que nous avons pris pour lombaires. Dans une les transverses sont terminées par une surface convexe inégale. Parmi les ossements & leurs débris il y a encore quelques vertèbres à trois apophyses semblables à celles que nous avons appellées lombaires. Il y a aussi deux fragments qui paraissent des parties de deux <term>Omoplates</term>.

translation:
We have taken them for lumbar vertebrae: here, then, are three kinds of vertebrae.

3. Besides the vertebrae contained in these two blocks, there is also a considerable number of detached vertebrae or fragments of vertebrae. Among these, there are 5 to 6 that have processes similar to the large vertebrae of the first block, several with 3 processes like those we regarded as lumbar vertebrae, and a much larger number still of oblong vertebrae similar to those of which the large block contains five. These oblong vertebrae form a decreasing series, interrupted here and there because of lost vertebrae, which ends almost in a point. The total sum of all the vertebrae arranged by the central school amounts to more than 80. There are still several in the hands of some private individuals who obtained them from the workers before the acquisition was made by the school. I flatter myself that most of these individuals, at least, will give the vertebrae they possess to the Cabinet <note>referring to a museum or scientific collection</note>. So far, as far as I know, only four teeth have been found, one of which—and the fragments of another—are in the Cabinet. They are hollow up to the point, which is slightly curved. The comparison of these teeth with the superb jaws that are in Paris will alone suffice to prove, contrary to what Citizen <term>Faujas</term> <gloss>Barthélemy Faujas de Saint-Fond, a French geologist</gloss> said in his letter, that the animal in question and the one whose head is in Paris are of different species.

There is a bone in a small block that some regard as a rib and others as a tibia. This is, in general, what is deposited in the Cabinet.

Another block and several detached bones have been found since. In this block, there is a sequence of ten vertebrae, arranged as in the living animal; their height is 16 lines <note>a French unit of measurement, approximately 36 millimeters</note>, that of each of the vertebrae of our large block. Their <term>apophyses épineuses</term> <gloss>spinous processes</gloss> are also wider and six inches long. Beside these vertebrae, one sees the impressions of 9 ribs, and part of a rib 8 to 9 inches long. I was very sorry to see that this block had been sawed at the place of the ribs and that no rib has been preserved whole; but the workers say that this was impossible for them given the state of consumption in which the ribs are found due to the infiltration of

<column-break/>

waters that occurred in that place. They say that these ribs were more than three feet long and that they broke into pieces as soon as they touched them, which seems credible, for I have found detached bones that were entirely friable. The piece of rib that is found in the block is almost round, very slightly flattened, and has a curvature. Among the bones that are still drying, there are five or six vertebrae quite different from those that are in the Cabinet. They appear to have been the vertebrae of the neck. The spinous process is well pronounced, and the transverse processes are of a different form from those of the vertebrae that we took for lumbar. In one, the transverse processes are terminated by an uneven convex surface. Among the bones and their debris, there are also some vertebrae with three processes similar to those we called lumbar. There are also two fragments that appear to be parts of two <term>Omoplates</term> <gloss>shoulder blades/scapulae</gloss>.

<meta>Decorative initial letter B containing a human face.</meta>Blessed be this gossip of mine, at least she says it as she understands it, and she understands it very well according to me. Since Pilucca affirms that the husband is dead; she says she wants another, and without the advice of relatives, young, foreign, and poor, and, to the reasons she assigns, she seems to me a wise woman, and a great fool this Gisippo would seem to me, whom she says she has already had tempted, if he did not take her. It feels like a thousand years to me that she passes by the shop here, as she is accustomed to every day, to make this match for the gossip: Here he is with that foreigner. The gossip does not have bad taste, no, a cover just right for widows. Have you found that friend of yours, a good man?

Dem. I have found M. Gisippo here, who is that same one.

Bar. I like him, but with your leave I would like to tell him a few words apart.

Camillo Paderni was one of the first into whose hands these papyri fell (a).

**892-909 + 917-928 + 910-916.** Altri segni della persistenza in noi, sia pure inconsciamente, dell'idea che dopo morte un certo senso sopravvive: noi piangiamo la morte di persona cara come una sventura toccatagli, come perdita e privazione delle dolcezze della vita — quasi che vi sia privazione o perdita laddove ogni bisogno o desiderio è spento. Ed anche quando nei nostri lamenti confessiamo bensì che non fu sventura la morte per la persona a noi cara e partita, fu anzi per essa l'entrare nella pace e nella tranquillità d'un sonno perenne, al riparo d'ogni cura o affanno; ma a questa sua pace contrapponiamo il nostro dolore, e in certo modo lo difendiamo come giusto, anche allora cadiamo in contraddizione; poichè in fondo consideriamo sempre come cosa dolorosa ciò che non ha nulla di doloroso, come è appunto, per nostra esperienza, quel sonno al quale facciamo simile la morte, durante il quale nessuna cosa della vita vegliata ci tocca. Anzi, se non consideriamo punto un male la sospensione imperfetta del sentire, che è nel sonno, perchè nel non sentire non c'è privazione o desiderio di alcun che; tanto meno sarà un male la morte, in cui è annullato affatto il sentire, e quindi è completa l'assenza di privazione o desiderio. Ma anche in tutt'altre manifestazioni s'annida, sebben meno evidente, sebbene ancora più inconscio, il cieco stimolo. È voce frequente — ed è voce anche di epicurei: "Breve è la vita e corre irrevocabile al suo fine; godiamo, dunque, e sollazziamoci il più che possiamo, fin ch'è tempo.", Chi parla così contrappone in cuor suo alla vita la futura privazione; pensa dunque ancora, melanconicamente, che la futura nostra non esistenza sarà appunto uno stato di privazione — che avremo sete e non potremo bere. Il sapiente gode la vita misuratamente e saggiamente; sa che non la quantità ma la qualità del piacere ha valore; e convinto soprattutto che l'esser morto è a lui cosa al tutto indifferente, non si cura punto dell'al di là della vita, non dà luogo nell'animo suo a nessuna speranza o timore rispetto a quel tempo, ma entro i termini della vita circoscrive il suo pensiero nel porre la regola della vita. That there was also the custom of cremation is useless to point out, and the previous verse refers to it. The poor, instead, were buried, and without a coffin, even if transported to the burial inside one. **892-909 + 917-928 + 910-916.** Other signs of the persistence in us, albeit unconsciously, of the idea that after death a certain sense survives: we weep for the death of a dear person as a misfortune that has befallen them, as a loss and deprivation of the sweetness of life—as if there were deprivation or loss where every need or desire is extinguished. And even when in our lamentations we indeed confess that death was not a misfortune for the dear departed person, but rather that it was for them an entry into the peace and tranquility of a perennial sleep, sheltered from every care or distress; but to this peace of theirs we contrast our grief, and in a certain way defend it as just, even then we fall into contradiction; because, at bottom, we always consider as a painful thing that which has nothing painful in it, as is precisely, by our experience, that sleep to which we liken death, during which no thing of the waking life touches us. Indeed, if we do not consider the imperfect suspension of feeling, which is in sleep, a evil at all, because in non-feeling there is no deprivation or desire for anything; much less will death be an evil, in which feeling is entirely annulled, and therefore the absence of deprivation or desire is complete. But the blind stimulus also hides in all other manifestations, even if less evident, even if still more unconscious. It is a frequent voice—and it is also the voice of Epicureans: "Life is short and runs irrevocably to its end; let us enjoy, therefore, and amuse ourselves as much as we can, while there is time." He who speaks thus contrasts in his heart the future deprivation with life; he thinks, therefore, still, melancholically, that our future non-existence will be precisely a state of deprivation—that we will be thirsty and will not be able to drink. The wise man enjoys life moderately and wisely; he knows that not the quantity but the quality of pleasure has value; and convinced above all that being dead is to him a matter of total indifference, he does not care at all about the beyond of life, he does not give place in his soul to any hope or fear regarding that time, but within the terms of life he circumscribes his thought in setting the rule of life. We yearn for this, for our dwelling which is in heaven, and we long to be clothed with it, for we would rather be clothed than unclothed. For as long as we are at home in the body, we are on a pilgrimage away from the Lord.

Therefore, my dear wife, watch diligently that you finish the time of your <term>pilgrimage</term> <gloss>the earthly life of a believer</gloss> with fear and trembling. Not with such fear and trembling that we should fear or tremble before the world, or because they are so furious with us, but we shall fear and tremble before the <term>Lord</term> <gloss>God/Christ</gloss>, so that we shall keep his commandments and laws. And thus, finishing the time of our <note>original: "pelgrimagie"</note> pilgrimage in the fear of the Lord, and bringing the end of our faith—namely, the salvation of our souls—we shall rejoice eternally with the <term>Lord</term> <gloss>God/Christ</gloss>, and then we shall meet him in the resurrection of the dead.

Therefore, do not fear the world, for the hairs of your head are all counted. They have no power, unless it is given to them from above. <margin>Francis Drake, in the South Sea.</margin>
When Lord Francis Drake had entered the South Sea through the Strait of Magellan on the 6th of September 1578, he was driven by a heavy storm with his ships southward to the latitude of 55 and one-third degrees. This may be seen in more detail in his own voyage description, but when the storm had passed, he returned to the mouth of the aforementioned Strait.

On the 1st of October, the ship *Elizabeth*, one of our fleet commanded by Captain Winter, passed out of our sight and returned home through the narrow passage of the Strait, as we later heard upon arriving in our fatherland, and as he himself reported in his travel account.

<margin>Had a sloop manned with 8 men, with orders to remain near the ship.</margin>
<margin>Which lost the ship due to bad weather</margin>

We received orders to attend to the ship wherever it might have need of us. They gave us only one day of provisions in the sloop, without a chart or compass. Poot, die, in eenen lagen en eenvou-digen staat geboren en opgevoed, alles van de Natuur ontvangen had, wat tot de ware Digtkunde vereischt word; die geene onderwyzingen behoefde om, door fraa-ye vindingen en stoute trekken, te behagen en te ver-rukken; maar wiens ryk vernuft slegts eenige beschaving noodig had, om zodanigen, die ook netheid van taal en spreekwyzen begeerden, verwondering in te boeze-men. —— Eene korte beschouwing van zyn leven zal ons doen zien, hoe hy door naarstigheid zynen aangeboren geest met veele wetenswaardige byzonderheden verrykt heeft, die hem egter dien trap van vorderingen, tot wel-ken hy gekomen is, niet zouden hebben doen bereiken, ware hy door zyne natuurlyke begaafdheden niet geschikt geweest om uit te munten.

We do not need to look outside our own Homeland to find an excellent example to support this observation. One need only think of our distinguished countryman Hubert Kornelisz. Poot, who, born and raised in a low and simple station, received everything from Nature that is required for true poetry <note>original: "Digtkunde," the art and theory of poetic composition</note>. He needed no formal instruction to please and delight through beautiful inventions and bold strokes. His rich genius required only a measure of refinement to inspire wonder in those who also desired precision in language and expression. A brief examination of his life will show us how he, through diligence, enriched his innate spirit with many noteworthy details. However, these efforts would not have allowed him to reach the heights he attained if he had not been suited by his natural talents to excel.

Hubert Kornelisz. Poot was born on the 29th of January in the year 1689. His birthplace was Abtswoude, an outlying area situated between the City of Delft and the Village of Ketel. His parents, Kornelis Poot and Katharina Groenheide, were honest and simple people. While they had not accumulated great wealth, they were nevertheless blessed with prosperity in their agriculture. From their marriage they had, besides the son of whom we intend to speak in more detail, four daughters, one of whom died very young. Powers are always established for protection;
But you abuse your power: for you, oh evil force!
Have made those you should help cringe before your weapons.
One may not use the power of the Land against the land.
Whoever draws the sword against friends is guilty of treason.

    The Winter has thereupon retreated to the harsh North:

You who give dear life to all that inhabits the earth,
To what hides in the water and appears in the air,
Be welcome in this court, full of half-destroyed trees.

He who created the weather is stronger than the weather.

And this is essentially the distinction that the large Mennonite <term>Mennonite — 'Doopsgezinde', literally 'baptism-minded'; the name preferred by the group to emphasize their focus on adult baptism over the more controversial history of 'Anabaptism'</term> Congregations emphasize when they wish to be relieved of the name *Anabaptists* <term>Anabaptists — 'Wederdoopers', or 're-baptizers'; a term associated with radical movements which these groups sought to distance themselves from</term>. Meanwhile, I am told of examples (*), of Frisian Teachers <note>original: "Vriesfche Leeraers"; referring to ministers or elders in the Frisian Mennonite tradition</note> who, a long time after they had been baptized in their Congregation, came to the thought that no Baptism was proper unless received by Immersion; and who, for that reason, had themselves baptized anew among the Collegiants <term>Collegiants — a Dutch religious group that practiced adult baptism by immersion and valued individual conscience over formal creeds</term>: nevertheless, they have retained their ministry. For the rest, this position remains firm among them: that whoever wishes to become a Member among them must have been baptized in their mature age (†). <meta>This page continues the technical discussion on the timing of Vedic rituals, specifically transitioning from the general rules of lunar days (tithis) to the specific observances of the month of Shravana, including the sacred thread renewal (Upakarma) and the festival of Raksha Bandhan.</meta>

### Ritual Timings and the Month of Shravana

Whether the ritual offerings should be performed on the earlier day or when there is a partial contact with the required time is a matter of debate; however, **Hemadri** <note>Hemadri Pant, a 13th-century scholar and author of the influential legal digest *Chaturvarga Chintamani*</note> argues for the earlier day. In the *Nirnaya-amrita* <note>a treatise on ritual timings</note>, it is decided that for the followers of the **Yajur Veda** <term>Yajur-shakhina</term> <note>practitioners of one of the four primary Vedas, focusing on sacrificial formulas</note>, the ritual of the herbs <note>part of the Upakarma ceremony</note> should be performed on the following day. 

In the *Rama-koshtaka* <note>an astrological or ritual manual</note>, the preference for the earlier day's pervasion is explicitly stated. Regarding new **Brahmacharis** <note>a student of Vedic knowledge who has undergone the Upanayana initiation</note>, the initiation into the study is mentioned here, though not its completion. Shaving the head is prescribed as a duty for these students and others authorized to perform the ritual.

The **Full Moon of Shravana** <term>Shravani Purnamasi</term> <note>the full moon day of the lunar month Shravana, marking the height of the monsoon</note> is the time for the ritual of **Pavitrarpana** <note>the offering of "pavitra" or consecrated silk/cotton threads to the deity</note>; this is a family duty that must be performed despite any minor ritual defects. On this day, the ceremonial oil bath is mandatory. On this same day, provided it is free from the influence of **Bhadra** <note>an inauspicious astrological period during which certain rituals are avoided</note>, the ritual of **Raksha Bandhan** <note>the "bond of protection," where protective threads are tied around the wrist</note> must be performed. For the **Shravana** ritual <note>the Upakarma</note>, it should be performed at sunset for those to be initiated. If the lunar day is partial, it may be performed during the remainder of the period.

<column-break/>

### The Festivals of Ganesha and Shitala

The annual **Sankata Chaturthi** <note>the "Fourth Day of Crisis," a fast dedicated to removing obstacles</note> is known as the day of the **Appearance of Ganesha**. This day should be observed when the fourth lunar day pervades the time of moonrise. If moonrise occurs during that lunar day on two consecutive days, the former day is chosen. 

However, **Madhava** <note>Madhavacharya, the 14th-century scholar and influential commentator</note> states that if the lunar day pervades the time when the ritual actually begins, the later day should be accepted. Regarding the third and fourth lunar days, they are preferred when they pervade the appropriate time; if they pervade both days, the former is chosen. 

For the **Shitala Vrata** <note>a ritual dedicated to Goddess Shitala, the "Cool One," to ward off smallpox and fevers</note> on the seventh lunar day, the earlier day should be taken. For the eighth lunar day <note>Ashtami</note> of the dark fortnight of **Shravana**, the day that pervades midnight should be accepted.

### Here is the <term>Svalpajataka</term> <gloss>Little Book of Birth</gloss>:

**"Here, etc."**: The subsequent verse is from another work. (43)

**"Whichever, etc."**: By the word "etc.," connections through trines and the like should be understood. The connection with the ascendant is the presence of the lord of the house in the ascendant, in an angle from it, or by its aspect. Otherwise, only the connection of the houses with the ascendant is certain. (43)

**"Of the planets, etc."**: They are spoken of in two verses. (44)

**"For benefics, etc."**: "Abhimati" is the enemy, the sixth house. Among these twelve houses. "Dharmatmaja" are the ninth and fifth. Among these three—the ascendant, the fifth, and the ninth—the auspicious or inauspicious result is the auspicious result for the good, and the inauspicious result for the bad. When the ascendant, fifth, and ninth are associated with benefics, there is prosperity even for other houses like wealth. When those three have malefic influences, there is generally a loss of others, is the meaning. (44)

**"Copper, etc."**: Even though it is stated that malefics are favorable in the sixth house, in the case of questions about disease and the like, they are unfavorable. This means they are auspicious in questions regarding work and the like. (45)

**"Here, etc."**: Here, in the matter of contemplating the house.

Lord Krishna said: There is no destruction, O Arjuna, for a yogi either here or hereafter. A transcendentalist is never put to grief, My dear friend. (6.40)

The less evolved unsuccessful yogi is reborn in the house of the pious and prosperous after attaining heaven and living there for many years. The highly evolved unsuccessful yogi does not go to heaven, but is born in a spiritually advanced family. A birth like this is very difficult, indeed, to obtain in this world. (6.41-42)

There he or she regains the knowledge acquired in the previous life, and strives again to achieve perfection, O Arjuna. (6.43)

**The unsuccessful yogi is instinctively carried towards God by virtue of the impressions of yogic practices of previous lives. Even the inquirer of yoga — the union with God — surpasses those who perform Vedic rituals. (6.44)**

The yogi, who diligently strives, becomes completely free from all imperfections after gradually perfecting through many incarnations, and reaches the Supreme Abode. (6.45)

->**WHO IS THE BEST YOGI**<-

The yogi, who is devoted to meditation, is superior to the ascetics. The yogi is superior to the Vedic scholars. The yogi is superior to the ritualists. Therefore, O Arjuna, be a yogi. (6.46)

**And I consider the yogi-devotee — who lovingly contemplates on Me with supreme faith, and whose mind is ever absorbed in Me — to be the best of all the yogis. (See also 12.02 and 18.66) (6.47)**

# Sāṃkhyasūtravṛttiḥ

The reasoning that "I have pain in my head, I have pleasure in my foot" is used to suggest the all-pervasiveness of the mind; however, the lack of simultaneous perception is due to the sequential movement of the subtle mind. All-pervasiveness is not proven by this. 69

He states another refutation:

Because of the scripture regarding its activity. 70

"Because of its activity" indicates the inference. "Because of the scripture of movement" indicates the text. 70

He addresses the argument that even if it is atomic, it will be eternal due to the absence of a cause:

It is not without parts, because of its combination, like a pot and the like. 71

It is not without parts, it is not without a cause. "Because of its combination"—because of the combination of parts. What is the cause of this? <term>Ahaṅkāra</term> <gloss>ego-principle</gloss>. The fact that atoms have parts is proven by the simultaneous connection with a six-fold [aggregate]. Therefore, the mind is non-eternal, like a pot. 71

He states the division between eternal and non-eternal:

Everything other than <term>prakṛti</term> and <term>puruṣa</term> is non-eternal. 72

This is clear. 72

He addresses the question: how is everything non-eternal, given that time, space, and so on are eternal?

There is no acquisition of parts for that which has parts, because of the scripture that it is without parts. 73

There is no acquisition of a cause for that which has parts—meaning the primordial cause of the world—because of the scriptural statement "Being the root cause, it has no other cause." 73

He refutes the idea that liberation is the manifestation of bliss:

Liberation is not the manifestation of bliss, because it is devoid of qualities. 74

For as much as a world is lacking, it is severed, and all temporal life <term>chayei sha'ah</term> <gloss>temporary life</gloss> is consumed by eternal life <term>chayei olam</term> <gloss>eternal life</gloss>. This exists in all those who are related, and so forth. For when it spreads into the aspect of the distinct—that is, the soul <term>nefesh</term> <gloss>the lowest of the five levels of the soul</gloss> which spreads into the aspect of the distinct—because the side of the soul in the distinct aspect, which had an <term>ontology</term> <gloss>a state of being</gloss> and is a form unto itself, is an emanation into the aspect of temporal life, not as a force within the body. And so they are consumed and nullified from above, the dead who are the female, the emanation of temporal life. There is a theory of <term>ontology</term> <margin>from the soul</margin> and the virtue that when this is severed by death, death is eternal life. This is not the case for the beast <term>chayah</term> <gloss>animal/beast</gloss>, which lacks <term>ontology</term> in knowledge, for its virtue was to be emanated into temporal life, and since it is only time, the power is emanated through eternal life. And this is why the beast is lacking in the wisdom of emanation, in contrast to man and his vitality. It is also lacking in the vitality of the virtue to enliven the virtue. Therefore, there is a lack in vitality regarding the wisdom that is in essence, for he is wise in the wisdom of conduct. And in the beast, that which has less wisdom of clarification, it is providence. And upon this virtue, it had a very high aspect and little vitality in the virtue of the beginning. And there is a lack also from the side and the wisdom of the Torah. Rightly, the side in man has no value of wisdom of the beast, even though they are among the side regarding the side of the beast. And thus, it has a matter in intellect, for this emanation is through eternal life. And therefore the Sages of blessed memory said: "They spoke of eternal life and are occupied with temporal life." And one must say from now on regarding Solomon, to whom the Holy One, blessed be He, said, "Ask what I shall give you," and he requested a heart to understand between good and evil; the King explained to him why he was lacking with Him and did not have it, and he asked for a good heart. And it seems that the language is that wisdom, understanding, knowledge, strength, loving-kindness, mercy, and judgment are upon the evil side, even though there were many lacks, he asked for wisdom and understanding.

And the essence of the Tetragrammaton is mentioned, that there is the ascent that belongs to the light in the Torah. It was considered that the Tetragrammaton is the root of the souls of Israel, for it is in the aspect of the Tetragrammaton, as in the souls—it was clean and pure, but until the end of the ascent, and they grasped it further. 

And there is from another side an aspect which is the aspect of the body in the world. We can say the Torah, which is a part, for the root of the soul are the mystery of the letters of the Torah. <meta>This page continues the allegorical interpretation of Song of Songs, moving from the description of the various social classes to the merits of the Jewish people that make them worthy of the Divine Presence. The previous page discussed the four classes of people in exile; this page explains how the acceptance of the Torah and the merit of the Patriarchs allow for the "ascent" from the wilderness.</meta>

# Song of Songs

<header>Song of Songs</header>
<sig>I 6 h</sig>
<page-num>21</page-num>
<meta>catchword: And therefore</meta>

Among them are those who are compassionate, making a place for the Divine Presence <note>original: *Shekhinah*</note> to dwell among them, having received it from ancient days. This refers to the acceptance of the Torah. For "Who is this?" <note>Song of Songs 3:6</note> implies that while all the other nations refused to accept it, Israel did. This is a great merit that draws the Divine Presence down to the lower worlds. This is as the Sages taught in *Midrash Rabbah* on the verse, "And let them take for Me an offering" <note>Exodus 25:2</note>, using the parable of a king who had an only daughter, and so on. This means the "bed" <note>a metaphor for the place of union with God</note> exists because the acceptance of the Torah causes the Divine Presence to dwell. 

This is the secret of "Who is this... coming up from the wilderness?" <note>Song of Songs 3:6</note> It asks: what is the cause of her elevation and ascent from the wilderness? It is because of the "wilderness"—namely, the reception of the Torah there, as is explained. If so, the worthiness of their merit is clear, reaching unto the heavens. This is the secret of the phrase "like pillars of smoke"; by this power, they are worthy of this high level. Furthermore, she possesses the "merit of the ancestors" <note>term: *Zechut Avot* — the spiritual credit inherited from the righteousness of the Patriarchs</note>, a great and strong center that gives power and strength to the "branches" of the tribe. 

This is the secret of "perfumed with myrrh and frankincense, with all the powders of the merchant." As our Sages of blessed memory interpreted: 
"Myrrh" refers to our father Abraham; just as myrrh is the head of all spices, so was our father Abraham the head of all the righteous. 
"Frankincense" refers to our father Isaac, who was offered up like a handful of frankincense upon the altar. 
"All the powders of the merchant" refers to our father Jacob, whose "bed was complete" <note>original: *mitato shelemah*; a traditional idiom meaning all of his children were righteous and none were rejected</note>, and no defect <unclear>like this</unclear> was found in them. For they are compassionate in all matters of holiness, and it is fitting that you should take pity on the body of Jerusalem, that you should receive the Divine Presence, about which I have adjured you.

It is also possible that "perfumed with myrrh and frankincense" refers to the parts of the Torah. The Written Torah contains two parts: positive commandments and negative commandments. The negative commandments are likened to "myrrh" <note>original: *mor*</note>, as the Sages said that anyone who harvests it finds their hands are embittered; so too a person is embittered and finds it difficult to turn away from the pleasure of sins and their indulgence. Regarding the positive commandments, he says "frankincense," for they are sweet, heartening to the soul, and supportive of it. And regarding the Oral Torah, which consists of the words of the seeker and the wise, he says "and from all the powders of the merchant."

---

### Behold the bed of Solomon; sixty warriors are around it, of the warriors of Israel. <note>Song of Songs 3:7</note>

He also mentioned a great preparation for this attachment: the place where the Divine Presence dwells in the lower realms. This ensures that the ministering angels will have no cause to complain. He calls it "the bed of Solomon," meaning the Holy Temple <note>original: *Beit HaMikdash*</note>. He calls it a "bed" because just as a bed is designated for the union of husband and wife, so the Temple is designated to maintain the union of the Holy One, Blessed be He, with the Assembly of Israel here below. It is fitting that this "bed" be made with perfect intention, directed toward the dwelling place of the Name, may He be blessed, and the dwelling of His strength. 

It is also written that "sixty warriors" surround it. This refers to all the priestly watches, all the Levite watches, and the twelve divisions of Israel. As they said in the Midrash, they are all righteous and "warriors" in their ability to conquer their internal desires <note>term: *Yetzer Hara* — the "evil inclination" or base impulse</note>. This is the meaning of "warriors of Israel." Their merit is sufficient to sustain the matter and to guard Israel, even if the community as a whole lacks merit. All of this is an argument against the angels—that God's submission to dwell below is not purely an act of unearned grace, for there indeed exists the merit of these individuals, and these merits cause the fulfillment of His word, as we have said.

---

### They all hold swords, expert in war; every man has his sword upon his thigh, because of fear in the night. <note>Song of Songs 3:8</note>

He explained the strength of the aforementioned "warriors": they are warriors against their own desires. They are always standing armed on guard so that the inclination does not overcome them and cause them to stumble, even slightly...

---

<summary>This page provides an allegorical interpretation of Song of Songs 3:6-8, linking the imagery of spices and warriors to the Torah, the Patriarchs, and the spiritual guards of the Holy Temple. It emphasizes that Israel's merit comes from accepting the Torah and overcoming internal moral struggles.</summary>
<keywords>Song of Songs, Solomon's Bed, Holy Temple, Patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Torah, Myrrh, Frankincense, Divine Presence, Shekhinah, Evil Inclination, Priestly Watches, Midrash Rabbah</keywords>

This is the intention of Hippocrates in his statement: "until it happens in it, it came out and blood flowed from it." The word "blood" is applied in two meanings: one is the aggregate of the humors, which is what came out at that time; and the second is the humor that is one of the four known ones. And the liquid at the time of surgery, even if it is not blood in this meaning, it is a metaphor indicating its existence in the body, because nothing else comes out with the remaining humors. His statement: "as long as he breathes, he inhales air and it exits in breathing," its meaning is as long as he has the effect of that action according to custom. For what counts as that is only with the soundness of one of the four. And there is no impossibility then that the body is missing one of the four, because the four, as for their necessity in the body, is because they are the limbs.

<summary>The author clarifies the two meanings of the word "blood" as used by Hippocrates—the aggregate of humors versus the specific humor—and discusses the role of breathing as a sign of life and constitutional balance.</summary>

...is of the nature of persuasive arguments. It has been their habit, and the habit of others among the pillars of wisdom—especially the early ones—to provide "reminders" <term>tanbīhāt</term> <gloss>intuitive pointers</gloss> regarding philosophical objectives. These may suffice for the seeker of perfection, even if they are not understood by the people of imagination. 

Others have imagined their pre-existence <term>qidam</term> <gloss>eternity</gloss> without the body. The mentioned proof only negates their pre-existence as abstracted from all bodies. Rather, their existence—not their pre-existence—by way of **transmigration** <term>tanāsukh</term> is not proven by demonstration, as reported from the commentator of *The Intimations*. Perhaps he had a delusion there and did not know that if they were, as they claimed, united in eternity before all bodies, what led them to depart from the **Holy World** <term>‘ālam al-quds</term> and Life—meaning pure abstraction, which is characterized by transcendence over material deficiencies and intellectual life—and to attach to the world of death and darkness—meaning the body, which is subject to natural death and material deficiencies? And who coerced the eternal and imprisoned it by attachment to the personal body, which is like a partner to it? And how was it subjugated to raise the nursing infant, or even the fetus, until it was drawn from the world of holiness and light to its body? 

All of these are persuasive reminders. He pointed to the demonstrative aspect by saying: "How was some of it distinguished from others in eternity?" Its explanation is that if they were eternal, they would either be multiple or one. Both have been shown to be false due to their agreement in species and its concomitants. As he said: "Their species is unified." Likewise for the third possibility, because if that "other" <note>the differentiator</note> were the subject or matter and its accidents, he pointed to its falsehood by saying: "There is no place, neither essentially nor accidentally, nor substrate"—meaning no matter and no subject. And if it were an inherent state within it, he indicated this by saying: "There is neither action nor passion before the body, nor acquired attributes" as occurs after the body—meaning after the attachment to the body is severed. For their individuation through those acquired traits <term>malakāt</term> is, in their view, a truth. Some of the "people of taste" <note>mystics/gnostics</note> said that these...

<margin></margin>
<unclear>state</unclear> within it. And the animal: the souls become individuated after their abstraction; rather, the abstracted lights are absolutely distinguished by the levels specific to them in terms of intensity, weakness, perfection, and deficiency. These do not add to their specific essences except conceptually. For the more intense light is not distinguished from the weaker light except by the specificity of the simple identity. And those acquired identities, if they are made additional to the soul and accidental to it in the knowledge of those specificities, then their individuation is in reality by that identity itself, not by those states that reveal it.
</margin>

<margin></margin>
<unclear>That is</unclear>, since the spirits were pure lights, and luminous things are not distinguished except by intensity, weakness, perfection, and deficiency—as in sensible lights—it must be that the spirits in eternity were distinguished by perfection and deficiency, etc.
</margin>

<margin></margin>
It is not hidden that this does not repel what he mentioned of the falsehood of multiplicity.
</margin>

translation:
<meta>continues from previous page: ...if the result were</meta>
<margin>
Because if it were not a statement, it would not be a proposition, and if it were not a proposition, it would not be a syllogism.
</margin>

<margin>
The truth is that the intent of "statement" is the intellectual meaning.
</margin>

...one of them, it would not lead to a syllogism. Every statement that is such is not a syllogism. This is how the Sheikh <note>Avicenna</note> mentioned it in *The Healing* <term>al-Shifāʾ</term>. 

It has been said that if this were not considered, it would necessitate that any two propositions would be a syllogism, however they were, because they would necessitate one of them <gloss>meaning they are identical</gloss>. But the necessity of the whole for the part is prohibited, because the meaning of "necessitating from them" is that each one of them must have a role in achieving that result, and neither of them has a role in achieving the other. 

If it is said: This definition applies to the composite proposition that necessitates its converse and its contrapositive, yet it is not called a syllogism. The answer is that these are not "statements" <note>plural</note>, but rather a single statement, so the definition does not apply to it. 

The investigation shows that the intent of his saying "**necessitate by their very essence another statement**" is that those statements must lead to the result by way of logical inquiry <term>al-naẓar</term>. This inquiry is understood because that which leads to a goal by way of inquiry is not a mere accident. How could it not be considered when the purpose of this art <note>logic</note> is to explain the methods of acquiring concepts and assents? Thus, the assent to one of the parts of a composite proposition, even if it necessitates its converse or contrapositive, is not reached by way of logical inquiry.

<margin>
Its being universal requires that it does not exclude other statements that lead to the objective. This requires the correctness of the technical term since they were in a state of leading by way of inquiry, not essentially. The contrapositive is not like that; rather, it holds true as long as the indication is not like the complete one.
</margin>

<meta>catchword: And it is</meta>

བསྟི་བྱས་ནས་བསྟི་བསྟང་བྱེད༴ བསྟིང་ཚིག་བ་འོག་ས་བསྡ་ཡིན༴ མཐའ་མེད་མཐོ་འཚམ་རྒྱུན་མཐུད་ན༴ མཐོ་ཡང་མཐུར་དུ་ལྟུང་བ་མཐོང་༴ མཐེ་བོང་མཐོ་ཡོར་མཐུ་བྱུང
ན༴། མི་མཐུན་མཐོལ་བ་མ་མཐའ་ཡིན༴ སེཾན་འཐས་སྤོས་འཐག་འཐོན་ནས་འཐོར༴ འཐིལ་འཐུག་འཐུན་པ་འཐད་ནས་འཐོན༴ འཐེང་པ་འཐབ་ཀྱིན་འཐིང་ཆུ་འཐུང་༴
འཐུན་ཕྱོཊ་རྣཾས་ནི་འཐུན་འཇུག་བྱེད༴ འཐོ་གང་དྲོད་འཐུལ་འ་འཐའ་ཡིན༴ ༈ གདན་པའི་གདན་སྟེངས་གསེར་གདུག་ཕུག༴ གདངས་སྙན་གདཾས་པ་གདོད་ནས་ཟབ༴ གདུལ་བྱའི་
