The one who holds many riches is bound. Teaching and listening are flawed and the mind is not in harmony. Evil thoughts arise and virtue does not remain. Not being in harmony, one will be summoned by death. To trick others, to hide and conceal. Searching and feeling is the <term>A-Chah</term> <gloss>the letter A prefixed to Chah</gloss>.

If one considers the penis and the tail, the fluids are not tolerated and are swallowed by the girl. In the end, there is regret if they did not meet. Paying taxes, though the neck is thick, it still decays. Clinging to the smooth white one, it becomes elongated. Even if the future is destroyed, there is no foundation. In the field that is exhausted, the <term>Jag-ma</term> <gloss>grass</gloss> flourishes. Milking the female yak while watching the rainbow. The result of entering is destroyed by another. Mañjuśrī and Bhairava are one in essence. To be stuck together by a bushel is the <term>A-Jah</term> <gloss>the letter A prefixed to Jah</gloss>.

A heavy tree grows in the valley. The green sprout sinks deep. This is the letter <term>Ja</term> with a <term>La</term> prefix.

The manager’s ferocity caused a contagious disease. Relatives and spiritual friends are destroyed by the antidote. In the state of the natural mind, one falls asleep, and the wrinkles on the necks of both are cleared. Being busy with a purpose is the <term>Ga-Ny-ah</term> <gloss>the letter Ga prefixed to Nya</gloss>. By listening to the Vinaya, the mental continuum becomes disciplined. Respect everyone, whether equal or unequal. By listening to the one lying down, one was pleased. Abandoning the flexible is the <term>Ma-Ny-ah</term> <gloss>the letter Ma prefixed to Nya</gloss>.

Acquiring new or old gains, one still finds them. The silt of muddy water is the <term>Ra-Nya</term> <gloss>the letter Ra superscribed over Nya</gloss>. Having attained the monastic seat, one looks down on others. The vows were placed in the womb of the noblewoman. An image is the <term>Ba-og Ra-Nya</term> <gloss>the letter Ra over Nya with a Ba prefix</gloss>. In the degenerate age, the oral lineage fills the heart. With compassion, others...

<leaf-break/>

The view and the viewer. Like a jewel, look at the belly-crawler <note>a snake</note>. This is the letter <term>Ta</term> with a <term>La</term> subscript. The physical eye's seeing is the letter <term>Ta</term> with a <term>La</term> subscript and a <term>Ba</term> prefix. On the beautiful tiger-skin mat. Showing emptiness and giving food and wealth. The birch tree of the festival. The lost axe and the small knife. This is the letter <term>Ta</term> with a <term>Sa</term> superscript.

The holder of the teachings explains and speaks words of praise. Having shown respect, one serves. A word of sarcasm is the <term>Ba-og Sa-Ta</term> <gloss>the letter Sa over Ta with a Ba prefix</gloss>. Endlessly seeking to compete, the connection continues. Even if high, one sees the fall to the bottom. If the thumb, the cairn, and power arise. Disagreeing and confessing is the <term>Ma-Tha</term> <gloss>the letter Ma prefixed to Tha</gloss>.

The fingernail is hard, the incense is ground, it comes out and scatters. Deep and thick, being in agreement, it emerges. The lame person fights while drinking the blue water. Those on the side of harmony practice harmony. A span of heat rising is the <term>A-Tha</term> <gloss>the letter A prefixed to Tha</gloss>.

On the seat of the sitter, a golden parasol was opened. The melodious sound and instructions are profound from the beginning. The radiance of the disciples has great strength. Released from the poisonous snake and the evil spirit. Relics and the body-relic is the <term>Ga-Da</term> <gloss>the letter Ga prefixed to Da</gloss>. To the seven Sugatas, the devotee offered. That we are chased by demons is true. Chattering, sharpening a knife, and being prepared with a peaceful mind. The enemy's flourishing is the <term>Ba-Da</term> <gloss>the letter Ba prefixed to Da</gloss>. An arrow, a spear, and an arrowhead cut the knot. The feather in front has bright radiance. White color, radiant oil, in front...

<leaf-break/>

...is the prefix.

Malicious thoughts always suppress the enemy. Now, swearing an oath, I contemplate. When going to the relentless hell, one is suppressed beneath. To endure hardship is the <term>Ma-Na</term> <gloss>the letter Ma prefixed to Na</gloss>. The pus in the ear of the yogi. Pierced by something sharp, it becomes calm. If distraction is abandoned, the pure state is nurtured. The flesh of the ear is eaten by the <term>Nang-nang</term> bird. This is the letter <term>Na</term> with a <term>Ta</term> prefix.

Covetousness is the <term>Ma-og Ra-Na</term> <gloss>the letter Ra over Na with a Ma prefix</gloss>. The patched robe, woolen cloth, and ink. Various kinds of woolen cloth are held by the end. The smell of incense, the nose smells in the light. The mucus of the nose is blown outside. Having removed the excess measure, the bright lamp was lifted. To smell a scent is the letter <term>Na</term> with a <term>Sa</term> prefix.

Increasing the fine, the ointment was applied by them. Crossing the hands, the pigment was ground. Abolishing is the <term>Sa-Na</term> <gloss>the letter Sa over Na</gloss> with a <term>Ba</term> prefix.

From the Stream of the Nectar of Orthography, this is the fifth chapter, the section on the <term>Ta</term> group.

On a Friday, the lute is played in the lap. The <term>Su-hrang</term> <gloss>straight</gloss> poto and the <term>pi-u-tu</term> <gloss>small box</gloss>. The god Pe-kar, a volume of books, and incense were hidden in the box. A brush and a small box are the plain letter <term>Pa</term>. The hero acts as the lord of the mind. Boundless wealth, estimated by example. Hang the silk scarf on the wish-fulfilling tree. Investigation, the winter, and the hip joint. Inside the shoulder of the target, the leader's army. The forehead is high, this is the letter <term>Pa</term> with a <term>Da</term> prefix.

The peak of the meadow mountain is adorned with clouds. The general meaning, a cane, and joining with glue. One who had wealth has become a beggar. Leave the <term>Pra</term> <gloss>a type of wax</gloss> and the monkey in the crowd. The glue is an emanation, let go of the elaboration. Shaking the hair, having shaken it, one shook it. Shaken...

Second, for the generation and invitation: <term>Om Svabhava</term> and so forth. Out of the state of emptiness, in the eastern direction of the great palace of the practice hall, in the center of an immense and vast jewel palace with perfect arrangements, upon the heart of a blossoming multi-colored lotus, from the complete transformation of a white syllable <term>Ham</term>, appears the Great King Dhritarashtra <note>Ulkhor Kyong</note>. His body is white like the kumuda flower. His left hand holds the celestial lute <term>pipa</term>, and his right is raised, proclaiming the sound of Dharma. His eyes are slightly wrathful at the corners, and his face is smiling and composed, yet he is seductive, heroic, and blazing with light and majesty. He wears firm jewel armor and is adorned with all ornaments. In the center of a host of Gandharvas and a hundred thousand lords of the pure family, he sits majestically. At his crown is <term>Om</term>, at his throat is <term>Ah</term>. From <term>Hum</term> at his heart, light rays radiate and invite the Wisdom Being, identical to himself, from its natural abode. <term>Vajra Samaya Jah</term>. <term>Jah Hum Bam Ho</term>. <term>Padma Kamalayé Stvam</term>. The commitment being and the wisdom being become inseparable. Thus, invite and dissolve them. Third, inviting from the life-essence and offering: Recite <term>Om Bheru Rajaye Hum</term> one hundred times. As in the preliminary torga offering—

<leaf-break/>

"Until... is fulfilled, may the four great kings who protect the directions offer a single boundary offering to those who cause obstacles to the accomplishment." Thus chant. <term>Ho</term>! Externally, you are the Great King Dhritarashtra; internally, you are the Blessed Vajrasattva; secretly, you are Vajra Heruka. You great kings who possess strength and skill, the enlightened activity I entrust to you is this: in this mandala of the body, speech, mind, qualities, and activities of the Guru, Chosen Deity, and Dakini, for the sake of accomplishing the intentions of us practitioners led by the Vajra King, we have generated the supreme mind of enlightenment tonight. From the beginning of this practice until the very end, do not allow any outer obstacles to enter inside, and do not allow any inner accomplishments to vanish outside. Please establish a holy boundary of protection. Please cause all enemies and obstacles who create interference to be no more. Furthermore, please subdue all those who lead astray, such as the <term>Damsri</term>. Thus, with the King and his entourage looking outward to protect, recite "The mind of the Victor" and so forth, and speak auspicious verses. Recite <term>Supratishtha Vajraye Svaha</term> to make it stable. Scatter flowers. Likewise—

<leaf-break/>

"Holding a stupa, the corners of the eyes slightly wrathful" and so forth, "with the entourage of hosts of Nagas and demons," thus recite. <term>Om Bheru Bakshaye Hum Jah</term> (one hundred times). Torga and offerings. <term>Om Bheru Bakshaye Balinta</term> and so forth. <term>Argham</term> and so forth. "Hum, Great Powerful One" and so forth. The distinction is: "King of the West, Virupaksha <note>Chenmizang</note>, red and clear, with a majestic and awesome form, holding the Stupa of Merit and the snake-lasso, protect and offer the boundary to the hosts of Naga demons." <term>Om Bheru Bakshaye Hum Jah Raksha Kuru Svaha</term>. "Yogi" and so forth. <term>Ho</term>! Externally, the Great King Virupaksha; internally, the Blessed One Amitabha; secretly, Padma Heruka and so forth. "The speech of the Victor" and so forth. Also "In the northern direction," and the syllable <term>Kumni</term> <note>green</note> completely transforms into Vaishravana <note>Namthöse</note>. His body is green like emerald. His right hand holds a victory banner and his left holds a mongoose hide-bag. "The corners of the eyes slightly" and so forth, "with the entourage of hosts of Yakshas," thus change the recitation. <term>Om Bheshramanaye Hum Jah</term> (one hundred times). Torga and offerings with the root mantra <term>Balinta</term> and so forth, and <term>Argham</term> and so forth. "Hum, Great Powerful One" and so forth, as before. "King of the North, Vaishravana, fierce activity—"

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>without falling into distraction, without letting virtue slip into ordinary speech, and without allowing the teachings to become mere intellectual habit. It is the meeting with the Teacher in the form of the Three Bodies <note>the Dharmakaya, Sambhogakaya, and Nirmanakaya</note>.

The signs and measures of purifying the grasping of appearances and mind are as follows. With the eyes, one attains the unobstructed divine sight, seeing directly through walls and other obstacles as if they were transparent. With the ears, one hears the languages of the six classes of beings, such as gods and <term>nagas</term> <gloss>serpentine spirits</gloss>. With the nose, one smells the fragrances of other pure realms. Because the stains of mental obscurations are purified, unimpeded clairvoyance arises, and one dwells in the exhaustion of contaminated states. Through the purification of grasping at appearances and mind, wisdom seizes its own ground. This is the attainment of the result: the Teacher as the Three Bodies, spontaneously present without effort. This is the sixteenth core instruction. <term>Samaya</term> <gloss>sacred bond</gloss>. <term>Tya tya tya</term> <gloss>seal, seal, seal</gloss. By unifying view, meditation, and conduct, the result of the Three Bodies is delivered to its own place. Thus it is said.

<leaf-break/>

Appearances that have never existed before arise. It is certain that liberation occurs by resolving the artificial duality of Buddhas and sentient beings. For example, just as one sees all four continents from the peak of Mount Meru, the views of all the individual philosophical schools are clearly understood here. One who knows this meaning is called a <term>rtogs ldan</term> <gloss>realized practitioner</gloss>. As for the nature of that realization: for a yogi who realizes this Teacher as the <term>Dharmakaya</term> <gloss>Truth Body</gloss>, there is nothing in all of appearance and existence that is not liberated. Having never been deluded, they do not dwell in delusion; delusion is impossible. Having never been a Buddha, they do not dwell in "Buddha"; there is no liberation <note>meaning they are beyond the duality of bondage and liberation</note>. The five poisons have not been abandoned but are self-liberated. Such a person dwells in the state where phenomena are exhausted and the conceptual mind is transcended. Because cyclic existence has become nameless, they are upright. Because the tenets of dualistic phenomena have collapsed, they are spacious within. Because awareness has recognized its own enlightenment, they are at ease. This chapter introduces the yoga of the ultimate view and summarizes its points.

<summary>This page describes the supernatural signs of successful meditation practice and the realization of the non-dual nature of the Buddha and ordinary mind. It emphasizes that a realized practitioner views all phenomena as spontaneously liberated and transcends conventional philosophical tenets.</summary>
<keywords>Three Bodies, clairvoyance, Mount Meru, Dharmakaya, non-duality, self-liberation, five poisons, awareness</keywords>

...and sitting there, the infinite host of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas abide in the manner of gathering clouds. I offer my body, all my possessions, and all sentient beings equal to space without exception as your subjects, O Supreme Being! Please consider us with compassion, accept us, and grant us protection! 

To the Teacher, the Secret Bliss Indra-bhūti; the Naga Yogini and Saraha; Nagarjuna, Aryadeva, and Nagabodhi; the elder and younger Dus-zhabs; Vajrasana; Abhaya and Tsami Pal-wa-lo; Tsultrim Jungne and Dorje Wangchuk; Phagmo Drupa, Zhang, and Lingre Tsangpa Gya; the nine named Senge, Magyal of Kashmir, and the father and sons who are emanations of the Three Families, the Lords of the Teachings; Chödrak Tobgyal and Pema Karpo; Chokyi Gonpo, Mipham Chogyal, and Ngawang Namgyal. Furthermore, I pray from my heart to all the gurus of the lineage of the empowerment and instructions of the Protector. Protect the teachings and grant the two types of accomplishments <note>common and supreme</note>! May the gurus dissolve into light and be absorbed into myself! 

May all sentient beings meet with happiness—thus one should abide in loving-kindness. May all sentient beings...

<leaf-break/>

**SAMANTA BUDDHĀNĀM GRAHE SHARI PRABHANJA JATI MAHĀ SAMAYA SVĀHĀ.** May all the guests act as my companions and helpers as needed. 

**HUM**. The expanse of primordial purity free from identification. The spring of the door of spontaneously present, unobstructed arising. From the expanse of equanimity and compassion, I myself am the body of Padmasambhava, possessing a slightly wrathful expression. On my head, I wear the lotus hat with the soaring vulture feather. I wear the brocade cloak and the dharma robes. I carry the vajra and the skull-cup of nectar. The <term>khaṭvāṅga</term> <gloss>trident-staff</gloss> is resting on my left shoulder. I sit in the posture of a great king at ease. 

To the right is the divine consort Mandarava, the blue-complexioned accomplished yogini. To the left is the lady of Kharchen, Yeshe Tsogyal. Both of them, white in color, offer nectar. On the body, speech, and mind are **OM AH HUM**. From them, rays of light radiate to invite <note>the wisdom beings</note>. 

**HUM**. From here, at the southwest border of the sun, in the center of the land of the Chamara continent, from the palace of Lotus Light at the peak of the Glorious Copper-Colored Mountain: King who establishes the <term>rakshasas</term> in the law, Padma Thötreng Tsal, father and mother! Surrounded by a retinue of heroes and <term>dakinis</term>! In rainbow and light "pu-ru-ru" <note>swirling</note>! Invited by our calling, please come here! Descend your blessings upon this supreme place! To the supreme practitioner...

<leaf-break/>

...please come! 

**HUM**. I am the Great Glorious Heruka! I am the Great Devourer! I am Vajrapani Humkara! I am the Terrifier, Vajra Bhairava! There is no Buddha except me. All abide by my command. The life-blood of all the proud gods and spirits of existence comes to me. You must accomplish the activity I entrust to you! If you are negligent and delay the work, you will be burned in the hell of the reversal of the command! 

**OM VAJRA SAMAYA HANA HANA HUM PHAT JAH HUM BAM HO**. We become non-dual. 

**HUM**. To offer you worship, like the four Vedas of the twice-born <note>original: "dvija"</note>. To follow the respective intentions of the mind. The pool for purifying the Body, Speech, and Mind. When Avalokiteshvara and Vishnu search, they see the smile of the Lady of All Flowers. From the swaying of the lotus-filaments' sidelong glance, she radiates the passionate expressions of yellow dust. Before Indra, the Lord of the Senses, the sweet fragrance of the Parijata tree wafts. From the direction of the gaze of the majestic Great God <note>Shiva, the fire that burns all demons appears. To bring peace to Brahma in the heart, it settles as the ointment of the meditative Ganges. Music sounds as spring to the ears, joined with supreme melodies. At the tip of the tongue that flickers like lightning, cloud-banks of nectar-food...

### Calculation of Service Tenure <term>Gi-sa</term>
The Tutor <term>Seol-seo</term> does not have their months of service counted to reach the Sixth Rank. Junior officials in the Office of Royal Decrees <term>Yemungwan</term> leave their post after one year and two negative performance reviews <term>bu</term>. If they do not have at least four negative reviews but have not completed their full term, they are not promoted. 

Officials in the Office of Diplomatic Correspondence <term>Seungmun-won</term> and the National Academy <term>Seonggyun-gwan</term> leave after two negative reviews in summer and one in winter. 

Officials in the Bureau of Books <term>Gyoseo-gwan</term> leave after one year and two negative reviews. 

For the top graduate of the civil exam <term>Tam-hwa-rang</term>, the fifteen months of service are counted from the month they first pay respects to the King. Even if they are not in the top registry during the personnel review, they are promoted to the Sixth Rank. 

For civil officials, service in the posts of Historiographer <term>Geom-yeol</term>, Clerk <term>Sa-rok</term>, Instructor <term>Hun-do</term>, and Inspector <term>Chal-bang</term> is counted by months, not by days, to reach the Sixth Rank after three thousand days <note>This represents roughly 8 years of service</note>. 

For privileged officials <term>Eum</term>, service as a Tutor <term>Geom-gyo</term> or in the Office of Punishment below the rank of high official is counted to reach the Sixth Rank after nine hundred days. Those on the merit list are promoted to the Sixth Rank. If a dismissed official is reinstated, their previous service is counted. 

Service as a Temporary Overseer <term>Ga-gam-yeok</term> is not counted. Once they move to a substantive post, their total service of nine hundred days is counted for promotion to the Sixth Rank. 

Service as a Temporary Ritual Usher <term>Ga-in-ui</term> is not counted. Once they move to a substantive post, their nine hundred days are counted. 

For specialists in astronomy, geography, divination, the medical clinic for tumors, the Bureau of Interpreters, the Bureau of Books, the Clerical School, the administrative clerks of the State Council and the Office of Royal Advisors, the service required to reach the Sixth Rank is one thousand three hundred and fifty days. 

For the post of Chief Clerk <term>Jik-jang</term>, service is counted from the month they pay respects, requiring four hundred and fifty days for promotion. 

Assistant Clerks <term>Bong-sa</term> are promoted to Chief Clerk after four hundred and fifty days. 

Service for various regional and palace inspectors <term>Chal-bong</term> is counted from the month they pay respects. For Tomb Wardens, it is counted by their months on duty. All require four hundred and fifty days to be promoted to Senior Clerk <term>Cham-bong</term>. 

Regardless of the type of inspector or assistant, even if they have not completed the full term, if they are at the top of the service list, they are promoted in order. Once they reach the required seniority, the vacancy is filled. They reach the Sixth Rank only after completing the required tenure. Even if they have extra days beyond the required tenure for inspectors or assistants, those days are not applied. When promoting, the person who appears first in the attendance ledger <term>Gong-jwa-bu</term> is nominated. During the major personnel review, if a Chief Clerk has served less than ten months, a request is made to promote them to the Sixth Rank. 

For officials of the Seventh Rank and below who are in similar "pools" of candidates, if they are moved to another bureau, their total service is counted. If they are in mourning or become an unassigned official without cause, their previous service is still counted. For privileged officials in Tomb offices...

<header>Impedimentum.i.</header>

Impediment i. The first part commonly concerns the obstacles to marriage. The first is about the impediment in general; the second, error of the person; the third, the impediment of condition; the fourth, the impediment of the vow; the fifth, the impediment of carnal kinship; the sixth, the impediment of spiritual kinship, that is to say, of godparenthood; the seventh, legal kinship, that is to say, adoption; the eighth, the impediment of sin; the ninth, of <term>diffulto</term> <gloss>difficulty</gloss>, that is, of disparate faith, and this is the tenth; the eleventh, of force or fear; the twelfth, of the impediment of holy orders; the thirteenth, of the bond to another woman; the fourteenth, of the justice of public honesty; the fifteenth, of affinity; the sixteenth, of the inability to unite; the seventeenth, of marriage made against the interdict of the church; the eighteenth, of the impediment of times and seasons. And of these said impediments, there are verses in which they are explained according to the said order, thus: Error, condition, vow, kinship, crime, disparity of cult, force, order, bond, honesty; if you are akin, if by chance you cannot copulate, these things known forbid marriages, it retracts the joined, the prohibition of the church, and also the forbidden times, they impede it from being made, they allow what is done to be held.

¶ Chapter 2. What things impede a marriage already made. It is answered: there are 12 which not only impede a marriage from being made, but even undo the one that is already made. Which things are placed in the first three verses in the nearby text. ¶ And they understand that they undo the marriage already made if they passed before the marriage, but if they supervened after the marriage was already rightly made, such as sister-in-law status or sin, they do not undo it. ¶ Even if it is not followed by carnal union. <note>see Summa Confessorum, book 4, title 30, question 1, B.</note> Saved for one case, this by the vow of religion with effect, when someone, having made the marriage, before the carnal union entered into religion. <note>see Extra, "On the conversion of married persons," chapter "Venit," c. "ex parte n." z. H.</note> There it is said clearly that a marriage contracted legitimately by words of the present can in no case be undone, even if one of the contractors were made a heretic, because while the other lives they pass to second vows, unless one enters into religion. <note>B. Of betrothals, "commissum." But it must be waited for until the profession is made, as Thomas puts it in the 4th, distinction 27.</note> He means until the religion in general is at least tacitly obligated, because if he did not want to change his life absolutely, the benefit of the one who enters is not to be given to another without his consent. <note>see in the chapter "beneficium," of rules, book 6, B. For at least it is not undone, nor even according to Pe. Similarly to this, see below "votum," 4, f. G., at the end.</note> And this is to be guarded the same for the reception of holy orders, for the marriage is as well undone as some wished to say, but the contrary is declared in an Extravagante of John XXII that begins "Antiqua."

<column-break/>

¶ Chapter 3. What things are those that impede a marriage that is to be made, but do not impede or undo the one that is already made. It is answered: the first are the two things mentioned above in the 1st section, that is to say, the development of the church, nor the time of the fairs, of which it will be said below in Impediment 16 and Impediment 17. Also there are some sins of which see below Impediment 8, section 1. Item, it impedes betrothals that were first begun with another; see it below under "sponsalia," section 8. Item, it impedes the catechism that is done before baptism; see it below Impediment 6, section z. Item, it impedes the simple vow; see it below Impediment 4, section i. n. z.

¶ Chapter 4. If any custom impedes a marriage that is to be made or undoes the one that is already made. It is answered according to Hostiensis: if the custom is approved by the Pope that the marriage is not to be made, or if it is already made that it be undone, certainly it will impede and undo in any cases that the canonical constitution can do this. <note>Extra, "On spiritual kinship," chapter 1, n. c. ff. c. Extra, "On consanguinity," n. thus.</note> That the choice of the Pope has the force of law. But if the custom is not approved by the Pope nor disapproved, then to avoid the scandal that could happen by acting against it, the marriage that is to be made they will impede; the one that is already made is not undone. This same thing says Bernard in his "Novella." A. The same in the "Summa Confessorum," title, question 2.

¶ Chapter 5. What is to be held or done when the doctors disagree concerning the impediments of marriage. It is answered according to Hostiensis: wherever the doctors say by their glosses that the marriage is undone, if they do not bring forward an express contrary law, you must adhere to those who say the contrary. <note>Extra, "On witnesses," l. 3, "ex quodam" at the end. A. The same in the "Summa Confessorum," same title, question 3.</note>

# The Barrier to be Broken

"Crossing over all suffering and disaster." Crossing is crossing over and liberation. "All suffering and disaster" means: If one realizes that the inside is originally empty and still, and that there is not a single particle that can be attained, one is liberated from the two types of birth and death: *phased* and *changing*. Disaster is the cause of calamity. The above passage is the separate preface. When Ananda compiled the dharma treasury, he narrated the meritorious action of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara in saving living beings. Below, starting from Shariputra, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara answers Shariputra's questions.

Next, the Bodhisattva's correct teaching for the benefit of others is divided into two.
First, the explicit teaching of *Hannya*. (A)
Second, the secret teaching of *Hannya*. (B)

First, summarizing the five *skandhas* and explaining them in two parts.
First, broadly explaining form. (Above) "Shariputra, form does not differ from emptiness; emptiness does not differ from form; form is exactly emptiness; emptiness is exactly form."

Gushan says: In the correct teaching section, there is the explicit *Hannya* and the secret *Hannya*. The reason for these two is that they follow the differences in the capacity of the listener. Some hear the explicit and rejoice; some hear the secret and are satisfied. Giving rise to good, breaking evil, and entering the truth are all the same. Thus, I know that the discussion of explicit and secret is both for the purpose of giving birth to wonderful wisdom. Question: If the secret cannot be understood,

<column-break/>

how can it also give birth to wisdom? Answer: If you reach the realization of "incomprehensible emptiness," this is the ability to give birth to wisdom. Therefore, the *Great Treatise* says: A heavenly being says to Subhuti, "The *Hannya* you preach is hidden and difficult to know; I cannot understand it." Then Subhuti replies by citing, "Not understanding is also empty. This is *Hannya*." You should know: if you recite it with a mind of attachment, the explicit only increases merit. If you recite it with a formless mind, the secret is then able to give birth to wisdom. Shariputra is called *Shariputra* in Sanskrit. *Shari* is translated as "body," and *putra* is translated as "son." Now, the two characters preserve the Sanskrit, and the one character follows the Chinese. Thus, it is called *Shariputra*. Because the mother had a beautiful body, the mother is named "Body." Because the body is the son, he is named "Body's Son." The above is the first among the Buddha's disciples in wisdom. He asks questions for the sake of the assembly. Therefore, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara calls his name and tells him. Shundai says: The transformed body returns to true emptiness. <margin>Shundai says: Saying that the transformed body returns to consciousness is not a delusion.</margin> It is because it is not originally the transformation of "extinction-emptiness." Extinction-emptiness is vacuous and extinct; it has no knowledge and no function, so it cannot manifest the myriad dharmas. It is like the emptiness outside a mirror not being the same as the emptiness inside a mirror. The forms are clearly present, yet when you seek them, they are unattainable. This is called "emptiness." "Emptiness does not differ from form" means true emptiness is definitely not different from form. Therefore, it is said emptiness does not differ from form. The governor of the Syrian frontiers has the chief command of it. The costs of a maritime expedition of this kind amount to approximately 100,000 <term>denares</term> <gloss>gold coins</gloss>.

After this description of the Roman frontiers, it will not be without use to give some information on the Romans. Let us begin with the organization of the army. The <term>patrice</term> <gloss>patrician</gloss> commands 10,000 men. He has under his orders two <term>toumarkhes</term> <gloss>division commanders</gloss>, who each command 5,000 men. Each <term>toumarkhe</term> has under his orders five <term>drungaires</term> <gloss>brigade commanders</gloss>, who <margin>256</margin> each command 1,000 men. Under the orders of each <term>drungaire</term> are five <term>comès</term> <gloss>counts or battalion commanders</gloss>, each commanding 200 men. Each <term>comès</term> has under his orders five <term>komtarches</term> <gloss>captains</gloss>, who each command 40 men. Each <term>komtarkhe</term> has under his orders four <term>dékarkhes</term> <gloss>squad leaders</gloss>, each commanding 10 men. Every soldier who experiences any injury reports it to his superior, that is to say to the <term>dékarkhe</term>, the latter to his superior, and so on up to the king. By this means, the king is better informed than any other of everything that happens in the army, and if someone happens to die, they can be replaced without delay.

As for the number of armies, the one found at Constantinople, the residence of the king, counts 24,000 men, of which 16,000 are cavalry and 8,000 are infantry. The cavalry are divided into four corps. The first, 4,000 men strong, is that of the <term>Scholârioi</term> <gloss>Imperial Guard units</gloss>, under the command of the grand <term>Domestique</term> <gloss>Domestic/Commander-in-Chief</gloss> who at the same time is commander-in-chief of the whole army and charged with ordering the levies. <meta>continues from previous page</meta>"The sound of the carriage is like <term>ju</term> <note>車</note>." Nowadays it has the <term>fanqie</term> <term>chi-she</term> <gloss>pronounced che</gloss>. Wei Zhao said: "In ancient times all pronounced it with the <term>fanqie</term> <term>chi-she</term>; only from the Han dynasty onward did the pronunciation <term>ju</term> first appear."

The "Hereditary House of Liu Ze, King of Yan" in the <term>Records of the Grand Historian</term> states: "Zhang Qing and the son of Tian Sheng persuaded him, saying: 'Now the Lady Lü's clan...'" The older text of the <term>Ya</term> originally had: "thrust the hub <note>original: "推轂"</note> for the High Emperor <note>Emperor Gaozu</note> to take possession of all under Heaven." The <term>Suoyin</term> commentary states: "<term>Tui</term> <gloss>to push or promote</gloss> has the <term>fanqie</term> <term>chang-shui</term>."

In the <term>Comprehensive Mirror</term> under the fourteenth year of Former Emperor Xiaowen: "Thrust the hub <note>original: "推轂"</note>." For the upper character, it has the <term>fanqie</term> <term>tong-hui</term>, meaning to push through or make open <note>original: "通也"</note>; the lower character has the <term>fanqie</term> <term>gu-lu</term>, meaning that where the spokes converge <note>original: "輻所輳也"</note>.

In the second year of Duke Cheng in the <term>Zuo Tradition</term>, Qiu Huan of Zheng said: "From the time the battle first joined, if there was danger, I certainly pushed the carriage from below." Lu's phonetic reading gives for <note>推</note> the <term>fanqie</term> <term>chang-shui</term>, and also the <term>fanqie</term> <term>ta-hui</term>.

In the Former Han biography of Zheng Dangshi: "Its thrusting the hub <note>original: "推轂"</note>." The upper character <term>tui</term> has no phonetic reading provided.

Master Dan'an, Hu Zhongjian <note>Hu Quan</note>, in his postscript to the "Record of the Baojing Hermitage," remarked: "<term>Jing</term> <gloss>quiet/still</gloss> was written as <term>jing</term> <gloss>ornamented/quiet</gloss> in ancient script. Upon examining the classics and histories, it has several meanings. The commentary to the poem 'Han Yi' states: '<term>Qiqi</term> means slowly; <term>jing</term> means slow.' Master Xu's <term>Shuowen Jiezi</term>

Yang Blade Pattern
</margin>

The <term>Yang Blade</term> <gloss>Yang Ren</gloss> and the <term>Established Salary</term> <gloss>Jian Lu</gloss> are quite similar. However, in cases where one sees the Salary, we do not speak of the Blade. This is because the day master and the month order are of the same substance, representing pure harmony. Furthermore, there is the "Back-stabbing Yang Blade" <gloss>Yang Ren Dao Ge</gloss>. This person will surely become a "headless ghost" <gloss>die by decapitation</gloss>. For example, if a <term>丙 Fire</term> day master has a four-pillar chart that is too prosperous, and <term>丁 Fire</term> is revealed and sits close to the body, the sharpness of the blade becomes even more blazing. How could the head and body not be separated? This was the case with the fate of **Xia Guizhou**. 

The Yang Blade, in the heavens, is the Purple Dark Star, which specializes in executions. On the earth, it is the Yang Blade, which is one position ahead of the <term>Killing Salary</term>. It likes the <term>Partial Official</term> and <term>Seven Killings</term> to restrain and subdue it. Then the Yang Blade arises at the border. One will attain wealth and nobility, becoming a general or a minister. When the Blade enters the Official or Killing stars, its majesty awes the borderlands. 

It likes the <term>Seal</term> to produce the body. It dislikes <term>Reversed Fuyin</term> and <term>Fuyin</term> <gloss>repeated or clashing cycles</gloss>. <term>Fuyin</term> occurs when, for example, <term>Jia</term> uses <term>Mao</term> as its blade and <term>Geng</term> uses <term>You</term> as its blade, and the year or luck cycles match the original fate. If one sees <term>Mao</term> and <term>You</term>, or sees <term>You</term> again, disaster will surely follow. This is what is called "the year and luck cycle arriving together; calamity reaches immediately." <term>Fanyin</term> <gloss>Reversed Fuyin</gloss> refers to clashing. For example, <term>You</term> clashing with the <term>Mao</term> blade, or the <term>Mao</term> blade clashing with <term>You</term>. Encountering this brings blame. This is the Yang Blade clashing with or combining with the <term>Year Sovereign</term> <gloss>the current year's stem/branch</gloss>, causing disaster to break out suddenly. 

Regarding the "Triple Combination with the Year Sovereign": For example, if the current year sees <term>Hai</term> and <term>Wei</term>, and the <term>Mao</term> blade forms a triple combination; or if the current year sees <term>Si</term> and <term>Chou</term>, and the <term>You</term> blade forms a triple combination. Also, if the current year sees <term>Xu</term> and the <term>Mao</term> blade forms a six-fold combination; or sees <term>Chen</term> and the <term>You</term> blade forms a six-fold combination. In that year, disaster will surely arrive quickly. This is the Blade combining with the Year Sovereign, causing calamity to erupt. It dislikes the <term>Kui Gang</term> <gloss>specific noble/harsh stars</gloss>, punishment, and harm. If there are no Official or Seal stars, nor any <term>Blessing Gods</term> to assist, then ten thousand disasters will occur. If there are Official and Seal stars...

<summary>This page discusses the dangerous and powerful aspects of the Yang Blade, including its potential for high military rank and the severe risks of decapitation or sudden disaster when it is clashed or combined.</summary>

To the supreme unique king, the Precious Lama. 
To the Precious Lama, the lord pervading all families. 
To the Precious Lama, the union of all lineages. 
To the Precious Lama, the union of all Buddhas. 
To the Precious Lama, the union of all sacred Dharma. 
To the Precious Lama, the union of the <term>Sangha</term>. 
To the Precious Lama, the union of all <term>Yidams</term>. 
To the Precious Lama, the union of all <term>Dakinis</term>. 
To the Precious Lama, the union of all Dharma Protectors. 
I pray to the Precious Lama, the union of all refuge objects. 
I pray: please bless me with your compassionate heart. 
Thus, by making this prayer, the great power of compassion of all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Lamas from the infinite realms of the ten directions is invoked. In the center of the expanse of space, entirely filled with the radiating and absorbing light and rays, within the great celestial palace of precious primordial wisdom, from the light rays of the body of the Glorious Lama, the incomparable King of the Shakyas, beginning from the teacher who first showed great kindness by teaching me to read, as well as the presiding teachers, the teachers of the secret instructions, the ritual teachers, the teachers of the time-gate, the causal teachers, the conditional teachers, the co-emergent teachers, and so forth—all those with whom there is a Dharma connection, as well as the holders of the <term>Tripitaka</term> <gloss>Three Baskets of Scripture</gloss>...

<leaf-break/>

Because I have not accomplished appearances as they truly are, I confess and disclose all my personal faults and regrets. Having accepted them with patience in the expanse of compassion, may the blessings of the Glorious Lama enter me. Whatever activities the lamas perform, I rejoice in them with wonderful devotion. Without seeing them as faults measured by my own mind, may respect for the Dharma arise, seeing whatever they do as excellent. Just as there is a Teacher within each of their retinues, I pray that all holders of the teachings turn the wheel of Dharma. In the places of the Sangha who have gathered in harmony, may the great wheel of Dharma emerge. May all the lamas be in good health, may their lives be long, and may their activities flourish. As long as <term>Samsara</term> is not emptied, may they always work for the benefit of others through their emanations. I, with a mind of impartial pure vision and devotion, pray to all the root and lineage lamas. May I be held by the compassion of all lamas, and may the blessings of all lamas enter me. The Buddhas of the ten directions scatter flowers of praise and prostrate to the actual Shakyamuni, the Lord of the Family, and to the assembly of Buddhas and Lamas, I bow. The heart of the Muni's teachings, the sacred Dharma, the <term>Vinaya</term> of the discipline section...

<leaf-break/>

I pray to the lamas of the lineage. I pray to the lamas of the lineage of the teachings of Maitreya. I pray to the lamas of the lineage of the practice of training. I pray to the lineage of the profound view. I pray to the lineage of the equality of existence and peace. I pray to the lineage of the Great Middle Way. I pray to the lineage of the instructional guidance on the view of self-emptiness. I pray to the lamas of the lineage of the instructional guidance on the view of other-emptiness. I pray to the lineage of the six-fold transmission. I pray to the lineage of the three stages of meditation. I pray to the lineage of the <term>Kadam Lamrim</term> <gloss>Graduated Path</gloss>. I pray to the lineage of the <term>Mahayana</term> <gloss>Great Vehicle</gloss> mind training. In brief, to all the teachers who show the various modes of the profound and vast in accordance with the Bodhisattva vehicle, I pray. Please bless me to fully realize the two types of the mind of enlightenment. The command of <term>Vajradhara</term>, the <term>Yidams</term>, and the <term>Dakinis</term>; the lineage of the adepts and knowledge-holders whose commitments are unimpaired, who possess the primordial wisdom of the <term>Vajra</term> <gloss>Indestructible</gloss> commitment. I pray to the lamas of the lineage of secret mantra vows. I pray to the lamas of the lineage of empowerment. I pray to the lamas of the lineage of blessings. I pray to the lamas of the lineage of authorization. I pray to the lamas of the lineage of the entrustment of awareness. I pray to the lamas of the lineage of the entrustment of the command. I pray to the lamas of the lineage of mantra recitation transmission. I pray to the lamas of the lineage of the generation and completion stages. I pray to the lamas of the lineage of pith instructions. I pray to the lamas of the lineage of the collection of activities. I pray to the lineage of the ocean of Tantras...

<meta>This page continues the translation of the second Mandala, third Sukta of the Rig Veda. This is an Apri hymn, used during animal sacrifices to invoke specific deities and personified ritual objects. The previous page discussed the sacred grass (Barhis) and the previous verse addressed the personified Doors of the sacrificial chamber. This page focuses on the twin goddesses of Dawn and Night, and the two divine invokers of the gods.</meta>

म० २. अ० १. सू० ३. ॥ Book 2. Chapter 1. Hymn 3. ॥ द्वितीयोऽष्टकः ॥ Second Octave ॥ ४३३ Page 433

-> ॥ The Sixth Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
Night and Dawn, the two who are ancient and exalted, move together like two skilled female weavers. They weave the stretched thread of the sacrifice, creating its beautiful form. They are bountiful and full of water. ॥ ६ ॥

> **Ancient/Exalted; actions/works; eternally; for us; sprinkled/worshipped; Dawn and Night; like two female weavers; praised/rejoicing; thread; stretched; weaving; moving together; of the sacrifice; form/beauty; bountiful; full of water.** ॥ ६ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Exalted** refers to those who are praised by our **actions**, meaning our sacrificial works. They are **eternally** worshipped through continuous songs of praise. Alternatively, the word for eternal refers to their perpetual nature. In this case, **sprinkled** means they are the ones who pour out the fruits of the ritual. **Dawn and Night** are the deities of the day and the night. They are described as being **like two weavers**, meaning they are as skilled as women who weave cloth. They are **praised** as they move past one another in succession. They are **weaving** the **stretched thread**, which represents the various parts of the sacrifice that are spread out over time. They work **moving together** in mutual cooperation to produce the ritual. Why do they weave? To create the **form** or the beauty of the **sacrifice being performed**. This means they cause the parts of the sacrifice to be carried out in the correct order. The sacrifices are spread out across the days and nights. They are **bountiful**, meaning they yield the fruits of the ritual. They are **full of water** because rain is produced by the cycle of day and night. May these two great deities of day and night carry out our sacrifice.

---

-> ॥ The Seventh Verse ॥ <-

## Hymn Text
The two divine invokers, the first and most wise, perform the sacrifice rightly with a sacred song. They have excellent forms. Worshipping the gods according to the seasons, they anoint them at the navel of the earth, upon the three heights. ॥ ७ ॥

> **Two divine; invokers; first; most wise; rightly; they sacrifice; together; with a song; most beautiful; the gods; worshipping; according to the season; together; they anoint; at the navel; of the earth; upon; the heights; three.** ॥ ७ ॥

---

## Commentary (Sayana)

**Two divine** refers to the divine Agni who exists in heaven. From that divine fire, two **invokers** are born. They are the ones who call the gods or perform the offerings. They are identified as the two fires: the terrestrial fire on earth and the atmospheric fire in the sky. They are the **first** to be worshipped. They are **most wise**, meaning they are the greatest of the learned. They have **excellent forms**. These two gods, through a **sacred song** or mantra, **sacrifice rightly**, which means they perform the worship perfectly without any defect. They **worship the gods** who are worthy of sacrifice **according to the seasons**, meaning at the specific prescribed times. These two gods—

<margin>
VOL. II. 5 S
</margin>

<note>
- **Dawn and Night** (Uṣāsānaktā): These are personified as twin sisters or two weavers who create the fabric of time and ritual.
- **Day and night**: The commentary links the natural cycle of time to the successful completion of the ritual.
- **Two divine invokers** (Daivyā Hotārā): These represent two forms of the fire god Agni, usually understood as the fire on the altar and the lightning in the clouds.
- **Navel of the earth** (Nābhā Pṛthivyā): This is a technical term for the central sacrificial altar, considered the center of the world.
- **Three heights**: This likely refers to the three levels of the world (earth, atmosphere, and heaven) or three specific locations on the altar.
</note>

<summary>
This page translates verses 6 and 7 of the third hymn in the second book, invoking the personified Night and Dawn and the two divine priestly fires. It explains their roles in maintaining the continuity and beauty of the sacrificial ritual.
</summary>

## Ueber das Podagra.

Vor allen Dingen muss ich bemerken, dass das Podagra in vielen und verschiedenartigen Ursachen seinen Grund haben kann. Die verschiedene Art der Entstehung ist auch, wie ich glaube, Schuld, dass man die Krankheit früher weder richtig zu diagnosticiren, noch gänzlich zu heilen verstand. In Folge dessen kam sie in den schlimmen Ruf, dass sie durch die ärztliche Kunst überhaupt niemals geheilt werden könne. Ich behaupte dagegen, dass diese Krankheit, wenn man die Verschiedenheiten und einzelnen Formen derselben nach Quantität und Qualität genau auseinander hält, von den Aerzten leicht geheilt werden kann. Wir wollen zunächst die diagnostischen Kennzeichen und nachher die Heilmethode besprechen. Wenn man sich genau an die angegebenen Vorschriften hält, so darf man hoffen, vielen Kranken zu helfen und zwar nicht blos im Beginn des Leidens, sondern auch, wenn dasselbe bereits längere Zeit besteht. <meta>This page concludes the discussion of the three primary axioms of logic as they apply to the Cosmos, focusing on the third axiom and how it proves that the universe must be governed by Law rather than chance or arbitrary whims.</meta>

III. **The Axiom of Excluded Middle**: "Everything must either be or not be; there is no other alternative or middle course."

These are established <term>axioms</term> <note>Self-evident truths or fundamental principles that serve as the starting point for all logical reasoning.</note> of Logic. A leading authority, Prof. Jevons <note>William Stanley Jevons (1835–1882) was an influential English logician and economist whose works were standard textbooks in the late 19th century.</note>, says of them: "Students are seldom able to see at first their full meaning and importance. All arguments may be explained when these self-evident laws are granted; and it is not too much to say that the whole of Logic will be plain to those who will constantly use these laws as the key."

Therefore, we must either hold that the Cosmos is under Law and Order, or else that it is not. And if it is not, then Chance or an <term>Arbitrary Decree</term> <note>A decision made by a ruler based on whim rather than established rules or reason.</note> rules the universe—and the Cosmos is merely Chaos. There is no alternative—there can be no "half-and-half" middle ground in this matter. Which is it? 

We hardly need to assure the student that the highest modern scientific thought agrees perfectly with the teachings of the ancient <term>occultists</term> <note>Here referring to those who study the "hidden" or underlying laws of nature and reality.</note>: that the Cosmos is governed by Law in every detail and as a whole, and that universal order, balance, and harmony are manifested through it. Not only is this true, but the ordinary human mind is capable of discovering the existence of Law in the universe in every way it manifests. The rising of the sun, the flow of the tides, the law of gravitation, the laws of mechanics, and "Natural Law" in all its forms show that Law exists in the Cosmos. 

Science shows us that the entire universe is held together by the operation of Law. If the tiniest atom were released from the operation of Law, the entire universe would dissolve into Chaos; its parts are so interdependent that even the slightest exception to Universal Law would be inconsistent with the whole system. The Laws of the Universe can never be "broken." If we come into contact with them and refuse to govern ourselves accordingly, we suffer—but the Law remains intact. We do not "break" the Law of Gravitation when we step over a cliff; we only prove its existence. If we could "break" even the smallest Law of the Cosmos, the Cosmos would become Chaos.

Furthermore, these Cosmic Laws are not the result of an arbitrary <term>fiat</term> <note>original: "fiat", a Latin word meaning "let it be done"; an authoritative decree.</note> or <term>dictum</term> <note>original: "dictum", a Latin word for a formal pronouncement or command.</note> of some Being. Instead, they are inherent in the very nature of—

<summary>This page applies the Axiom of Excluded Middle to argue that the universe must be entirely governed by Law, as the only alternative is total Chaos. It asserts that these laws are not external commands but are inherent to the nature of the Cosmos itself.</summary>
<keywords>Axiom of Excluded Middle, Logic, Prof. Jevons, Law and Order, Cosmos vs. Chaos, Gravitation, Natural Law, Determinism, Occultism</keywords>

### IIII.

It is proposed against him who is bound to us by no right, yet possesses the thing we claim as our own. Law "Officium", Law "Is qui destinauit", under this title; § 2, Institutes on Actions; or who ceased to possess it with intent to deceive <term>dolo</term> <gloss>maliciously</gloss>. Law "Si autem", § "Si homo petitus", verse "Sed et is, qui", under this title. Bartolus and the Doctors on Law "Quia", § "Finis", on the alienation of a judge changed.

### V.

This judgment is also transferred in various ways to the heir of the possessor. For after the contestation of the suit <term>litis contestatio</term> <gloss>the formal framing of the issue in court</gloss>, both the fault and the deceit of the heir are taken into consideration. But before the contestation of the suit, if the possessor was involved in the matter with malicious intent, the heir shall not be compelled to undergo the action in rem. Although an action *in factum* <gloss>based on the specific facts</gloss>, for restitution if he was made richer by it, ought to be granted against him. Law "Si in rem", 42, and Law "Si in rem", § 1, where the gloss and Bartolus [comment]. Law "Cum autem", under this title.

### VI.

This action has a place in all movable things, both animate and inanimate, and those things which are contained by the soil. Law 1, 4, 5, 23, 35, under this title. However, those free persons who are within our legal power are not recalled into our power through this action (unless some specific cause is added), but rather through interdicts, or prejudicial inquiries, or other praetorian cognition. Said Law 1, § 1, under this title.

### VII.

Pomponius testifies that not only are individual things to be vindicated in this way, but sometimes also sets of corporeal things, as is a herd, a stud of horses, and other things of that kind which are grazed collectively. This holds true even if the individual heads do not belong to us in the least. Law 1, § "Finis", under this title; Law "Vendicatio", in the same.

### VIII.

I believe that incorporeal rights, since they are not properly held nor possessed, are not subject to vindication; although I would not rashly deny that they can be sought in effect through real actions, as is taught in the title on the vindication of services and the petition of usufruct. § "Aeque", Institutes on Actions.

### IX.

If someone has so combined the property of another with his own that it became a part of it, I conclude with Paulus that it cannot be sought as our own, just as sacred or religious places cannot be. Law "In rem", 23, § 1, 2, & 5.

La différence des opinions dépend encore de la manière dont chacun détermine l'influence des données qui lui sont connues. La théorie des probabilités tient à des considérations si délicates, qu'il n'est pas surprenant qu'avec les mêmes données, deux personnes trouvent des résultats différens, surtout dans les questions très-compliquées. Exposons ici les principes généraux de cette théorie.

### *Principes généraux du Calcul des Probabilités.*

<margin>Ier Principe.</margin>
Le premier de ces principes est la définition même de la probabilité qui, comme on l'a vu, est le rapport du nombre des cas favorables à celui de tous les cas possibles.

<margin>IIe Principe.</margin>
Mais cela suppose les divers cas, également possibles. S'ils ne le sont pas, on déterminera d'abord leurs possibilités respectives dont la juste appréciation est un des points les plus délicats de la théorie des hasards. Alors la probabilité sera la somme des possibilités de chaque cas favorable. Éclaircissons ce principe par un exemple.

Supposons que l'on projette en l'air, une pièce large et très-mince dont les deux grandes faces opposées, que nous nommerons *croix* et *pile*, soient parfaitement semblables. Cherchons la probabilité d'amener *croix*, une fois au moins en deux coups. Il est clair qu'il peut arriver quatre cas également possibles, savoir, *croix* au premier et au second coup ; *croix* au premier coup et *pile* au second ; *pile* au premier coup et *croix* au second ; enfin *pile* aux deux coups. Les trois premiers cas sont favorables à l'événement dont on cherche la probabilité qui, par conséquent, est égale à 3/4 ; ensorte qu'il y a trois contre un à parier que *croix* arrivera au moins une fois en deux coups.

<meta>The previous page discussed the astrological signs of Mediterranean coastal cities and their trade connections to the Greeks and the Nile Delta. This page moves to a specific geographic survey of the Mediterranean islands, focusing entirely on Cyprus.</meta>

# Description of the Fifteenth Section on the Islands of the Sea

> The purpose of this book is not to describe all inhabited islands. Rather, the intent is to highlight what was mentioned for those who understand Arabic and seek it in our book titled "The Encompassing" <note>original: "al-Muhit"</note> concerning the descriptions of all sea boundaries, according to our ability and the extent of our knowledge. God is the helper in what His generosity deserves. # Map of the Island of Cyprus and Its Harbors

<note>A large rectangular diagram represents the island of Cyprus. The diagram is framed by a green border. Inside, there is a grid structure. An outer border contains sixteen individual rectangular compartments, each containing the name of a harbor <term>marsa</term> and the winds it is sheltered from or affected by. Each compartment features a red circular dot representing the harbor's location. Inside this outer ring is a central area divided into a top horizontal box, a middle section with nine vertical columns representing more harbors, and a bottom horizontal box. The central boxes contain descriptive text about the island's geography, history, and the names of its harbors.</note>

->The length of the island is forty-five parasangs and its width is twenty-two parasangs.<-
<note>A parasang, or farsakh, is an ancient unit of distance roughly equal to 3.5 miles or 5.5 kilometers.</note>
->Its beginning faces Alexandria and its end aligns with Syria.<-

# The Names of Its Harbors

<margin>
**Harbor descriptions in the outer compartments (starting top left, clockwise):**

1. The Western Tabyun Harbor: protected from the East wind <note>original: "al-Auri"; from the Greek "Euros"</note> and the South wind <note>original: "al-Natus"; from the Greek "Notus"</note>. 2. Butis Harbor: protected from the "Head" wind <note>likely a local nautical term for a wind coming from a specific headland</note>. 3. Qablasi Harbor: suitable for a single ship. 4. Fadlah Harbor: for a ship, protected from the South wind and other winds. 5. Harbor of the Seven Springs. 6. Harbor of Wadi Lid: protected from the North wind <note>original: "al-Bulus"; from the Greek "Boreas"</note>. Harbor of the Fortress: protected from the Head wind and the "Bear" wind <note>original: "al-Dub"; likely referring to a North wind associated with the Great Bear constellation</note>; it guards the village. 3. Salwah Harbor: protected from the South wind, used by large merchant ships. 4. Latiyah Harbor: large, protected from the Butis and Frankish winds, and a large valley. 5. Harbor of Reproach <note>original: "al-Malamah"</note>: protected from the land wind and the North. 6. Al-Adi Harbor: protected from the South wind. 7. The Fort Harbor: protected from the East and South winds. 8. Harbor of "So-and-so" <note>original: "Kadha"; used when a name was missing in the source manuscript</note>: protected from the South and Frankish winds. 9. Al-Adni Harbor: protected from the South wind and other winds. </margin>

> When Jabbara of the Umayyad dynasty conquered the island, he made peace with its people for fourteen thousand dinars. He stayed there to take a third of the tribute in kind, a third in cash, and a third deferred. This occurred during the days of Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan <note>the first Umayyad Caliph, reigning 661 to 680 AD</note>. ---

> This island produces pearls, lapis lazuli, gold, copper, iron, salt, and cotton. It also produces all kinds of textiles and other goods that are brought from the land of the Romans <note>the Byzantine Empire</note> to the city. <summary>This page provides a detailed maritime and economic survey of Cyprus, featuring a schematic map of its many harbors and their safety from various winds. It also notes the island's historical conquest by the Umayyads and its reputation as a source of precious minerals and textiles.</summary>
<keywords>Cyprus, Mediterranean, navigation, harbors, Umayyad Caliphate, Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, trade goods, copper, textiles, winds</keywords>

Inscribed within the circles is a square, and within that square is a diamond shape. emet ve-tzedek." **Inner Square Sides**

**Top side:** Nuriel <note>The "Light of God" or "Fire of God," an angel often associated with Uriel and the element of fire in Kabbalistic tradition.</note>

**Bottom side:** Gabriel <note>Meaning "Strength of God," the messenger angel who represents divine justice.</note>
**Left side:** Raphael <note>Meaning "God heals," the angel associated with healing and physical restoration.</note>

**Inscribed Diamond Sides**

<note>The following lines are the first four words of the "Ana B’Koach," a mystical prayer from the 1st century attributed to Rabbi Nehunya ben HaKanah. It is believed to invoke the 42-letter name of God.</note>

**Bottom right side:** the greatness of Your right hand <note>original: "gedulat yeminekha."</note>

<note>The inner circle represents the heart of the divine presence.</note>

The Lord, The Lord, The Lord, The Lord <note>original: "YHWH," the Tetragrammaton, repeated four times around the inner circle.</note>
I Shall Be <note>original: "Ehyeh," from the phrase "Ehyeh Asher Ehyeh" (I Am That I Am) spoken to Moses at the burning bush in Exodus 3:14.</note>

<meta>Focusing on the historical identification of the Ram and the He-Goat as the Persian and Greek empires.</meta>

### Wellspring 9, Branch 4

Darius the Mede and Cyrus the King of Persia joined together. Darius the Mede was king in Media, and Cyrus came to the throne in Persia. They united Media and Persia and conquered toward the west, the north, and the south. This is why the text says the ram "pushed westward, northward, and southward" <note>Daniel 8:4</note>. Cyrus and his son after him conquered many lands, as recorded in the history of the Persian kings. Cambyses, the son of Cyrus, sent his generals to conquer the entire East. The reason the East is not mentioned in the ram's pushing is that Persia was already in the East; they did not need to conquer the direction they already occupied. The text says, "no beast could stand before him," meaning the surrounding kings and princes could not withstand the Persian power. The text says he came "from the west" and "on the face of the whole earth," and he "did not touch the ground." This describes the incredible speed of Alexander’s conquests. He did not linger; it was as if he were flying on the clouds of heaven. The he-goat came to the "ram that had two horns" <note>Darius III of Persia</note>. He ran at him in "furious power." This describes the three major battles Alexander fought against Darius, where he eventually destroyed the Persian monarchy and took over the empire. The "notable horn" was Alexander, as Gabriel later explains: "the rough goat is the king of Greece, and the great horn between his eyes is the first king" <note>Daniel 8:21</note>. He is called "notable" because of his fame and his association with the teachings of Aristotle the philosopher; he was a man of great intellect as well as military might. He reached the "ram" and broke his two horns, signifying the total collapse of Median and Persian power. <summary>This page identifies the ram as the Medo-Persian Empire and the he-goat as Alexander the Great, highlighting the speed of Alexander's conquests and his defeat of Darius III.</summary>

Nicahtacah se llamaba el ídolo que sacó Yquibalam, y solamente les acompañaron los Quichées y tambien los de Tanub, y así tambien es el ídolo de los de Tanub, el ídolo Tohil. # On Faith. <meta>catchword: maer</meta>

<margin>Heb. 11:33.</margin>
Practicing righteousness is truly a work of faith. Now it seems to me that if the histories of Christ are believed, and especially the resurrection, that the other things should also be believed. For there is no doubt that if it were believed that Jesus Christ is risen, by the same token it would also be believed that he is truly the Son of God, and consequently all his words would be believed. That is why John has said: "These things are written so that you might believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, and that believing you might receive life through his name."

<margin>John 20:30.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the analysis of the relationship between names and objects, specifically addressing the conceptual attachment to labels within the Mind-Only school of Buddhist philosophy.</meta>

Furthermore, the conceptualization that thinks, "just as a name possesses an inherent nature, the objects symbolized by it, such as a vase or cloth, likewise exist in that same way," is called conceptualization through attachment to objects according to their names. As an antidote to this, the *One Hundred Thousand Verse Prajnaparamita* <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom Sutra</gloss> states that names are false <note>The OCR notes a variant reading between "false" (brdzun) and "falsehood" (rdzun).</note>. This means that things designated by names, such as vases and cloths, are false and like an illusion; they do not possess an inherent nature. As an antidote to being attached to names according to their objects, the Buddha taught that a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>an awakening being</gloss> does not perceive any of those names; because they are not perceived, there is no attachment to them. Regarding the line: "One with virtuous intelligence who has attained supreme diligence," a Bodhisattva who abides in the search for dharma is called "one with virtuous intelligence" because they possess the qualities of searching for the dharma. Because they abide in diligence that is free from exhaustion, struggle, discouragement, or agitation when searching for the dharma, they are said to have "attained supreme diligence." This does not refer to diligence performed through mere force or compulsion, but rather means having attained diligence characterized by skillful methods. Regarding the line: "Because of perceiving the true nature of reality possessing the two truths," because they have attained such supreme diligence, they are said to "possess the two truths." This refers to the ultimate truth... <summary>This text explains the Buddhist philosophical view that names and the objects they represent lack inherent existence, using the Perfection of Wisdom sutras as an authority. It also begins a poetic summary of the qualities of a Bodhisattva, focusing on their diligence and understanding of the two truths.</summary>
<keywords>Prajnaparamita, Bodhisattva, inherent nature, two truths, diligence, conceptualization, Mind-Only, philosophy</keywords>

Venerable ones, since I committed that earlier offense, I have been under probation. Regarding this intermediate offense, it is not appropriate to set aside the legal action of the <term>mula-parivasa</term> <gloss>probation from the beginning</gloss>, so I request that it be granted properly. The monks decided that for the first offense, it was not appropriate to set aside the valid legal action, so they granted the <term>parivasa</term> <gloss>probation</gloss>. For the intermediate offense, since it was appropriate to set aside the invalid legal action, they granted the <term>mula-parivasa</term> <gloss>probation from the beginning</gloss>. Knowing that intermediate offense himself, and knowing that the community had granted him the six-day <term>manatva</term> <gloss>penance to gladden the community</gloss> by setting aside the invalid action, he said: "Venerable ones, for my earlier offense I performed the penance, and for this intermediate offense, since it is not appropriate to set aside the valid legal action for penance from the beginning, I request that it be granted properly." Those monks, for the earlier offense, granted the penance since it was not appropriate to set aside the valid action. For this intermediate offense, they granted the penance from the beginning, as it was appropriate to set aside the invalid action. While he was performing that penance from the beginning, he again committed a <term>sanghadisesa</term> offense similar to the intermediate one, which he did not conceal. He recognized that repeated offense. Knowing that the community had granted the penance from the beginning for that intermediate offense by setting aside the invalid action, he spoke to the monks: "Venerable ones, I committed a <term>sanghadisesa</term> offense similar to the intermediate and earlier ones, which I did not conceal. persona nimirum, cum assumpta Natura humana minimè permixta est: ita nec humana cum diuina.

V.

Sed potius, differentia duarum diuersissimarum Naturarum seruata, vsq; adeò duæ istæ Naturæ inter sese non miscentur, vt potiùs cuiusque Naturæ essentiales proprietates, quotquot sunt, in perpetuum seruandæ & retinendæ: nec vllo modo vel ratione, quacunque id fiat, vnquam inter sese commiscendæ sint.

VI.

Porrò nec talis vnio vel Commixtio in Christo duarum istarum Naturarum vnquã vel fingenda vel concedenda est in qua ex duabus Naturis, tanquam ex duobus integris vel corruptis, tertiũ aliquod singulare mixtum genus constituatur quod nec perfectè diuinum nec perfectè humanum sit: sed partim ex diuina, partim verò ex humana Natura, in vnam quandam peculiarem commixtam substãtiam & Naturam coaluerit.

VII.

Quod sanè in rebus naturalibus fieri perlibenter concedimus: quippe quod & Ratio physica & ipsa experientia quoti-

<vocab>Natura, Christo, Commixtio, vnio, substãtiam, Ratio physica</vocab>
translation:
<header>ON THE PERSONAL VNION.</header>

the person indeed, since the assumed human Nature is not in the least mixed: thus neither is the human with the divine.

V.

But rather, the difference of two most diverse Natures being preserved, those two Natures are so far from being mixed among themselves, that rather the essential properties of each Nature, however many they may be, must be perpetually preserved and retained: nor in any way or manner, by whatever means that may happen, are they ever to be mixed among themselves.

VI.

Furthermore, neither is such a union or Commixture in Christ of those two Natures ever to be imagined or conceded in which, from two Natures, as if from two wholes or corrupted parts, some third singular mixed genus is constituted which is neither perfectly divine nor perfectly human: but which has grown into one certain peculiar mixed substance and Nature, partly from the divine, and partly from the human Nature.

VII.

Which, to be sure, we willingly concede happens in natural things: for both physical Reason and experience itself daily testify: namely, that when qualities are broken and to some extent corrupted within one another, some third Mixed thing is thereby made.

<header>A letter from Jeronimus Segersz.</header>

<sig>P. 5.</sig>

<margin>Mark 12:30</margin>

to serve with a whole heart and to follow his footsteps; for we know that if our <term>earthly house</term> <gloss>the body</gloss> of this dwelling is broken, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, but one that is eternal in Heaven. We yearn for this, for our dwelling which is in heaven, and we long to be clothed with it, for we would rather be clothed than unclothed. For as long as we are at home in the body, we are on a pilgrimage away from the Lord.

<margin>1 Pet. 1:17</margin>
Therefore, my dear wife, watch diligently that you finish the time of your <term>pilgrimage</term> <gloss>the earthly life of a believer</gloss> with fear and trembling. Not with such fear and trembling that we should fear or tremble before the world, or because they are so furious with us, but we shall fear and tremble before the <term>Lord</term> <gloss>God/Christ</gloss>, so that we shall keep his commandments and laws. And thus, finishing the time of our <note>original: "pelgrimagie"</note> pilgrimage in the fear of the Lord, and bringing the end of our faith—namely, the salvation of our souls—we shall rejoice eternally with the <term>Lord</term> <gloss>God/Christ</gloss>, and then we shall meet him in the resurrection of the dead.

<column-break/>

<margin>Matt. 10:30</margin>
Therefore, do not fear the world, for the hairs of your head are all counted. They have no power, unless it is given to them from above. And Christ says: Do not fear those who kill the body, but fear him who, after he has killed the body, also has power to cast the soul into hell. There shall be <term>weeping</term> <gloss>mourning</gloss> of the eyes and gnashing of the teeth, and their <term>worm</term> <gloss>a symbol of eternal conscience/torment</gloss> shall not die; they shall rest neither day nor night. The Almighty, eternal, and powerful God will so strengthen and comfort you with his blessed word that you may remain a <term>faithful servant</term> <gloss>loyal follower</gloss> until the end. Then you shall also come under the <term>altar</term> <gloss>the resting place of martyrs</gloss> with all the dear children of God; there all <term>tears</term> <gloss>sorrows</gloss> shall be washed from our eyes. The mind of the ascetic, which was inclined towards ignorance and directed outwards—bowed down towards objects, and having the experience of objects as its fruit—is now turned towards discrimination. That is, it enters the right path and is directed inwards toward "Isolation"—it has Isolation as its result, or is possessed of the germ of Isolation.*

Now, by describing the causes of the impediments that occur to the mind flowing in the path of discrimination, he mentions the means of abandoning those obstacles:—†

->तच्छिद्रेषु प्रत्ययान्तराणि संस्कारेभ्यः ॥ २६ ॥<-

*Aph. 26.* In the intervals thereof, other thoughts arise from the self-continuant impressions.

Different thoughts, characterized by "non-abstraction," which arise in the intervals or gaps in the mind of the ascetic abiding in meditation, spring up in the shape of "I," "mine," etc., from the former impressions of the mind produced by the perceptions of non-abstraction, even though these are now weakened.‡

Therefore, such thoughts must be abandoned by extirpating their causes. This is what is to be stated.

He now states that the methods of abandoning these are as they have been described before:§

->हानं तेषां क्लेशवदुक्तम् ॥ २७ ॥<-

*Aph. 27.* The means of the avoidance of these are explained to be as in the case of the afflictions.

<margin>* The mind that was previously leaning toward ignorance, outward-facing, and bearing the fruit of object-enjoyment, is now leaning toward discrimination and the path of truth, bearing the fruit of Isolation or starting the process of Isolation.</margin>
<margin>† He mentions the way to renounce these by explaining their causes in the mind that is flowing toward discrimination.</margin>
<margin>‡ In the intervals of the ascetic's meditation, thoughts of distraction arise from previous impressions of worldly experience, even if those impressions are waning. The meaning is that one must destroy them by cutting off the root of the internal organs.</margin>
<margin>§ He states that the means of removal has been described previously.</margin>

## ARTICLE I.

# THE TWENTY-EIGHT CHINESE CONSTELLATIONS (BT),

# EUL-CHE-PA-SIEOU 二十八宿.

The twenty-eight Chinese asterisms are divided into four groups, each containing **7** constellations; they have been scientifically classified in the work of Father Zottoli, <italic>Cursus litteraturæ sinicæ</italic>, Vol. II, p. 51, and in the <italic>Calendar-Yearbook of Zi-ka-wei</italic>; we refer the reader to these data. <meta>continues from previous page</meta>He rose in official rank to Academician of the Hanlin Academy. He had a poetry collection circulated in the world and gave himself the sobriquet Woodcutter of Jade Mountain <note>original: "玉山樵人"</note>. The songs and poems he composed were quite numerous. Among them, several hundred pieces were ornate and especially well crafted, often winning widespread praise and recitation by the public. At times, musicians set them to musical tones and meters. Those who secretly chanted them on whitewashed partitions and pepper-scented walls could not be fully recorded. He said of himself that he chewed the five-colored divine mushroom of immortality <note><term>lingzhi</term></note> and swallowed the auspicious dew of the Three Purities <note>original: "三清", referring to the three highest Daoist heavens</note>, asking: "Were it not so, how could such clear diction and elegant lines be so exceptionally brilliant?"

When examining his calligraphy, although it enjoyed no fame in his own time, his running script is nonetheless delightful. I once read his poem inscribed on the cursive calligraphy of Huaisu, which ran: "Strange boulders rush down an autumn torrent; withered vines hang from an ancient pine. If brought beside the water's edge, every character, I fear, would turn into a dragon." Without immersing his mind deeply in the study of calligraphy, his poetic phrasing could not have attained such mastery.
