v. 8. *With the example showing the way* <note>original: "Exemplo monstrante viam"</note>.] For they handed down these annotations to posterity as examples and *rhuseis pragmatikas* <gloss>practical observations</gloss>. Ptolemy: *because of agreeing with them, as they were assigned back to the degrees by the practical observations held by them*. For he calls them *exemplar births*, which they recorded from observations into tables, as we have already shown from Sextus Empiricus.
v. 10. *And the whole alternating* <note>original: "Et totum alterna"</note>.] If it is not an error, he calls "alternating" that which returns into a circle. But I remember that these three words, *aeterna* <gloss>eternal</gloss>, *alterna* <gloss>alternating</gloss>, and *aetheria* <gloss>ethereal</gloss>, are interchanged among themselves in this author by the fault of copyists. Therefore, it is more consistent with the author's mind that *eternal* should be read. For how often is it read thus?
v. 11. *To discern the changes of the Fates by certain signs* <note>original: "Fatorumque vices certis discernere signis"</note>.] Who would doubt that it should be read *to discurre by signs* <note>original: "discurrere signis"</note>, unless someone who had not noticed the lines above? *Discurrere* crept in from the verse that is eighth from this one.
v. 15. *As if mourning for the lost* <note>original: "Tam velut amißis mærens"</note>.] Literally for the Greeks: "The Egyptians, when they saw the sun descending under Cancer and Capricorn, when it was shortening the days from longer ones, would mourn, fearing that the sun might leave them with too little. And that is the time, which is the year of their solstice." When it began to ascend again and make the days longer, they would then celebrate and wear crowns. These things were without doubt written from the *Octaeteris* <gloss>eight-year cycle</gloss> of Eudoxus. In which Eudoxus began the solstice, from which he started his year of *prytaneis*, from the Ides, at which time the sign of the solstice was completed. But see the second book of our work *On the Amendment of Times* regarding this matter.
v. 17. *Nor with the Sun returned* <note>original: "nec Sole regreſſo"</note>.] Gemblacensis and Bonincontrius: *now with the Sun returned* <note>original: "iam Sole regreſſo"</note>. Which is true.
v. 22. *And unknown new* <note>original: "Ignotuſque nouos"</note>.] Better Gemblacensis: *And motionless new* <note>original: "Immotuſque nouos"</note>. He did not speak of "new" spheres in vain because of Britain, discovered by C. Julius Caesar shortly before his own times, which they called a new world.
v. 23. *Nor to trust sails to the winds* <note>original: "ventis nec credere vela"</note>.] Gemblacensis and Bonincontrius: *nor to trust vows to the winds* <note>original: "nec ventis credere vota"</note>. Which is better.
v. 27. *Fortune ordered him to watch over himself by pressing* <note>original: "Aduigilare fibi iußit Fortuna premendo"</note>.] Fortune sharpens them by pressing, as if he were saying, Necessity sharpens cares. As,
— *And poverty urging in harsh matters.* Theocritus:

The philosopher La Mettrie would have been an excellent dancer in this ballet, but poor Epicurus would have played a sad part there, as would Lucretius <note>The Roman poet and philosopher of Epicureanism</note> and his other disciples. I believe I can also ensure that Spinoza, Collins, and Hobbes would hardly have been amused by it. But so that one does not believe we have embellished the narration of this feast, we will place here, following our custom, the original words of the historian.

<note>original Latin: "On the last Sunday of the month of October, fifty honest prostitutes, called courtesans, held a supper with the Duke of Valentinois in his room in the Apostolic Palace. After supper, they danced with the servants and others present, first in their clothes, then naked. After supper, the table candlesticks with burning candles were placed on the floor, and chestnuts were thrown on the ground before the candlesticks, which the naked prostitutes gathered up on their hands and feet as they moved. The Pope, the Duke, and Lucrezia his sister were present and watching. Finally, gifts were displayed, silk tunics, pairs of shoes, caps, and other things for those who could carnally know the most of these prostitutes, who were carnally handled there in the hall publicly at the discretion of those present, and the gifts were distributed to the winners. Ibid, page 77."</note>

This little gallant feast must have produced a good effect; for a few days later the most Holy Father gave a second one, in a different manner, which was no less suited to incite the desire to fulfill the duties of marriage. <header>Impedimentum.i.</header>

Impediment i. The first part commonly concerns the obstacles to marriage. The first is about the impediment in general; the second, error of the person; the third, the impediment of condition; the fourth, the impediment of the vow; the fifth, the impediment of carnal kinship; the sixth, the impediment of spiritual kinship, that is to say, of godparenthood; the seventh, legal kinship, that is to say, adoption; the eighth, the impediment of sin; the ninth, of <term>diffulto</term> <gloss>difficulty</gloss>, that is, of disparate faith, and this is the tenth; the eleventh, of force or fear; the twelfth, of the impediment of holy orders; the thirteenth, of the bond to another woman; the fourteenth, of the justice of public honesty; the fifteenth, of affinity; the sixteenth, of the inability to unite; the seventeenth, of marriage made against the interdict of the church; the eighteenth, of the impediment of times and seasons. And of these said impediments, there are verses in which they are explained according to the said order, thus: Error, condition, vow, kinship, crime, disparity of cult, force, order, bond, honesty; if you are akin, if by chance you cannot copulate, these things known forbid marriages, it retracts the joined, the prohibition of the church, and also the forbidden times, they impede it from being made, they allow what is done to be held.

¶ Chapter 2. What things impede a marriage already made. It is answered: there are 12 which not only impede a marriage from being made, but even undo the one that is already made. Which things are placed in the first three verses in the nearby text. ¶ And they understand that they undo the marriage already made if they passed before the marriage, but if they supervened after the marriage was already rightly made, such as sister-in-law status or sin, they do not undo it. ¶ Even if it is not followed by carnal union. <note>see Summa Confessorum, book 4, title 30, question 1, B.</note> Saved for one case, this by the vow of religion with effect, when someone, having made the marriage, before the carnal union entered into religion. <note>see Extra, "On the conversion of married persons," chapter "Venit," c. "ex parte n." z. H.</note> There it is said clearly that a marriage contracted legitimately by words of the present can in no case be undone, even if one of the contractors were made a heretic, because while the other lives they pass to second vows, unless one enters into religion. <note>B. Of betrothals, "commissum." But it must be waited for until the profession is made, as Thomas puts it in the 4th, distinction 27.</note> He means until the religion in general is at least tacitly obligated, because if he did not want to change his life absolutely, the benefit of the one who enters is not to be given to another without his consent. <note>see in the chapter "beneficium," of rules, book 6, B. For at least it is not undone, nor even according to Pe. Similarly to this, see below "votum," 4, f. G., at the end.</note> And this is to be guarded the same for the reception of holy orders, for the marriage is as well undone as some wished to say, but the contrary is declared in an Extravagante of John XXII that begins "Antiqua."

<column-break/>

¶ Chapter 3. What things are those that impede a marriage that is to be made, but do not impede or undo the one that is already made. It is answered: the first are the two things mentioned above in the 1st section, that is to say, the development of the church, nor the time of the fairs, of which it will be said below in Impediment 16 and Impediment 17. Also there are some sins of which see below Impediment 8, section 1. Item, it impedes betrothals that were first begun with another; see it below under "sponsalia," section 8. Item, it impedes the catechism that is done before baptism; see it below Impediment 6, section z. Item, it impedes the simple vow; see it below Impediment 4, section i. n. z.

¶ Chapter 4. If any custom impedes a marriage that is to be made or undoes the one that is already made. It is answered according to Hostiensis: if the custom is approved by the Pope that the marriage is not to be made, or if it is already made that it be undone, certainly it will impede and undo in any cases that the canonical constitution can do this. <note>Extra, "On spiritual kinship," chapter 1, n. c. ff. c. Extra, "On consanguinity," n. thus.</note> That the choice of the Pope has the force of law. But if the custom is not approved by the Pope nor disapproved, then to avoid the scandal that could happen by acting against it, the marriage that is to be made they will impede; the one that is already made is not undone. This same thing says Bernard in his "Novella." A. The same in the "Summa Confessorum," title, question 2.

¶ Chapter 5. What is to be held or done when the doctors disagree concerning the impediments of marriage. It is answered according to Hostiensis: wherever the doctors say by their glosses that the marriage is undone, if they do not bring forward an express contrary law, you must adhere to those who say the contrary. <note>Extra, "On witnesses," l. 3, "ex quodam" at the end. A. The same in the "Summa Confessorum," same title, question 3.</note>

They certainly honored memory very much and applied great exercise and care to it. In learning, they would not let go of what was being taught until they had firmly grasped the things of the first lesson, and they practiced recollection of things said daily in the following manner. (165) A Pythagorean man did not rise from his bed before he had recollected the events of the previous day. He performed the recollection in this way: he tried to recover in his mind what he first said or heard or ordered for the household after rising, and what was second, and what was third. The same logic applied to subsequent events. And again, upon going out, whom he first met and whom second, and what words were spoken first, second, and third; and the same logic for all other things. For he tried to recover in his mind everything that happened in the whole day, desiring to remember them in the order in which each of them happened to occur. If he had more leisure upon waking, he tried to recover the events of the third day in the same way. (166) They tried even more to exercise the memory, for nothing is greater for knowledge, experience, and wisdom than the ability to remember. From these practices, it happened that all of Italy was filled with philosopher men, and though it was previously unknown, it was later called Great Greece because of Pythagoras, and many philosophers, poets, and lawmakers arose among them. For the rhetorical arts, the demonstration speeches, and the written laws were brought from them into Greece. And regarding natural philosophers, whoever makes mention of them, they happen to bring forward Empedocles and Parmenides the Eleatic first; and those wishing to say something wise about life bring forward the thoughts of Epicharmus, and almost all philosophers possess them. <note>Regarding section 163, compare Cramer's notes: the Pythagoreans, as Aristoxenus said, used purification of the body through medicine and of the soul through music. Also Diodorus x 5. Regarding section 164, compare Iamblichus 110-111.</note>

2. Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras* 137. I wish to show from the beginning the principles of the worship of the gods which Pythagoras and the men after him established. Everything they define regarding acting or not acting is aimed at communion with the divine; this is the starting principle, and their whole life is organized toward following God. The logic of this philosophy is that men act ridiculously when seeking the good from anywhere other than from the gods. It is similar to a person in a kingdom who serves a minor official of the citizens but neglects the ruler and king of all. For they think humans do such a thing. Since there is a God and He is the lord of all, and it is agreed that one must ask the lord for the good—and everyone gives good things to those they love and in whom they delight, but the opposite to those they are against—it is clear that those things must be done in which God happens to delight.

# <term>Juan</term> <gloss>Volume</gloss> 30

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>to the name Kingdom of Wu. During the Yongjian reign period <note>126–144 CE</note>, Kuaiji Commandery was established as a separate partition. Under the Jin dynasty, it became the Kingdom of Kuaiji. In the third year of the Xianhe reign period <note>328 CE</note>, Wang Shu was appointed General Who Pacifies the Army and Internal Historian of Kuaiji. Shu submitted a memorial stating that his father's personal name was Hui <note>written with the same character 会 as Kuai</note>, requesting a transfer to another commandery. The imperial court thereupon changed Hui <gloss>Kuai</gloss> to Kuai <note>鄶</note>. Or perhaps at that time it was originally referred to as the Kingdom of Hui <gloss>Kuai</gloss>, and later annotators and catalogers accordingly changed it to the Kingdom of Kuai <note>鄶</note>.

Chen Renshan's *Examination of the Four Books* <note>original: "四書考"</note> states: "The 'Treatise on Astronomy' in the *New Book of Tang* <note>original: "唐志"</note> states that the asterisms of <term>Chunshou</term> <gloss>Quail Head</gloss> and <term>Shishen</term> <gloss>Orion</gloss> correspond to the West Sea; their presiding deity is centered on Mount Hua, where <term>Taibai</term> <gloss>Venus</gloss> resides. <term>Taibai</term> is the place where Master Guigu imparted to Su Qin the arts of statecraft."

I note that the Treatise of the Tang states that <term>Jianglou</term> <gloss>Aries</gloss> and <term>Xuanxiao</term> <gloss>Aquarius</gloss> correspond to the East Sea; their presiding deity is centered on Mount Daizong <gloss>Mount Tai</gloss>, where <term>Suixing</term> <gloss>Jupiter</gloss> resides
